sens: percevoir par les yeux, regarder
constater, remarquer, observer
examiner, inspecter, vérifier
apparaître, se montrer, être visible
montrer, faire voir, révéler
pourvoir, choisir, pourvoir à
H7200G.detail:
1. Perceive by the eyes, look: the simplest sense, the act of directing one's gaze towards something or someone. When God "saw that the light was good" (Genesis 1:4), He observes the created work. When Abraham "saw the place from afar" (Genesis 22:4), he glimpsed Mount Moriah.
2. Notice, remark, observe: to see attentively in order to understand, judge, or recognize a state or reality. Jehoiada "showed the king's son" (2 Kings 11:4) by making him clearly visible to the military leaders so they would know whom to support.
3. Examine, inspect, verify: to see with particular attention, in order to check or judge. "Look and do according to the pattern that is shown to you" (Exodus 25:40): to carefully examine the divine model.
4. Appear, show oneself, be visible: when the subject is a person or thing, the verb expresses that it becomes visible or manifests itself. Jacob "saw" the angels (Genesis 32:2): they appeared to him.
5. Show, make visible, reveal: in the active form, to make someone see. God shows a model, an angel reveals a vision.
6. Provide, choose, supply: less common, the sense of "foresee" or "provide" in the expression "God will provide" (Genesis 22:14).
H7200G.origine: Very ancient Hebrew root, belonging to the order of the most primitive senses. It belongs to the family of perception verbs: see, hear, touch. In Hebrew, as in all languages, the verb "see" extends figuratively: to see is to understand, notice, inspect, and even in certain contexts to direct one's gaze with intention to choose or provide. The root עיד (ʿīd) or the noun עַיִן (ʿayin, "the eye") are close.
H7200G.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible: over one thousand one hundred occurrences. It is found everywhere, from historical narrative to psalm, from law to prophecy. Its meanings vary according to context: at the beginning of Genesis, God "sees" at each stage of creation (Genesis 1:4, 1:9, 1:10), judging the work as good; Abraham "sees" a ram for the sacrifice (Genesis 22:13); the prophets "see" visions (Jeremiah 6:16: "look to the ancient paths"). The verb is also used to express divine revelation: God shows Himself to Abraham (Genesis 12:7), Noah "saw" his father's nakedness (Genesis 9:22). In the active form, it can also mean that God shows, makes known, or reveals.
H7200G.portee: This verb reminds us that vision is at the heart of the relationship with God: to see His creation, to see His works, to receive His revelations. But "seeing" is never passive in the Bible: one must look, observe attentively, discern the signs of God. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to spiritual vigilance and awareness of God's gaze upon our lives: God sees us.

sens: Percevoir par les yeux, regarder
Observer attentivement, examiner
Remarquer, comprendre, se rendre compte
Considérer, réfléchir à, prendre en compte
Faire apparaître, montrer, révéler
H7200H.detail:
1. Perceive by the eyes, look: it is the simple act of seeing, directing one's gaze towards something. Jacob "saw" that there was grain in Egypt (Genesis 42:1); it is perceiving a concrete reality by sight.
2. Observe attentively, examine: to go beyond a mere glance to scrutinize, inspect, consider with attention. The king of Israel is invited to "examine" and "see" what he must do in the face of the Syrian threat (1 Kings 20:22).
3. Notice, understand, realize: to grasp the importance or nature of something, to see clearly in a situation. Micah "saw" that the sons of Dan were stronger and understood that he could not stop them (Judges 18:26).
4. Consider, reflect on, take into account: to mentally focus on something, to weigh it. The psalmist asks the Lord to "consider" his love for the divine ordinances (Psalms 119:159).
5. Make appear, show, reveal: to allow someone to see, to perceive reality. God makes "see" or reveals hidden things to those who seek Him.
H7200H.origine: The Hebrew verb רָאָה (ra'ah) is one of the oldest and most fundamental roots in the Bible. It primarily evokes the physical act of seeing, perceiving by sight. It has given rise to many derived words, such as רְאִית (vision) and צְפִיָּה (gaze). In biblical Hebrew, "to see" encompasses not only visual perception but also understanding, attentive observation, and even judgment. It is a verb that opens the world of senses and intelligence alike.
H7200H.emploi: The verb רָאָה is one of the most used in the Hebrew Old Testament, with over 1300 occurrences. It is found in all literary genres: historical narratives (Genesis, Samuel, Kings), poetry (Psalms), wisdom (Ecclesiastes, Proverbs), and prophecies (Ezekiel). Its usage varies according to context: in narratives, it denotes the action of seeing an event or reality (Genesis 42:1, Judges 18:26); in the Psalms, it rises to a plea addressed to God, begging Him to "see" the psalmist's distress (Psalms 25:18); in wisdom literature, it carries a nuance of thoughtful contemplation and discernment (Ecclesiastes, Proverbs 6:6).
H7200H.portee: For the believer, this verb invites a dual vision: that of the eyes of the body and that of the heart. To see is not to be a passive spectator, but to actively perceive, examine, understand, and respond. When the psalmist begs God to "see" his misery, he is not merely asking God to look, but to take into account, to remember, to act. This word teaches that spiritual vision—knowing how to discern God's will, understanding His truth—is as important as physical sight.

sens: Perceive with the eyes, look
Observe carefully, examine
Notice, discover through observation
Understand, become aware of
Show, make something visible to someone
Consider, judge, recognize
H7200I.detail:
1. Perceive with the eyes, look: this is the simplest meaning, seeing with one's eyes what is in front of oneself. In Genesis 39:14, Potiphar's wife cries out: "See, he has brought in a Hebrew" — she calls the servants to look at the man she accuses.
2. Observe carefully, examine: going beyond the simple glance, it is to scrutinize, inspect, seek to understand what one is looking at. In 1 Samuel 23:23, Saul says: "Examine all the places where he hides" — this refers to a thorough search.
3. Notice, discover through observation: this is to perceive something that was unknown, to learn through sight or experience. In Ecclesiastes 7:27, the Preacher says: "Here is what I have found," revealing what his examination has uncovered.
4. Understand, become aware of: the word also encompasses the meaning of "know," to access knowledge. In Exodus 35:30, Moses declares: "Know that the Lord has chosen Bezalel" — this is to make a spiritual reality known.
5. Show, make something visible to someone: this is to place something before the eyes of another, to give them the vision. In Deuteronomy 30:15, God says: "See, I have set before you life and good" — He places the choice before the people.
6. Consider, judge, recognize: this is to evaluate, weigh, take into account what one sees. In 2 Samuel 24:22, Araunah says to the king: "See, the oxen will be for the burnt offering" — he recommends that he recognize what he is offering.
H7200I.origine: The Hebrew word רָאָה (ra.ah) comes from a very ancient root denoting the act of seeing. It is one of the most fundamental verbs in the Hebrew Bible. The word belongs to a broad family: nominal forms like "vision" (mar'eh) and the idea of "appearance" or "what is seen" can be found. In Hebrew as in French, "see" quickly transcends the simple physical gaze to mean "understand," "know," "discern" — the eye accesses the mind.
H7200I.emploi: The verb "see" is extremely frequent in the Hebrew Bible, with 43 occurrences listed here and many more besides. It appears in all literary genres: historical narratives (Genesis, Kings), law (Deuteronomy), wisdom (Ecclesiastes, Job), prophecy (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). The word consistently retains its dual meaning: to see physically (Genesis 39:14, where the woman looks at Joseph) and to see spiritually, that is, to understand, discern, access hidden knowledge (Exodus 35:30, where Moses announces God's choice of Bezalel). In Deuteronomy 30:15, "see" becomes a call to consider, to weigh the consequences. In Ecclesiastes 7:27, it is the patient examination that reveals wisdom. The word can also mean "show" or "make visible" (causative form), as when one "makes visible" a reality to someone.
H7200I.portee: For the believer, this verb reminds us that God sees everything — our actions, our hearts, our secrets — with a clarity that we cannot match. But it also invites us to "see" ourselves: to examine our lives, to discern good from evil (as in Deuteronomy 30:15), to not remain blind to spiritual realities. It is a verb of commitment: to see is also to be responsible for what one has seen, for what one has understood. It teaches us that true knowledge comes through careful observation, reflection, and openness to what God reveals.

sens: Perceive with the eyes, look
Observe, examine carefully
Understand, discern by the spirit
Choose, select
Provide for, procure
Appear, show oneself
H7200J.detail:
1. Perceive with the eyes, look: the primary and most common meaning, the physical act of directing the gaze toward something. Abraham says to his son: "God will provide for Himself the lamb," where the same Hebrew verb "see" takes on the meaning of "choose" and "provide" (Genesis 22:8).
2. Observe, examine carefully: going beyond the simple glance, it is to scrutinize, inspect, pay attention to what is happening. David orders his servants to "pay attention" when Amnon is made merry by wine (2 Samuel 13:28).
3. Understand, discern by the spirit: "see" rises from the physical to the mental, it is to perceive with intelligence, to recognize what is hidden. Samuel must go to Jesse because the Lord has "seen" among his sons the one He desires for king (1 Samuel 16:1).
4. Choose, select: "see" takes on the meaning of distinguishing and recognizing as worthy, of making a choice. Pharaoh must "choose" a wise and discerning man to lead the country (Genesis 41:33).
5. Provide for, procure: the verb expresses the action of ensuring, taking care to meet a need. Abraham believes that God "will provide" a lamb for the sacrifice (Genesis 22:8).
6. Appear, show oneself: in the passive form, "see" means to present oneself to view, to be visible. This is how one expresses the fact that a person or thing shows itself, becomes visible.
H7200J.origine: The Hebrew verb "see" (ra'ah) is one of the most fundamental roots of the biblical language. Its starting image is very concrete: the act of directing the gaze. But as in many languages, "see" quickly extends into the mental and moral realm: to see is to understand, discern, choose. The root also generates forms that mean "appear" or "show oneself." This shift from the physical to the mental reflects a biblical conviction: true vision comes through intelligence and will, not just through the eye.
H7200J.emploi: The verb "see" appears eleven times in the provided occurrences, and it is one of the most frequent words in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis and Exodus, it primarily denotes physical sight, but it quickly shifts toward discernment: Abraham "sees" the sacrifice that God will provide (Genesis 22:8), the Lord "sees" in Jesse's sons the one who will be king (1 Samuel 16:1). In the royal narratives (2 Samuel, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles), the verb often emphasizes choice and selection: Pharaoh must "choose" a wise man (Genesis 41:33), David must "see" that is, consider his options for punishment (2 Samuel 24:13). In the Psalms and Lamentations, "see" rises to a spiritual dimension, that of moral discernment and intimate knowledge of God. The context almost always determines which meaning of the verb is dominant.
H7200J.portee: This word "see" invites the reader to understand that biblical vision is not passive. To see is also to choose, judge, discern, act. When the Lord "sees" a man to be king, it is not a mere glance: it is a thoughtful selection, a discernment of hidden value. For the believer today, "see" reminds us that true knowledge of God comes through sincere attention, spiritual discernment, and the ability to recognize His action in history and in daily life.

sens: See, look, perceive
Contemplate, observe attentively
Savor, taste, take pleasure in
Experience well-being, satisfaction
H7200K.detail:
1. See, look, perceive: the primary meaning of the verb is the action of directing one's gaze towards something to know it, examine it, or simply notice it. It is the physical gaze that opens knowledge.
2. Contemplate, observe attentively: to look not just in passing, but with intention, to examine, discern, and understand what one sees. In Psalms 106:5, the psalmist asks to "see" the happiness of the chosen ones, meaning to contemplate and share in their joy.
3. Savor, taste, take pleasure in: the verb extends from sight to the pleasant experience of the senses and the heart. In Ecclesiastes 2:1, the Preacher says, "you will taste happiness," meaning you will experience it joyfully.
4. Experience well-being, satisfaction: to enjoy means to possess and benefit from well-being, a good life. It is to take one's share of the legitimate goods and pleasures of life. In Ecclesiastes 2:24 and 3:13, "enjoying well-being" amidst one's work is presented as a gift from God, a wisdom of living.
H7200K.origine: The Hebrew verb רָאָה (raah) comes from a root that expresses the idea of sight. In biblical Hebrew, "to see" is often more than just a physical perception: it is to know, understand, and even experience. The idea of enjoyment naturally adds to this, as seeing something beautiful is to enjoy it. The verb appears in several grammatical forms that nuance the meaning: seeing actively, being seen, being shown to someone.
H7200K.emploi: The verb raah is extremely common in the Old Testament. In the provided usages, it almost always denotes the action of enjoying, savoring, taking pleasure — particularly in Ecclesiastes, where the author repeatedly returns to the idea that enjoying well-being amidst one's work is a gift from God (Ecclesiastes 2:24; 3:13; 5:17). In Job 33:28, "to flourish in the light" also expresses this notion of vivifying enjoyment. In Psalm 106:5, "to see happiness" means to contemplate it and enjoy it. Thus, it is a verb that Ecclesiastes uses to affirm that it is good and worthy for man to enjoy the legitimate goods of life.
H7200K.portee: This word invites the Christian not to reject the simple and legitimate goods of existence — eating, drinking, enjoying the fruit of one's labor — as if they were bad. It is a biblical call to gratitude and wisdom: to recognize good things as gifts from God and to savor them in faith, without making them idols. It also protects against melancholic asceticism: an authentic Christian life does not exclude joy and well-being received from the hand of God.

sens: perceive by sight, look
observe attentively, examine
understand, grasp mentally
appear, show oneself to someone
have a vision
show, make visible
H7200L.detail:
1. Perceive by sight: this is the simplest action: open the eyes and look at what is happening around oneself. In 2 Samuel 15:27, the king says to the priest Zadok, "do you understand?" where "see" also means to hear and grasp what is said.
2. Observe attentively, examine means to look with intention, scrutinize, study something closely — not just to glance, but to truly consider.
3. Understand or grasp mentally: "to see" can also mean to perceive mentally, to hear in the sense of "to grasp the message." That is why one can "see" a truth without images before one's eyes.
4. Appear or show oneself is the opposite: when the angel of the Lord "appeared" to Manoah (Judges 13:21), he made himself visible, he presented himself to the eyes. This is "to see" from the perspective of one who becomes visible.
5. Have a vision: to see God or His angels in extraordinary experiences. In 2 Chronicles 26:5, Zechariah had "the understanding of the visions of God," experiences where he saw what is normally hidden.
6. Show or make visible: to cause someone to perceive something. This is an active usage where the one who sees is led to see by someone else.
H7200L.origine: This Hebrew verb is one of the most fundamental roots in the Bible. Its starting image is very simple: to open the eyes and look. The root ra'ah has given rise to several names in the same family: ro'eh (seer, prophet — one who sees divine visions), mar'eh (vision, appearance), and marah (which sometimes means "to come into view"). The verb appears in its various biblical forms (Qal, Niphal, Hiphil) amplifying this notion: from simple "seeing" to "showing oneself" and "showing to others."
H7200L.emploi: This verb is extremely frequent in the Hebrew Bible: it appears hundreds of times in all the books, from the narratives of Judges to the wisdom of Psalms and the prophecy of Isaiah. In the given usages, "to see" or "to appear" mainly designates encounters with angels or divine visions (Judges 6:12, 13:3, 13:10, 13:21): the angel of the Lord "appeared" to Manoah and his wife. But "to see" also carries the meaning of "to understand" or "to grasp" (2 Samuel 15:27: "do you understand?"). In 2 Chronicles 26:5, we speak of the "visions" of God, intimate experiences where the prophet perceives the divine will. The word thus circulates from the concrete (opening the eyes) to the spiritual (receiving a revelation).
H7200L.portee: For the Christian, this verb reminds us that seeing is not just a matter of the eyes. To see God is also to welcome Him into one's heart, to perceive Him by faith. The angels who "appear" in the narratives of the Bible show that God makes Himself visible, that He does not remain distant: He shows Himself to His servants. The word also invites to spiritual vigilance: to see is to observe, examine, discern — essential qualities for following God with wisdom and obedience.

sens: perceive by sight, look
observe, examine attentively
show oneself face to face, meet
understand, discern
show, make visible
H7200M.detail:
1. Perceive by sight, look: the most elementary meaning, that of directing one's gaze towards something or someone to discern it. It is the movement of the eyes towards an object (2 Chronicles 25:21: "they saw each other face to face").
2. Observe, examine attentively: to go beyond a mere glance, to scrutinize, inspect something with care. This includes the idea of considering, taking into account, monitoring (2 Kings 25:19: "a eunuch who was in charge").
3. Show oneself face to face, meet: to be in each other's presence, to confront visually. Two people "see" each other when they are face to face, in a direct relationship.
4. Understand, discern: to see is not just physical; it is also to grasp mentally, to perceive with intelligence, to distinguish what is hidden or obscure.
5. Show, make visible: in the active forms of the verb, to mean to allow or cause another to perceive something, to reveal, to present.
H7200M.origine: The Hebrew verb רָאָה (raah) expresses the action of directing the gaze, but also of perceiving and understanding. Its root suggests the idea of opening the gaze and the knowledge that follows. This verb is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, used to describe both physical vision and spiritual or intellectual perception. It encompasses the entire process: to see, then to consider, then to understand.
H7200M.emploi: The verb "to see" appears here three times in specific contexts of the history of Judah and Israel. Two occurrences speak of "counselors" of the king (2 Kings 25:19 and Jeremiah 52:25), where the Hebrew word is translated not as "to see" but as "counselor" — probably a nuance of the meaning "to examine attentively" or "to observe" that has evolved towards the idea of those who scrutinize affairs and counsel. A third occurrence (2 Chronicles 25:21) uses the verb in its most direct sense: "they saw each other face to face," when two kings meet in battle. The verb thus manifests itself in moments of direct contact or authority relationship.
H7200M.portee: Understanding the verb "to see" in biblical Hebrew helps to grasp that vision is never passive in the Bible. To see is also to observe, judge, know. When God "sees" sin or justice, He does not look passively: He discerns, He knows, He acts. For the reader, this enriches their understanding of key verses like "God saw that it was good": it is an active perception, a divine approval.

sens: Observe, look carefully
Examine, inspect, verify
Notice, become aware of something
Take care of, provide for needs
Understand, discern (figurative)
H7200N.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is the action of seeing, of directing one's gaze at something: to observe an object or a person attentively. It is the gaze that scrutinizes and examines.
2. In Hebrew, this verb also means to verify or inspect: to look closely at something in order to judge its quality or condition. Abraham must verify what is happening on the mountain of sacrifice.
3. Seeing often leads to knowledge: to ascertain for oneself, to become aware of a reality. When one truly sees, one understands.
4. By extension, to see also means to provide, that is, to take care of and satisfy a need. On the mountain where God is about to receive Abraham's sacrifice, the Lord will see (that is, provide) for the necessary lamb. This is the meaning of the name "Jehovah-Jireh" in Genesis 22:14: the Lord who sees our needs and satisfies them.
5. Figuratively, to see can mean to understand, to discern with intelligence, to perceive the truth of a situation.
H7200N.origine: The Hebrew root רָאָה (raah) is one of the oldest and simplest in the Semitic vocabulary: it expresses the act of seeing. It gives rise to many derivatives that retain this idea of vision and discernment. The divine name Jehovah-Jireh (Genesis 22:14) is a compound of this root: it literally means "the Lord will see" or "the Lord will provide," based on this same root, expressing that God sees and responds to the needs of His people.
H7200N.emploi: This verb appears very frequently in the Old Testament, particularly to express the action of seeing, observing, and especially God's ability to see, monitor, and provide. In Genesis 22:14, Abraham names the place "Jehovah-Jireh" in recognition that the Lord saw his distressing situation (having to sacrifice his son) and provided (by supplying a ram in his place). The context of the sacrifice shows how the verb shifts from the literal sense (to see, to observe) to the theological sense: God sees the heart, the faith, and responds with His providence. This is why the French translation renders the name as "why" ("that is why... it will be provided"), explaining the reason for calling the place this way.
H7200N.portee: This word reveals the nature of God as one who truly sees our needs and difficulties, not by chance or from a distance, but with vigilant attention. For the believer, it affirms that God never turns His eyes away, that He discerns the heart and responds generously. The name "Jehovah-Jireh" becomes a comforting promise: the Lord who has seen us will provide for us, not because we have sought Him, but because He has cared for us with love.

sens: Bird of prey with swift flight
Impure creature according to the Law of Moses
H7201.detail:
1. The kite is a bird of prey, swift and a hunter, that soars in the sky to catch its food—small birds and rodents. It is probably a kite or a hawk, raptors that are easily identified in the Mediterranean and the Middle East (Deuteronomy 14:13).
2. The Law of Moses classifies the kite among the impure birds that the Israelites must not eat. This prohibition is based on rules of ritual purity that mark predatory or carnivorous species as incompatible with the status of the holy people that God has chosen (Deuteronomy 14:13).
H7201.origine: The Hebrew word רָאָה (ra'ah) specifically designates this bird of prey. The biblical context suggests that it is an agile and carnivorous raptor, identified by ancient Greek translators as a kite or a falcon. The term belongs to the concrete and observed vocabulary of the nature of the Levant.
H7201.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 14:13, in the list of impure birds that God forbids the Israelites to consume. This list is part of the dietary code of the Mosaic Law, which distinguishes between pure and impure creatures. The kite is listed alongside the hawk and the vulture, all three being predators.
H7201.portee: This mention of the kite invites the reader to meditate on what Scripture teaches: holiness is not an abstract matter; it is rooted in concrete and daily life, including what we eat. Even though the ceremonial law no longer applies to Christians after Christ, it reveals God's thoughts on purity and His desire to form a separated people for Himself.

sens: be entirely occupied by something
have all one's attention focused on a subject
be immersed in a concern or emotional state
H7202.detail: 1. The word describes total concentration, the mind entirely taken by a reality. In Job 10:15, Job says he is "absorbed in his misery": this means that shame and suffering completely fill his heart and attention; he cannot think of anything else. The image is that of a person drowned in a feeling, unable to detach from it. 2. It is also the idea of being overwhelmed, having lost the ability to lift one's eyes or head—physically or morally. Job cannot lift his head because he is inwardly absorbed by his condition, his gaze turned downwards, towards his own distress.
H7202.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the idea of seeing or fixing one's gaze. To be absorbed is to have one's gaze and thought riveted on something so strongly that nothing else exists for oneself. The same root designates the act of contemplating or being fixed on an object.
H7202.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 10:15. In this passage, Job, struggling with the enigma of his suffering despite his innocence, expresses that he is so crushed by shame and misery that they fill him entirely. The context shows a man grappling with profound inner distress, unable to escape this state.
H7202.portee: This word reminds us that suffering and guilt can completely absorb us, paralyzing us within. For the reader, it expresses a deep human experience: there are moments when the human heart is so occupied by pain that it sees nothing else. Job helps us to name this reality before God, without hiding it.

sens: One who sees, who has sight
One who sees the visions of God, who receives divine revelations
Prophet, a man inspired by God to speak in His name
H7203A.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one who sees, who possesses the ability to see in a physical sense. It refers to the man with open eyes, capable of perceiving what others do not see.

2. The seer is one who sees the visions of God — the revelations, images, and messages that God sends to His chosen servants. Samuel is called "the seer" because he receives the words of God (1 Samuel 9:19).

3. He is a prophet, a man chosen by God to be His spokesperson to the people. The text of 1 Samuel 9:9 clearly explains that one who is called a "prophet" was formerly called a "seer" — two names for the same role. Samuel the seer is respected as one who knows the secrets of the heart (1 Samuel 9:19) and who established the order of worship (1 Chronicles 9:22).
H7203A.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "to see" (ראה, ra'ah): a seer is literally one who sees. It is an agent noun formed from this verb. The word first designates the physical act of seeing, then takes on the spiritual meaning of one who sees divine visions, who receives and perceives the revelation of God. It is an ancient term from the prophetic tradition in Israel: before the term "prophet" (navi) was used, the term "seer" (ro'eh) was used to designate the same inspired figure.
H7203A.emploi: The word appears about 10 times in the Bible, mostly in the ancient accounts concerning Samuel. 1 Samuel 9 provides the explicit definition: the seer is the former title of the prophet (verse 9), and people come to consult him to know the will of God (verses 11, 18-19). Samuel, called "the seer," enjoys great authority: he knows the innermost thoughts (1 Samuel 9:19) and has established the ordinances of worship (1 Chronicles 9:22). The term emphasizes less the act of speaking than the ability to see and perceive what is hidden. In later passages (Isaiah 30:10, 2 Chronicles 16:7), the seer remains one who conveys the message of God, and attempts are made to silence him when his message is unwelcome.
H7203A.portee: This word reminds the believer that the biblical prophet is not a diviner or magician, but a man to whom God opens the eyes to see His will and plans. It is an invitation to seek knowledge from those whom God inspires about what exceeds our natural vision. It also teaches us that true prophecy requires integrity: the seer speaks what he sees, without fear or compromise, even if it displeases others.

sens: To speak in the name of God as a prophet
To make a divine word public or official
To predict the future or announce the will of God
To express oneself under the influence of the Spirit of God
H7203B.detail:
1. To prophesy is to speak in the name of God: the prophet does not invent his words, he receives and transmits them to the people or the king. It is a sacred function, that of the bearer of divine message.
2. It is not only to predict (to announce the future), but primarily to announce the will of God for the present moment, to call for obedience, to denounce evil — and sometimes also to describe what is to come. Isaiah 28:7 illustrates this well: the priests and prophets were supposed to "prophesy" (declare God's judgments), but drunkenness prevented them from doing so.
3. The word can also refer to the vision or the word received itself — what comes directly from God, without human calculation.
H7203B.origine: The Hebrew word רֹאֶה (ro.eh) literally means "one who sees" — for the prophet is primarily one who sees the divine vision. It comes from the root ראה (ra.ah, "to see"). In ancient Hebrew, a prophet was first called a "seer": one who receives the vision of God, who "sees" what others do not see. This shows that prophecy is primarily a matter of spiritual perception.
H7203B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Segond (Isaiah 28:7), where it designates the expected activity of priests and prophets. The context is critical: these men were "absorbed by wine" and "staggered," so they could no longer "prophesy" or "render justice" as they should. This shows that to prophesy requires clarity, sobriety of mind, and attentiveness to God. It is a sacred charge that cannot be fulfilled in a state of drunkenness.
H7203B.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the prophetic word is not a private or personal matter, but a public word that commits the one who pronounces it to God and to the people. It also shows that to listen to a prophet is to listen to God Himself — and that to despise prophecy is to despise God. Finally, it emphasizes that receiving such a charge requires a righteous life, free from the entanglements of sin.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
H7204.detail: Haroé is a character from the Old Testament belonging to the tribe of Judah. He is mentioned as one of the sons of Shobal, the father of Kirjath-Jearim, in the genealogy of the descendants of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:52). His name is sometimes written as "Reaiah" in other genealogical passages.
H7204.origine: The name Haroé means "vision" in Hebrew, formed from the root that evokes the act of seeing or receiving a vision. It is a name of spiritual significance borne by this member of the lineage of Judah. The variant "Reaiah" refers to the same root and designates the same person in other genealogical listings.
H7204.emploi: Haroé appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:52, where he is listed in the genealogy of the sons of Judah. He is presented as a descendant of Judah through the line of Shobal. This brief mention is part of the list of tribes and families of Judah, intended to establish kinship ties within the people of Israel after the exile. Although he is not well-documented, his presence in the genealogies shows the importance that Scripture attaches to the transmission of family lineages.

sens: The firstborn of Jacob's twelve sons, born of Leah
The tribe of Israel descended from Ruben
The territory located east of the Jordan, inhabited by the tribe of Ruben
H7205.detail:
1. Ruben is the firstborn son of Jacob and Leah. His name means "Behold, a son" (Genesis 29:32), because Leah, seeing that the Lord had heard her humiliation, hoped that this birth would win Jacob's love. Although he is the firstborn, Ruben loses his birthright due to his transgression (1 Chronicles 5:1); this right passes to Joseph. Among his four sons mentioned in Exodus 6:14 and 1 Chronicles 5:3 (Hanok, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi) later arise the families of the Palluites and the Hezronites.

2. During the Exodus and the journey through the desert, the tribe of Ruben is counted and organized militarily (Numbers 1:5-21; 2:10-16). It participates in the events of the desert, notably during the rebellion of Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, which provoked the Lord's anger (Deuteronomy 11:6).

3. In the conquest of Canaan, Ruben receives in inheritance the territory east of the Jordan, between the Dead Sea and the river Amon, including cities like Betser and Jahzah (Joshua 13:15-23; 21:36-37). It is a region of pastures, suitable for livestock, which explains the tribe's initial request (Numbers 32:1-33).
H7205.origine: The Hebrew name רְאוּבֵן (Reuben) literally means "behold, a son" (ראה, see, and בֵן, son). It expresses Leah's joy and surprise at this birth, summarizing her hope that she would regain her husband's favor. This name is specific to this individual and his descendants; it is not a word used elsewhere in Scripture.
H7205.emploi: Ruben appears 68 times in Scripture, mainly in Genesis and in the books of the desert and conquest (Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua) and in Chronicles. In Genesis, we see him as a child and an adult: he protects Joseph from his brothers' jealousy (Genesis 37:21-22, 29), then attempts to reconcile with Jacob by offering his two sons as hostages for Benjamin (Genesis 42:37). After Jacob's death, Ruben loses his advantage as the firstborn (Genesis 49:3-4; 1 Chronicles 5:1). During the desert, his tribe is listed, participates in battles, and, after the conquest, settles east of the Jordan, where it remains throughout Israel's history.
H7205.portee: Ruben illustrates that the position of firstborn or divine favor does not guarantee faithfulness or the promised blessings: his moral failures have lasting consequences. His story reminds the Christian reader that God's grace is transmitted not by birthright or human status, but through obedience and faith. The tribe of Ruben, established east of the Jordan, also symbolizes Israel in its collective life, separated yet still part of the chosen people.

sens: member of the tribe of Ruben
descendant of Ruben, son of Jacob and Leah
H7206.detail:
1. Rubénite refers to a member of the tribe of Ruben, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. This tribe received a territory east of the Jordan, in the region of Gilead and Aroer (Deuteronomy 3:12). The Rubénites are counted among the warrior tribes that fought alongside Joshua for the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 1:12).

2. More broadly, a Rubénite is a descendant of Ruben, the firstborn son of Jacob and Leah, born in the time of the patriarchs. It is thus a genealogical and tribal identity that marked an Israelite's belonging to this particular lineage, with its rights, duties, and territorial inheritance.
H7206.origine: The word Rubénite comes from Ruben (Hebrew Reubhen), whose name means "behold, a son" — an expression of joy at the birth of Jacob's first child. The term with the suffix -ite (Hebrew suffix -i) marks belonging to a tribe or family group, as in French one would say "the Parisians" for the inhabitants of Paris. This is the usual way to form the names of the twelve tribes of Israel from their eponymous ancestors.
H7206.emploi: The term "Rubénites" appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the books of the Pentateuch and in historical narratives. It regularly designates the members of the tribe of Ruben during their territorial settlement east of the Jordan (Deuteronomy 3:12, Joshua 13:8), during calls to war (Joshua 1:12, 2 Kings 10:33), and during censuses (Numbers 26:7). The tribe of the Rubénites maintained its identity and lands despite Assyrian invasions and political upheavals (1 Chronicles 5:26). This word reflects the tribal structure of Israel and the land inheritance system that defined the organization of the chosen people.
H7206.portee: Knowing the term "Rubénite" helps the reader follow the history of Israel and understand how God organized His people into tribes with assigned territories. It shows the importance of inheritance and birthright in the Bible: Ruben, although the firstborn, lost his preeminence due to his sin (Genesis 35:22), but his tribe retained an honorable place in God's people. It also reminds us that the promise made to the patriarchs was concretely realized in the sharing of the Promised Land among the twelve tribes.

sens: Woman of the patriarchal era, concubine of Nahor
H7208.detail: Réuma is a woman mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 22:24. She was the concubine of Nahor, Abraham's brother. She bore four sons: Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah. Her name appears in the genealogical context where the Bible lists Nahor's descendants, showing how Abraham's family extended through several generations and multiple women.
H7208.origine: The name Réuma means "exalted" in Hebrew. It likely reflects a particular position or esteem, although few details are given about this woman in Scripture.
H7208.emploi: Réuma is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Genesis 22:24. The Bible identifies her as Nahor's concubine and the mother of four sons. She appears in a family genealogy, alongside other women of Nahor, which shows that patriarchal families had multiple wives and concubines.

sens: smooth and shiny surface that reflects an image
object made, of metal or other material, used to see oneself
H7209.detail:
1. A mirror is a shiny surface capable of reflecting the image of the one who looks into it. In its only biblical use (Job 37:18), God is compared to someone who can stretch the heavens as solid and smooth as a molten mirror — a polished metal surface that perfectly reflects light.
2. The word refers to the object itself, crafted by man. In biblical times, mirrors were made of metal (copper, bronze, or tin), carefully polished, as reflective glass did not yet exist. It is a precious object, synonymous with clarity and perfection.
H7209.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to see" or "to look." A mirror is literally an object of vision — that in which one sees oneself. It is an evocative image: the surface of the mirror allows the one looking into it to see themselves as they are, like an act of reciprocal vision.
H7209.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 37:18. It is part of Elihu's discourse on God's power and the beauty of His creation. The sky is described as solid and bright, stretched by God like a worker stretches a sheet of precious polished metal — an image of absolute perfection and divine mastery.
H7209.portee: This passage reminds us that the creation of the heavens reveals God's power and artistry. Just as a molten mirror requires patient work and technical mastery, the universe testifies to the intelligence and beauty of the Creator. The Christian can contemplate the heavens as a work revealing divine glory.

sens: The physical appearance of someone, their general look
The act of seeing, looking at something
The aspect that something takes on, its visible state
A spectacle, what is exposed to the sight of all
H7210.detail:
1. The figure is the physical appearance, the way one presents oneself: the expression, the features, the silhouette. When Samuel seeks the future king of Israel, the Lord directs him to David, who had "a beautiful figure" (1 Samuel 16:12) — not to judge by appearances, but the appearance here reflected a quality of the heart.
2. This word can also refer to the act of seeing or looking, the movement of the gaze: when Job says, "The eye that sees me will see me no more" (Job 7:8), he speaks of the Lord's gaze that soon will not see him anymore.
3. The figure is what becomes visible, what is exposed to the eyes: the flesh that "wastes away" appears in a state of decay (Job 33:21).
4. In the sense of spectacle or public exhibition, the figure refers to what is laid bare to the gaze of the crowd, often for humiliation: God says to Nineveh, "I will make you a spectacle" (Nahum 3:6), meaning you will be the object of mockery and contempt from all.
H7210.origine: The Hebrew root ראה (rā'āh) means "to see" — it is the fundamental verb of vision. The word רֳאִי (ro'î) is a nominal derivative: it speaks of what comes from seeing, what pertains to vision or appearance. It is close to the noun מַרְאֵה (mar'è), which also means "appearance" or "vision." This lexical family is central in the Bible: to see is to perceive, to know, and it encompasses both the physical act and spiritual understanding.
H7210.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in biblical poetry (Job) and prophetic words. In 1 Samuel 16:12, it describes David's physical appearance. In Job 7:8 and 33:21, it takes on the meaning of gaze or the visible aspect of things. In Nahum 3:6, it takes on a public hue, that of a demonstration of humiliation. The word thus plays on a tension between the visible surface and what it expresses: the bodily figure, the judging gaze, the apparent state of the suffering body, the spectacle of shame.
H7210.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible is concerned with what is seen — not out of superficiality, but because appearance tells a story. God looks not only at the outside, but at what it reveals. For the believer, this invites a healthy awareness of one's own appearance and self-presentation, while bringing them back to the essential: what God sees in us is the heart. The word also calls for vigilance when it speaks of spectacle: exposing someone to ridicule is a serious form of humiliation before which God does not turn a blind eye.

sens: man of the tribe of Reuben during the time of the divided monarchy
H7211G.detail: Réaja is a man belonging to the tribe of Reuben, mentioned in the genealogy that lists the descendants of Reuben after the captivity of Israel. He is the son of Micah and the father of Baal, as indicated in the genealogical list of 1 Chronicles 5:5.
H7211G.origine: The name means "the Lord has seen" or "Jehovah has seen": it is formed from the Hebrew root meaning "to see." This name expresses the confidence that God sees and knows the fate of His people, even during times of trouble or exile. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, like many Hebrew names.
H7211G.emploi: Réaja is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:5, in a genealogy of the sons of Reuben. He appears in the direct succession: Micah (father) — Réaja — Baal (son). He is a descendant of Reuben living during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. Although not well-known compared to other biblical figures, his mention in the genealogy shows the importance that God places on the continuation of the lineages of the covenant people, even those of the northern tribes.

sens: Chief of a family of temple servants returned from exile
Descendant of Shobal son of Judah
Son of Micah, father of Baal, from the tribe of Reuben
H7211H.detail:
1. Reaja is a man who lived during the time of the Babylonian exile and the return to the land of Israel. His name means "the Lord has seen." He is mainly known as the chief of a family of temple servants (in Hebrew, the "Nethinim"). These servants performed the material tasks of worship at the temple in Jerusalem. When Zerubbabel brought the exiles back from Babylon, Reaja's family was among those who returned to rebuild the temple (Ezra 2:47; Nehemiah 7:50).
2. In the genealogy of Israel, Reaja was a descendant of Shobal, who was the son of Judah. He thus belongs to the lineage of Judah, one of the great tribes of Israel.
3. Another person of the same name was a Reubenite, that is, a man of the tribe of Reuben. He was the son of Micah and the father of Baal, according to the genealogies of Israel.
H7211H.origine: The name Reaja comes from the Hebrew רְאָיָה (reayah) and literally means "the Lord has seen" or "what the Lord has seen." It is composed of the root ראה (raah), "to see," and the divine name "Jah" (abbreviation of Yahweh). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, expressing the conviction that God sees and watches over the one who bears this name.
H7211H.emploi: Reaja appears twice in the Bible, in two parallel books that recount the return of the exiles. In Ezra 2:47 and Nehemiah 7:50, we read the lists of families that returned from Babylon under the leadership of Zerubbabel. Reaja is mentioned there as the chief of a family of Nethinim, that is, temple servants. These two references are essentially identical, as Ezra and Nehemiah report the same events and the same lists of return.

sens: Descendant of Shobal, from the tribe of Judah
Father of Jachath according to the genealogy of Judah
H7211I.detail:
1. Reaja is a man of the tribe of Judah, born during the time of the divided monarchy. He belongs to the genealogical line of Shobal, one of the sons of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:2).
2. He is the father of Jachath, who himself had children named Achumai and Lahad. These descendants form the families of the Tzorathites, a community established in the territory of Judah.
H7211I.origine: The name Reaja means "Yahweh has seen" or "God has looked" in Hebrew. It combines the root "ro'eh" (to see, to look) with the divine name Yah, expressing the idea that God has seen or approved this person. This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common among the Hebrews.
H7211I.emploi: Reaja appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:2, in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is situated several generations after Judah himself, in a line of descendants from the clan of Shobal. This passage lists the ancestors of the Tzorathites, a family or group from Judah. His role in this text is purely genealogical: he represents one of the many ancestors whose memory the Bible preserves to establish the lineages of God's people.

sens: Action of seeing, looking
Fact of perceiving something with the eyes
What is offered to the gaze, spectacle
H7212.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the simple act of seeing, of looking at something: it describes the moment when the eyes perceive an object. In Ecclesiastes 5:10, the rich man "sees" his possessions with his eyes — he contemplates them, enjoying them through his presence and gaze.
2. More broadly, it refers to the visual experience itself, the fact of having something in front of one's eyes. This implies direct, immediate knowledge: one only sees what is present before oneself.
3. By extension, the word can also refer to what is shown to the sight, the spectacle or appearance that manifests itself to someone's eyes.
H7212.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root רָאָה (to see, to look), one of the most common in biblical Hebrew. Here, רְאוּת is a nominal form — a noun of action that designates the act or fact of seeing. Aramaic has a very similar word, רֵו, which means "appearance": the two languages share this image of the gaze that captures what manifests itself.
H7212.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ecclesiastes 5:10. There, it expresses a truth that the Wise meditates on: the wealth that accumulates around a man brings him nothing more than to "see" this wealth with his own eyes — a vain and fleeting enjoyment. The context shows that "seeing" is not merely a passive perception, but a kind of savory contemplation of what one possesses that ultimately proves sterile.
H7212.portee: This passage reminds us that possessing is not enough to fill the human heart. Having things "before one's eyes" — seeing them, contemplating them — does not replace the deep satisfaction sought in accumulation. For the Christian, this invites one not to seek contentment in the gaze cast upon material possessions, but to fix one's eyes on what endures: the work of God and one's relationship with Him.

sens: to ascend in height, to stand up towards the sky
to occupy a higher position, to overlook
to be elevated, to be raised in relation to a reference level
H7213.detail: 1. The verb describes the physical movement of ascending, of standing up towards the sky. In Zechariah 14:10, Jerusalem "will be raised" — the city will rise, its lands will ascend above the surrounding plains, marking its importance and future transformation. 2. The word also expresses the idea of occupying a more prominent position than the surroundings: Jerusalem will remain "elevated" compared to the rest of the land which becomes plain. 3. The image is one of elevation: what is high stands out, is seen from afar, dominates the horizon. It is both a geographical fact and a symbol of dignity and exaltation.
H7213.origine: The root verb ra'am literally means "to rise" or "to go upwards." It describes the elementary action of standing up, of soaring vertically. This Hebrew root expresses the upward movement in a concrete and visible way, without the idea of abstraction: it is an image drawn from daily life, from the behavior of beings and things that rise up.
H7213.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (in Zechariah 14:10), in a prophetic vision. Zechariah describes the future transformation of Jerusalem and the surrounding territory: the lands will be leveled into a plain, but Jerusalem itself "will be raised," standing above this leveling. This context is one of restoration and exaltation of Jerusalem on the day of the Lord. The uniqueness of this usage underscores its importance for the theology of final redemption: the holy city, brought low by judgment, will be lifted up and established in its true place.
H7213.portee: This word reminds believers that God is capable of raising up what has been brought low. The vision of elevated Jerusalem inspires hope: those who confess the Lord will not be left on the ground, but will be lifted up and exalted. It is a word of consolation for the people of God in times of despair.

sens: A large wild animal with powerful horns, probably an extinct aurochs
The strength and power of this animal
A symbol of divine or warrior power
The image of vigor and dominance
H7214.detail:
1. The "buffalo" (réem in Hebrew) refers to a large and feared wild animal, probably an aurochs or wild bull, extinct since antiquity. It is a powerful creature that cannot be domesticated. In Job 39:12, it is asked: "Will the buffalo serve you? Will it spend the night at your crib?" — the answer is clearly no: it is an untamed and fierce animal.
2. The word primarily evokes brute strength and the capacity for destruction. In Numbers 24:8, God is compared to a buffalo: "He devours the nations that rise against Him, He breaks their bones, and brings them down with His arrows." The image emphasizes an irresistible and terrible power.
3. In blessings and royal contexts, the buffalo symbolizes divine power or the warrior strength of a people. In Deuteronomy 33:17, the horns of the buffalo represent the strength with which the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh "will strike all the peoples, to the ends of the earth."
4. The word can also refer to a sense of threat or imminent danger. In Psalms 22:22, the psalmist asks God to "deliver me from the horns of the buffalo," where the animal embodies a peril that could destroy him.
H7214.origine: The Hebrew word réem comes from a root expressing elevation or height, evoking the imposing stature of this animal. It has been translated into Greek and Latin terms designating large and strong creatures. The term remains surrounded by mystery: no precise description allows us to know exactly which animal the ancient Hebrews had in mind, but all indications point to a colossal, powerful, and dangerous beast, well known in the ancient world but now extinct.
H7214.emploi: The buffalo appears 9 times in the Bible, almost always in a context of power or destruction. It is used mainly in prophetic blessings (Numbers 23:22 and 24:8, where God is compared to this creature for Israel) and in royal descriptions (Deuteronomy 33:17, where the "horns of the buffalo" are mentioned). Job refers to it to show that no earthly creature is truly tameable by man (Job 39:12-13). The psalms invoke it as an image of danger or peril against which the believer seeks protection (Psalms 22:22). In every occurrence, the animal represents a superior force, impossible to control or master by man alone.
H7214.portee: The buffalo teaches the reader that true power does not come from control or domestication, but from submission to a superior force. When the Bible compares God to a buffalo, it affirms that His strength is absolute and terrifying, irresistible against the enemies of Israel. For the believer in danger, the image of the "horns of the buffalo" reminds us that only God can protect us from the powers that threaten us — which is why the psalms ask God to deliver us from them.

sens: hard and colorful material formed by certain marine polyps
precious substance used as adornment or decoration
wealth and beauty compared to divine wisdom
H7215.detail:
1. Coral is a hard material formed by tiny marine creatures (polyps) that live in colonies. It can be white, red, or pink, and is found in the Mediterranean and tropical seas. The ancients valued it highly, just like pearls or precious stones.
2. In ancient trade, coral was a highly sought-after luxury commodity, so precious that it was among the rich offerings that cities exchanged with one another. Ezekiel 27:16 lists coral alongside purple, fine linen, and rubies that Syria brought to Tyre.
3. Coral symbolizes earthly goods of great value. But Job 28:18 puts it into perspective: even the most beautiful material treasures — coral, crystal, pearls — do not equal the value of true wisdom, which comes from God.
H7215.origine: The Hebrew word ramah specifically refers to coral. Its exact origin is debated by scholars, but it may be related to a root evoking the idea of "to rise" or "to grow," as coral develops in branches. The word describes a specific material reality, well-known to merchants and the wealthy of the ancient Levant.
H7215.emploi: The word ramah appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the Old Testament. Job uses it to illustrate the incomparable value of wisdom: even the rarest treasures of the world (27:18) cannot compare to it. Ezekiel mentions it in his lament over Tyre, listing the luxuries that this great trading city exchanged — coral is one element among many that attest to its vanished splendor.
H7215.portee: Coral reminds us that earthly riches, however beautiful and precious, are worth nothing compared to divine wisdom and true spiritual riches. It is an invitation not to cling to the goods of this world, but to seek above all that which remains eternal.

sens: City of heights in the land of Israel
Levitical city of the tribe of Issachar
Levitical city in Gilead, territory of Gad
H7216G.detail: 1. The name Ramoth literally means "heights" in Hebrew, reflecting the geography of the place — a city built on elevated land. 2. In 1 Chronicles 6:73, Ramoth appears as one of the cities given to the Levites of the tribe of Issachar, with its suburbs reserved for livestock and crops. 3. In 1 Chronicles 6:80, another Ramoth in Gilead is mentioned among the Levitical cities in the territory of Gad, also with a suburb — indicating that at least two cities bore this name in Israel.
H7216G.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew root meaning "height" or "eminence." This type of geographical name often described the terrain's relief. Several places in Israel and Judah were named Ramoth, as "heights" was a common descriptive term.
H7216G.emploi: Ramoth appears twice in the book of Chronicles, both times in the passage listing the Levitical cities assigned to the descendants of Levi. The first Ramoth (1 Chronicles 6:73) was in Issachar, the second in Gilead (1 Chronicles 6:80), in the territory of Gad. These two cities served as residences for the Levites, who had no territorial inheritance of their own but received cities distributed among the territories of other tribes.

sens: Levitical city of Gilead, in Israel
H7216H.detail: Ramoth is a city located in Gilead, a territory east of the Jordan River. It is one of the three cities of refuge that Israel established on this side of the river, alongside Betser and Golan. It was situated in the territory of the tribe of Gad and served as a refuge for someone who had committed unintentional homicide (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8).
H7216H.origine: The name Ramoth literally means "heights" in Hebrew, which likely reflects the geography of this region of Gilead. It is a spelling variant of Ramoth-Gilead, often referred to simply by this geographical nickname to distinguish it from other locations bearing the same name in Israel.
H7216H.emploi: Ramoth appears twice in the Old Testament, exclusively in passages that list the three cities of refuge established east of the Jordan. These two occurrences — in Deuteronomy 4:43 and Joshua 20:8 — are found in parallel lists presenting the cities intended to protect the innocent from the blood avenger by the victim's relatives.

sens: part of the body that contains the brain and face
seat of thought, spirit, or visions
chief, one who commands or directs
sum, total, essence of a matter
H7217.detail:
1. The head is literally the upper part of the human body: the part that bears the hair and face. In Daniel's vision of the statue, the head of gold represents the kingdom of Babylon (Daniel 2:32), and when Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are thrown into the fire, the hair of their head is not burned (Daniel 3:27).
2. The head also denotes the seat of mental and spiritual life — the mind or thinking soul. When Daniel has visions "from his mind" while lying down, it is in his head that these heavenly images are born (Daniel 4:10; Daniel 7:1).
3. A head can also be a chief or leader: someone who directs, who is "at the head" of a group. Ezra asks to be named the men who are at the head of these workers (Ezra 5:10).
4. Finally, the word can denote the principal, the essential, the summary of a matter — what constitutes the head or the summit. Thus, Daniel "tells" the main things of his dream (Daniel 7:1).
H7217.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to be in front," "to be elevated." The head is naturally what is in front of the body and what dominates it. In Aramaic (the language spoken by the Jews during the Exile), the same word exists in the form "resh" and denotes both the physical organ and the function of command or the essence of a thing.
H7217.emploi: This word appears 13 times in the provided usages, primarily in the books of Ezra and Daniel — texts written partly in Aramaic, notably Daniel's visions. The usages show a gradation: from the literal sense (the physical head: hair, face, part of the statue) to the figurative sense (the mind as the seat of spiritual vision, the chief who directs, the essence of a narrative). The context of Daniel's visions enriches the word: the head becomes the place where spiritual knowledge is born and forged, what God reveals to His servant.
H7217.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites an understanding that the head — both the body and the spirit — belongs to God and must be devoted to His will. In Daniel's visions, the head is the focal point of divine revelation: it is through the spirit, through enlightened thought, that man receives the word of God. This word also reminds us that in the Church, Christ is the head: He governs, directs, and provides direction and unity to the entire body.

sens: The part of the human or animal body that carries the face, the eyes, and the brain.
The top or highest point of something.
The person who leads, commands, or has authority.
The beginning, origin, or commencement of an action or period.
The total, sum, or complete count of a quantity.
What is best, most important, or most remarkable.
H7218A.detail: 1. The head is primarily the upper part of the human and animal body: the part that carries the eyes, mouth, and brain. It is anointed with oil as a sign of consecration (1 Samuel 10:1: Samuel pours oil on Saul's head), adorned for beauty (2 Kings 9:30: Jezebel adorns her head), and covered with dust as a sign of mourning (Lamentations 2:10). It is also the seat of hair and beard (Leviticus 13:29). 2. The head denotes the summit or peak: the top of a mountain, the uppermost part of an object. In the language of sacrifices, the "head" of the animal is offered, meaning its upper part (Leviticus 1:8; 4:11). 3. The head represents the one who leads, governs, or has authority: the chief of a nation, city, or family. This is why crushing the head of an enemy signifies complete victory (Genesis 3:15: the serpent will be crushed on the head). 4. The head can also mean the beginning, the commencement: the starting point of an action or period. 5. This word also expresses totality, the complete sum: counting "per head" means counting each individual. 6. Finally, the head can denote what is best, principal, or most eminent: the choice, the elite.
H7218A.origine: The Hebrew word rosh (רֹאשׁ) comes from a very ancient root that expresses the idea of "lifting up," "rising," or "going forward." The head is naturally the part that rises at the top of the body and precedes it when moving forward. This word has also given rise to related words that mean "principal" or "first." In Greek, the corresponding word is kephalè, which has the same range of meanings.
H7218A.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, used about 258 times. It appears mainly in Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and the historical books. The concrete sense (the head of the body) predominates in Leviticus, where details of sacrifices and skin diseases are enumerated (Leviticus 1 and 13). The figurative sense of "chief," "authority" appears in historical accounts and the Psalms (Psalms 83:3: the enemies "lift their heads"). In Genesis 3:15, the verb "to crush the head" of the serpent expresses a decisive victory, while wounding the heel remains a less serious injury. In Genesis 47:31 and 48:14-18, placing a hand on someone's head is a gesture of blessing or the transfer of power. The word is also used for the summit of a mountain or the beginning of a series.
H7218A.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader grasp how the Bible speaks of the body, authority, and victory. The head, as the seat of consciousness and command, represents the whole person and their honor. In Genesis 3:15, "crushing the head" of the serpent announces Christ's ultimate victory over evil. Recognizing that someone "lifts their head" means acknowledging them as victorious or restored in their honor. This concrete language anchors faith in the body and tangible actions, not in abstraction.

sens: Leader or sovereign of a people or region
Person who exercises supreme authority
One who commands and governs
H7218B.detail:
1. The word designates a leader or sovereign — someone who directs a people or region with authority. In Ezekiel 38:2, the prophet addresses Gog: "Son of man, set your face against Gog, of the land of Magog, prince of the chief of Meshech and Tubal," showing that this title applies to one who dominates and governs.
2. It is also the person who exercises supreme power and makes decisions for their people. The context of Ezekiel 38-39, where God announces judgments against this prince's armies, shows that this title recognizes a position of political and military command.
3. In biblical usage, the prince is one who leads, has authority, and governs; it is a role of responsibility towards those they lead.
H7218B.origine: The Hebrew word rosh comes from a root that literally means "head" — the idea of chief or prince naturally comes from this, as the head directs the body. It is a universal image: the one who thinks and commands is at the head. In Hebrew, it is used to designate anything that is first, principal, or in a position of command, and the French word "prince" accurately translates this notion of supreme authority.
H7218B.emploi: This word appears in the Book of Ezekiel to qualify Gog, an enemy leader that God announces (38:2-3 and 39:1). The prophet repeats this title three times when addressing this prince, emphasizing his importance and status as a sovereign. The usage shows that in biblical prophecy, the title of prince applies to a political and military leader who governs nations and whose actions have consequences that God controls and judges.
H7218B.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that all the princes and sovereigns of the earth are known to God and subject to His ultimate authority. Even the greatest leaders, who seem all-powerful, are under the gaze of the Creator and execute His plans, whether they know it or not. It is an assurance that the history of the world never escapes God's control.

sens: The head of the human or animal body
The summit or highest point
One who commands, leads, or has authority
The beginning, opening, commencement
The best, most excellent, principal
A group, division, or company of people
H7218H.detail: 1. The head is the upper part of the human or animal body, the part that carries the face and intelligence. This is the concrete and literal sense of the word. 2. The summit denotes the peak of a mountain or the highest part of something (Joshua 11:10 speaks of the "head" of Canaan, its main region). 3. A chief is one who leads, commands: this is the most frequent sense in the Bible. The "chiefs" of families (Exodus 6:14) are the patriarchs who govern their clan; the "chiefs" of tribes (Numbers 1:16) are the representatives of Israel before God and Moses. A chief of war (2 Samuel 23:8) is a top-ranking warrior. 4. The beginning: something has its "head" when it starts (like a year that begins). 5. The best: God asks for the "firstfruits," the things of the head, meaning the most beautiful, the purest. 6. A division or company is a "head" of men, an organized grouping (1 Chronicles 15:12: the "chiefs" of the families of the Levites).
H7218H.origine: The Hebrew word rosh comes from an ancient root meaning "eminence," "elevation." Its basic image is the head that rises above the body, from which it extends to everything that is "high," "first," or "principal." In Greek, the word kephalè often translates rosh in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), with the same range of meanings: literally the physical head, but also the chief, the leader, one who occupies the highest position.
H7218H.emploi: The word appears more than 160 times in the Old Testament, especially in historical and legislative books. Its most common usage is the sense of "chief" or "leader": we speak of chiefs of family (Exodus 6:14), chiefs of tribe (Numbers 1:16), chiefs of army (2 Samuel 23:8). In legislative and administrative texts, the "chiefs" are those who make decisions and represent their group (Joshua 14:1, Joshua 24:1). The word also applies to political and military leaders: the one who reigns is at the "head" of the people (Deuteronomy 33:5, 2 Chronicles 13:12: God and His priests are at the head of Israel). Sometimes it retains its physical sense (the head of a man or animal) or geographical sense (the head of a region). The context always determines which of the six senses is appropriate.
H7218H.portee: Understanding that "chief" in Hebrew comes from the image of the head helps the reader grasp how the Bible views power and authority: the one who is at the head is not separate from the body; they are responsible for it and embody it. Jesus is called "the head" of the Church (Colossians 1:18) — this biblical image means that He leads, supports, and animates the entire body of believers as the head governs the body. Meditating on this word allows for reflection on just authority: a true chief shares the life of their people and is accountable for them.

sens: Summit of a mountain or hill
Upper part of a construction or object
Leader, one who directs a group or nation
What is best, first
Beginning or commencement of a period
Division or organized group
H7218I.detail:
1. The summit is the highest point of a mountain or elevation: it is the peak, where the view extends the farthest. When the Flood ceases, "the summits of the mountains" appear first (Genesis 8:5); this is also what God shows to Moses from a mountain, to see all the land (Deuteronomy 34:1).
2. It is also the upper part of any constructed object: the top of a column, the capital or head that crowns it. The temple of Jerusalem has columns whose "summit" bears an ornate work of lilies (1 Kings 7:22); the columns of the tabernacle have silver capitals (Exodus 38:19).
3. A leader or ruler is called the "head" of a people, city, or family, because he is above and directs others as the head directs the body. Moses "ascends to the summit" of the mountain to receive the Lord, marking his authority in that place (Exodus 19:20).
4. What is best, most excellent, is also called the "head" or first rank — the finest riches, the best things (see Esther 5:2 and the context).
5. The beginning or starting point of an action is expressed by this word: it is where one departs, the first moment (Exodus 30:23).
6. A band, group, or division of an army is a "head": a distinct unit led (Numbers 14:40).
H7218I.origine: The Hebrew word rosh comes from an ancient root that evokes the idea of "to rise," "to elevate" — that which ascends, that which is high. It is found in many families of Hebrew words that speak of height, elevation, and direction. In Greek, this word is often translated as kephalé (κεφαλή), which literally means "head" and is used in the same way: the summit of an object, the leader of a community. This image of the "head" that dominates, directs, and represents an entire body is very common in the Bible.
H7218I.emploi: Rosh is one of the most frequent words in the Old Testament (87 times in the provided passages). It primarily refers to the summits of mountains and the upper parts of objects (columns, temple constructions) — very concrete and visual uses. But it then extends to the meaning of "leader," "political chief," or "responsible person": Moses at the summit of the mountain, a leader of a military division. Finally, it can mean "the best" or "the beginning." The Bible uses it interchangeably for a geographical summit, a part of a building, a community leader, or the excellence of a thing — always with the common idea that it is what is "above," that dominates or is first.
H7218I.portee: This word reminds us that the "summit" is the point of perspective: the one who reaches the top sees far (Moses from the top of the mountain). It also states that the leader is one who is "above," responsible, and that excellence consists of being "on high." For the believer, this suggests that seeking "above" — towards God, towards what is elevated — is a natural spiritual direction, and that true authority comes from the one who dominates, who sees all and guides.

sens: the upper part of a person's or animal's body
the highest point, the summit of something
the moment or event by which something begins
the one who leads, the chief or responsible person
the entirety or integrity of a thing
H7218J.detail: 1. The head is the upper part of the human or animal body (Genesis 2:10 speaks of the "arms" of the river, the branches that spring from it, like a head from which the branches flow). 2. The summit is the highest point: in Psalm 19 or Ecclesiastes 3:11, when speaking of the "first" atom of dust, it evokes the beginning of things (Proverbs 8:26: "the first atom of the dust of the world"). 3. The beginning is the moment when something starts: Isaiah 41:4 speaks of the one who "has called the generations from the beginning"; Ezekiel 40:1 situates a vision "at the beginning of the year." 4. The chief is the one who leads: the word rosh designates the head of a family, a city, a nation. 5. The whole or entirety: in Numbers 5:7, "in its entirety" translates this word to mean the full restitution, the complete sum of what was owed.
H7218J.origine: The Hebrew word rosh comes from a root that means "to be high, to rise." It belongs to a family of words describing what ascends, what exceeds. In Aramaic, rosh has the same form and meaning. The word evokes the image of the head as the highest point of the body, from which comes its broad meaning: first, principal, the one who presides. This root is very common in the Old Testament to speak of what begins or of the one who commands.
H7218J.emploi: The word rosh appears 18 times in the cited passages. It is used in a very concrete way: Genesis 2:10 speaks of the "arms" of the river (its branches stemming from the head of the river). It also designates the moment: "beginning" of the watch (Judges 7:19), "beginning" of the year (Ezekiel 40:1), "beginning" of the generations (Isaiah 41:4). The sense of chief or first appears implicitly in several passages where order and hierarchy are at play. Finally, "entire" in Numbers 5:7 translates rosh in the sense of totality, complete sum.
H7218J.portee: This word teaches us that God is the origin of all things (Isaiah 41:4: "the one who has called the generations from the beginning"). It also reminds us that all order, all authentic leadership is rooted in God, who is the head of all creation. Understanding rosh helps to grasp that repentance and restitution require total integrity (Numbers 5:7), not a half-measure.

sens: Group of people, organized band
Military division, contingent of soldiers
Set, totality (broad sense)
H7218K.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a group of people gathered and organized for a common action. In Judges 7:16, Gideon divides his three hundred men into three "troops," meaning three distinct groups, each with their trumpets and jars, for a coordinated operation. This conveys the idea of a unit of people forming a whole.

2. In a military context, rosh often refers to a division of soldiers or a contingent: in 1 Samuel 11:11, Saul divides the people into three troops before attacking the Ammonites at dawn. Similarly, in Judges 9:34 and 9:43, Abimelech organizes his troops into four or three separate bodies to encircle the city. It is a tactical term that describes how forces are distributed and organized in combat.

3. More broadly, the word can express a totality or a whole: in Job 1:17, the Chaldeans form unified bands that strike together. The meaning shifts towards that of a collection or an organized mass.
H7218K.origine: The word rosh is at the root of many biblical terms. It comes from a fundamental image: the "head" (the primary meaning of the word in Hebrew), which dominates and directs. From this come the meanings of "chief" (one who is at the head), "beginning" or "commencement" (what is in front), and by extension, "group" or "troop" (a division that has its own direction). The word appears in names of places and people, and structures many biblical expressions around the idea of preeminence or organization.
H7218K.emploi: The word rosh appears more than 600 times in the Old Testament in various forms and meanings. In the provided usages, it almost always designates a "troop" or a "military" or tactical "division": it is primarily found in the historical books (Judges, 1 Samuel) with this precise meaning. Saul, Gideon, and Abimelech divide their forces into several troops to carry out strategic operations (dawn attacks, ambushes, encircling maneuvers). In Job 1:17, the Chaldeans also gather in organized bands. The military or collective action context is constant. The word can also denote, in other passages, a totality ("the sum of your words" in Psalms 119:160), but it is primarily retained in the sense of division or group in the French translation as "troop."
H7218K.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, organization and tactics are not opposed to faith. The leaders of Israel wisely divide their troops to be effective in battle. For the Christian, this shows that God is not an enemy of strategy or order: He values clear organization and clarity in action. It is also a reminder that believers together form an organized people with roles and direction.

sens: action of counting the people of a group
totality of the counted people or goods
register or list of counted persons
H7218L.detail:
1. Counting is the action of counting head by head, person by person. In Numbers 1:2, Moses is commanded to "take a census of the whole assembly of the children of Israel," which means to count each member individually "head by head."
2. Counting produces a total, a sum: the result of the counting. It is this overall number that is obtained after enumerating the people or goods. In Numbers 31:26, the "count of the spoils" is made to establish the total of what has been taken.
3. By extension, counting can also refer to the register or the list itself of the counted persons, the document where names and numbers have been recorded. It is the fruit of the counting action, preserved for memory and administration.
H7218L.origine: The Hebrew word rosh literally means "head" (the head of a person or an animal), the organ that is at the top of the body. From this concrete image arises the idea of "chief" or "principal," one who is "at the head." When counting "head by head," each individual is counted as a distinct unit: this is where the meaning of "counting" or "total" comes from. The same root produces words for "summit," "beginning," "chief of a group."
H7218L.emploi: The word appears seven times in the provided texts, all in the book of Numbers. It is an administrative and religious context: the counting of Israel by Moses at God's command. In Numbers 1:2 and 26:2, the "whole assembly" of the children of Israel is counted to know the total number of warriors. In Numbers 1:49, it is specified that the Levites are not counted, setting them apart. In Numbers 4:2 and 4:22, the clans of the Levites responsible for transporting the tabernacle are counted. In Numbers 31:26, the counting applies to the spoils taken from Midian. It is always a precise counting operation, necessary for the organization of the people and the management of its resources.
H7218L.portee: The biblical counting is never a neutral act: it is God who commands the counting of His people, thus recognizing each member of Israel. This gesture affirms that the people belong to God and that He knows their exact number.
