For the Christian reader, this suggests that God counts each of His children, none are forgotten; our value comes from our unique place in the community He has chosen.

sens: Toxic substance, deadly venom
Bitter, corrosive, destructive character
Malicious word or lie
Bitter consequence of a bad action
H7219.detail:
1. Poison is primarily a venomous substance that kills or injures: the venom of snakes (Deuteronomy 32:33), the poisoned water forced to drink (Jeremiah 9:15). It is concrete and deadly.
2. The word also designates what is bitter and destructive in a figurative sense: a root that produces poison and bitterness symbolizes a spiritual deviation that corrupts a whole people (Deuteronomy 29:18), like a poisonous plant that grows in the fields (Hosea 10:4).
3. Poison characterizes malicious words or lies: putting poison in someone's food means overwhelming them with wickedness (Psalms 69:22, Lamentations 3:5). It is an image of betrayal and hostility.
4. Poison can also represent the bitter retribution one reaps: as one sows injustice, one harvests poison (Amos 6:12)—the natural and terrible consequence of one's actions.
H7219.origine: The Hebrew word literally means what injures or is bitter. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of tearing or piercing: like the venom of a snake piercing. In Aramaic and elsewhere, similar forms are found. The basic image is therefore physical: it is primarily the poison that can be touched or drunk, then it extends figuratively to describe anything that corrupts, injures, or spiritually kills.
H7219.emploi: The word appears about 12 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the prophetic and wisdom books. It is first used in the literal sense: the venom of snakes (Deuteronomy 32:33). But very quickly, it becomes figurative: a root of poison symbolizes religious unfaithfulness that spreads in a community (Deuteronomy 29:18), the poisoned water that God gives to drink represents His judgment (Jeremiah 9:15). In the Psalms and Lamentations, poison characterizes the cruelty of enemies who inundate the righteous with spiritual poison (Psalms 69:22, Lamentations 3:5). It is also the natural harvest of injustice (Amos 6:12). The word thus encompasses both the physical and the moral, divine punishment and human malice.
H7219.portee: This word reminds us that evil is not trivial: it has toxic effects, either immediately or over the long term. It warns us that malicious words, dishonesty, and unfaithfulness act like a slow poison. For the Christian, meditating on poison prompts vigilance over one's words, thoughts, and alliances: what seems bitter or toxic today is often the rotten fruit of bad roots. And it is also a call to turn to God to escape what destroys.

sens: Son of Benjamin, mentioned during the time of Egypt and the desert
H7220.detail: Rosh is one of the sons of Benjamin listed in Genesis 46:21, during Jacob's migration to Egypt. He is also referred to as Rapha in the parallel account of 1 Chronicles 8:2. His name literally means "head" in Hebrew, a common image in Hebrew names to denote the firstborn or a son of high rank.
H7220.origine: The name Rosh (רֹאשׁ) comes from the ordinary Hebrew word meaning "head." This concrete meaning transformed into a personal name to designate a son of Benjamin at the time of the settlement in Egypt. The parallels between the genealogies (Genesis 46:21 and 1 Chronicles 8:2) show that the same character bears two names: Rosh and Rapha (רָפָא), a common practice in ancient Israelite families.
H7220.emploi: Rosh appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 46:21, among the ten sons of Benjamin who go down to Egypt with Jacob. This genealogy situates the family of Benjamin at the time of the great famine, before the slavery in Egypt. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 8:2 designates him by the name Rapha, without contradiction: it is the same character. He is simply listed among the ancestors of the Benjaminites, without a detailed account of his life.

sens: the time that preceded, which elapsed before the present moment
an ancient, bygone era
H7221.detail:
1. The word designates the past, what has occurred before. In Ezekiel 36:11, God promises Israel to restore it and make it more fruitful "as formerly" — that is, as it was once, before desolation. The image is one of returning to a previous, happier state.

2. In a broader sense, it refers to an ancient, bygone era that can be evoked with nostalgia or admiration. The word carries the idea of a period that belongs to the past but remains present in memory or in the desire for restoration.
H7221.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "head" or "beginning." Literally, "head" can evoke the "beginning" or the "first time." This image of the beginning extends to the idea of original time, of what was at the start — hence the idea of past and ancient time.
H7221.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 36:11. It is found in a promise of divine restoration: God announces to the land of Israel that it will be repopulated and more fruitful than "formerly." The context is one of consolation for the exiles, where God promises to return to His people and restore their former prosperity. It is a rare word, but filled with hope.
H7221.portee: This word reminds us that the past can serve as a reference point for future hope. God promises not only restoration but even "more good than formerly" (Ezekiel 36:11): His grace surpasses mere repairs. For the Christian, this invites us to see how God can transform a loss or a time of desolation into an opportunity for even greater blessing.

sens: the highest stone, the one that dominates
the key stone of a construction, the one that is its heart and key
H7222.detail:
1. The cornerstone is the highest stone, the one that overlooks and is highlighted. In Zechariah 4:7, the prophet sees Zerubbabel laying this cornerstone amidst acclamations, a moment of triumph and grace for the rebuilt temple.
2. It is also the key stone, essential, without which the construction does not hold. It symbolizes the completion of a major work and the fulfillment of a project of great importance.
H7222.origine: The Hebrew word *roshah* comes from the root meaning "head" or "summit." It is formed from the same family as *rosh*, the most common Hebrew word for "head" or "chief." This image of the head applied to a stone naturally evokes what is first, what dominates, or what is essential in a structure.
H7222.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Zechariah 4:7. It describes a key moment in the restoration of the temple of Jerusalem after the exile: Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, lays the cornerstone while the people acclaim him, shouting "Grace, grace!" This stone symbolizes not only the end of the work but also the continuity of the divine promise and God's favor upon His people and His sanctuary.
H7222.portee: This cornerstone reminds the believer that God completes His work and that obstacles, even the greatest, will be leveled before His will. It invites us to recognize the decisive role of foundational stones — what is essential, what remains when the superfluous collapses — and to place our trust in God's plans even when everything seems impossible.

sens: Who comes before others in time, in succession
Who occupies the place before others in space or order
Who took place in the past
Who is principal, of first rank, the most important
H7223G.detail:
1. The most common meaning: what happened or exists before everything else in a sequence of events or things. For example, "the first month" of the year (Exodus 12:2), or "the first day" of the flood when Noah sees the dry land (Genesis 8:13). It is the order in time.
2. What is found in front, at the head, in a position that precedes others. Thus, in the march of the people of Israel, the first group advanced before the others (Numbers 2:9), and the first sacrifice was the one presented as a priority (Leviticus 9:15).
3. What belonged to the past, what was "formerly." This concerns ancestors or what existed in ancient times: for example, those who "had seen the first house" of the temple remembered its splendor (Ezra 3:12).
4. What is principal, of first rank, or commands the others. "Your hand shall be lifted first against him" (Deuteronomy 13:9) means that one acts first, with primary responsibility. "At the head" (Isaiah 60:9) designates one who is in the first rank, who leads.
H7223G.origine: The Hebrew word רִאשׁוֹן (ri.shon) comes from the root ראש (rosh), which means "head." The head is naturally what comes in front of the body, hence the idea of "first," of "what is in front." This word is formed with a suffix that makes it an adjective. This same root is found in other words of the family: ראש means literally the head of the body, but also the chief, the principal. The image is very vivid: what is "first" is what is "at the head," just as the head directs the body.
H7223G.emploi: This word is one of the most common in the Hebrew Bible, used 121 times. It appears in every book: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, to indicate moments, orders of succession, events in time. In the laws of Moses, it is used for religious festivals, the first days of months or of Passover, and for the ranks of one who acts "first." In the historical books, it is used for ancestors or past generations, and for one who occupies the first rank in an army or a position. The meaning nuances: sometimes it is a pure indication of rank or succession, sometimes it is a priority or responsibility ("your hand shall be lifted first"), sometimes it is a nostalgia for the past ("the first house").
H7223G.portee: This word reminds us that in God's plan, order matters: there is a first and there is a sequence. Understanding that Jesus is "the first and the last" (even if this word is not used in this exact verse) helps the reader grasp that He has absolute primacy. For the believer, it is a lesson: putting essential things first in one's life, as God ordains, is to walk wisely.

sens: That which comes before others in time; original, initial
That which existed or occurred in a past time; prior, ancient
That which occupies the first place, the highest rank; principal, first-rate
Before, first (adverbial sense)
H7223H.detail:
1. The word designates what occurs first in a temporal succession: the first famine in Genesis 26:1 is the one that took place during Abraham's time, before the current famine. It is the beginning, the origin of a series.

2. It also evokes what belongs to the past, what was once: the ancient practices of 2 Kings 17:40 are the customs that were followed in the past. Similarly, the former predictions of Isaiah 48:3 are those that God made long ago.

3. In certain contexts, the word marks preeminence, the principal or eminent character: the first husband in Deuteronomy 24:4 is the one who has the first place in marriage. The ancient dominion of Micah 4:8 is that which prevailed in the past.

4. Adverbially, it means "before," "first," "at the beginning": this indicates the chronological or logical priority of an action.
H7223H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "head" or "beginning." Its fundamental meaning is therefore that which comes first, at the start. This same root gives related words such as "rishon" (the first) and expressions marking order or succession. The idea is always one of priority, either in time or in rank or importance.
H7223H.emploi: This word appears about fifty times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical and prophetic books. It is used first in the strict temporal sense: the first days, the first year, the first ancestors (Leviticus 26:45, Deuteronomy 4:32). It also describes past events or states that serve as reference: the ancient law of Deuteronomy 10:4, the ancient practices of 2 Kings 17:40. In prophecies (Isaiah 41:22, Isaiah 42:9, Isaiah 43:18), God evokes His first acts or His ancient words to show His continuity and faithfulness. Sometimes, it emphasizes preeminence: the first husband has the first right. The nuance can thus shift from "chronologically prior" to "previously established" or "of primary importance."
H7223H.portee: This word reminds the reader that God acts in history, creating a continuity between the past and the present. By evoking God's first acts, the Bible invites recognition of His constancy and power: He acted in the past, He acts now. This strengthens trust in His word and His covenant, passed down from ancestors to descendants. Finally, the concept of the "first" underscores the importance of the order established by God: what is first in His plan deserves respect and obedience.

sens: That which comes before others in time or order
That which occupies the highest rank, the most important
That which is the oldest, the eldest
That which was before, which belongs to the past
H7223I.detail:
1. The word describes what comes forward, at the head: the sons of David were the "first" before the king (1 Chronicles 18:17), meaning those who stood in the front rank, closest to royal power.

2. It designates one who prevails over others, who occupies the place of chief: the word applies to "principal" leaders, the most important among the leaders (Daniel 10:13), those who command.

3. It can also qualify one who is the oldest: in 2 Chronicles 22:1, the "eldest" are the greatest of the sons, those who should have reigned before the youngest.

4. It evokes the past, antiquity: the "first" peoples to commit a sin are its initiators (Ezra 9:2), they did it before all others.
H7223I.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be at the head, to lead." It is related to the idea of preceding, of going before. The same root produces words for "head" and "prince." This word captures the image of one who walks ahead, showing the way to others.
H7223I.emploi: This word appears 4 times in the provided passages, always to qualify a position of preeminence or priority. In 1 Chronicles 18:17, it designates the high rank of the king's sons. In 2 Chronicles 22:1, it qualifies the relative age of the sons (the eldest compared to the youngest). In Ezra 9:2, it marks the principal guilt, that which inaugurates a sin. In Daniel 10:13, it identifies the greatest of the heavenly leaders. The meaning oscillates between hierarchical order and temporal order.
H7223I.portee: This word reminds us that God establishes an order: some are chosen to be "first," to lead and bear responsibility. It is an invitation to consider who the true leaders are, and for those who occupy a place of first rank, a call to faithfulness, as the example of the "first" has consequences for all.

sens: that which comes before all others in a succession
that which is at the beginning
H7224.detail:
1. This word designates what occupies the first place in an order or sequence — the beginning, the priority. In Jeremiah 25:1, it qualifies the "first year" of Nebuchadnezzar's reign, the one that precedes all other years of his power over Babylon.
2. More broadly, it can mean "initial" or "original" — that which marks the beginning of a period, an event, or a series.
H7224.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root רֹאשׁ (rosh), which means "head" or "chief." A "first" word is literally one that is at the head, in front. The family of the word also includes terms for "principal" and "beginning." It is the natural image of Hebrew: that which comes first is that which "leads" or "directs" the course, like a head guides the body.
H7224.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible in Hebrew (Jeremiah 25:1), where it precisely indicates the first year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign. It is a chronological usage, marking the starting point of a historical period. The usage is simple and direct: qualifying what is "first" in time.
H7224.portee: This term reminds us that history flows in order, with a precise beginning. For the believer, recognizing what is "first" — the origins of events, the beginnings of periods — helps to understand God's plan that unfolds in time according to an established order.

sens: The starting point in time, the moment when something begins
The first part of an action, period, or story
The first fruits, that is, the first harvest or the first fruits offered to God
What is first in rank, the most important or the best
H7225G.detail:
1. The beginning refers to the initial moment, the starting point of a reality. It is the word that opens the Bible: "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1), marking the instant when everything began to exist. It is also used to date the start of a prophecy (Jeremiah 26:1) or a reign (Jeremiah 27:1).
2. The beginning can also mean the first phase or the start of a process: "The beginning of a dispute is like the breaching of a dam" (Proverbs 17:14), where "beginning" describes how a conflict starts.
3. The first fruits are the first fruits of the harvest, consecrated to God as a sign of gratitude: "You shall offer to the Lord a contribution of the first fruits of your dough" (Numbers 15:21). They express dependence on God and the importance of giving Him the first and best fruits, not the leftovers.
4. When speaking of people or things, the word denotes what is first in dignity, the best. The firstborn is "the first" of God's works, the most honored (Job 40:14); Israel was "the first fruits of His harvest" (Jeremiah 2:3), His chosen people among all nations.
H7225G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be at the head" or "to lead." It is related to other words in the same family that denote the head (chief, leader). The basic image is therefore that of what comes first, in front: the beginning is what "stands at the head" of all other moments. This idea of priority in time or dignity is found in all the meanings of the word.
H7225G.emploi: This word appears 39 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Pentateuch, the Psalms, and the Prophets. It is used first in a literal and temporal sense: the beginning of the world (Genesis 1:1), the start of a prophecy (Jeremiah 26:1, 27:1, 28:1). Very often, it designates the first fruits offered to God — the first fruits, the first part of the dough — in the laws of worship (Numbers 15:20-21, Leviticus 2:12, Deuteronomy 18:4). It is also used to denote quality or rank: the firstborn (Deuteronomy 21:17), what is first or best (Job 40:14, 42:12). The last usages give it a more reflexive sense: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord" (Proverbs 1:7, 111:10), where it describes what is fundamental, essential.
H7225G.portee: This word reminds us that everything comes from God and begins with Him. "In the beginning" establishes that God is before all things and controls the origins. The use of first fruits teaches us to offer to God our first fruits, our best efforts, not our leftovers: it is to recognize His lordship over our lives. And the connection between "beginning" and "wisdom" invites us to seek in God the foundation of all true understanding.

sens: The first fruits or products harvested from a crop
What is best, most excellent in a category
The beginning, the start of an action or period
The main or most important part of a whole
H7225H.detail:
1. The first fruits are literally the first fruits picked at the harvest. In Israel, these first products had to be presented to the Lord as a recognition of His blessing (Exodus 23:19: "You shall bring the first of the first fruits of your ground to the house of the Lord your God").
2. The word also designates what is best and most excellent: the finest, most precious part of an offering. In 1 Samuel 2:29, the priest Eli is reproached for fattening himself on the "first fruits of all the offerings of Israel," meaning the best part.
3. By extension, "first fruits" can mean the beginning or what comes first. In Deuteronomy 33:21, the text speaks of the "first fruits of the land," the territory received as the first inheritance.
4. The word can also express the main force or capital element: in Jeremiah 49:35, the Lord "breaks the bow of Elam, its main strength," where "main" translates the same Hebrew word.
H7225H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "head" or "beginning." This family root expresses the idea of what is first, what presides. The noun "first fruits" retains this image of priority and superiority: what comes first is also what has the greatest value.
H7225H.emploi: This word appears about 10 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is particularly used in the Law (Exodus, Deuteronomy) to designate the prescribed offerings: the first fruits that the people were to offer at the temple. It is also found among the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos) to describe what is excellent or principal. In 1 Samuel, it qualifies the best part of the sacrifices. Its usage thus varies from the concrete (physical fruits) to the figurative (excellence, principal), but the central idea remains that of what is first and therefore most esteemed.
H7225H.portee: Understanding the first fruits reminds us that in Israel, honoring God began with giving Him the first fruits, not the leftovers. This teaches a lasting spiritual principle: to recognize God in what is best in us and to give Him the first place. This word invites the believer not to offer to the Lord what is worn out or second-rate, but the first fruits of their time, attention, and resources.

sens: The place where a person's head rests when sleeping or lying down
By extension, the area located at the head of the bed or resting place
H7226.detail:
1. The bedside is literally the place where the head rests when one sleeps or lies down. In the account of 1 Samuel 26:12, David stealthily approaches Saul during his deep sleep and takes the spear and the water jug that are at the king's bedside — that is, right next to his head, as objects within reach of the sleeper.
2. The word more broadly designates the area, the space located at the head of the bed or the place where someone rests, as opposed to the other sides. It is a concrete detail that helps visualize the scene: David acts with remarkable discretion, removing the personal belongings of the sleeping king without waking him.
H7226.origine: The Hebrew word רַאֲשֹׁת (ra'ashoth) is constructed from the root רֹאשׁ (rosh), which means "head." The form used here (with the suffix indicating place) makes it a place name: literally "the place of the head." It is a compound that localizes the action or object: the bedside is the place designated by the head, where it is located.
H7226.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 26:12, in the context of the narrator David being pursued by Saul. David quietly enters the camp of the sleeping king and takes the spear and the water jug placed at his bedside — the objects closest to his head. This detail highlights David's boldness and caution: he acts just inches from the king, in the darkness of the night, without waking him. The unique usage of the word confirms its concrete and spatial meaning: it precisely describes the location of the king's objects.
H7226.portee: This word speaks to us of David's quiet courage and his trust in God to act under divine protection. By approaching the sleeping Saul, David steals his personal belongings to prove to the king that he could have killed him but did not — a lesson in humility and respect for the one anointed by God, even when he might seek vengeance. The detail of the bedside also reminds us how God can cover us with a deep sleep when we need protection.

sens: That exists, is found in large numbers, in significant quantity
That lasts a long time, that extends over a considerable period
That is important, considerable in size, intensity, or value
That is abundant, sufficient in quantity
That is strong, powerful, intense
A lot, enormously (adverbial sense)
H7227A.detail:
1. Numerous describes a multitude of people or things: "The children of Israel captured two hundred thousand prisoners among their brothers" (2 Chronicles 28:8), showing that the number is considerable and impressive.
2. When it comes to time, the word means a long duration: "You have not abandoned your brothers for a long time until this day" (Joshua 22:3), where "long" translates this same root to express a significant period.
3. Great can describe something imposing or intense: "The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great on the earth" (Genesis 6:5), where the extent of evil is emphasized.
4. The word also expresses abundance or sufficiency: "They took a lot of plunder from him" (2 Chronicles 28:8) shows that the quantity was more than sufficient.
5. It can qualify a force or power: when speaking of a "great" assembly (Psalms 40:11), it describes both the number and importance of the gathering.
6. Used as an adverb, it reinforces intensity: "I will strike many peoples with astonishment" (Ezekiel 32:10) expresses the magnitude of the action.
H7227A.origine: This Hebrew root, very ancient and very common, comes from a fundamental idea: that of quantity increasing, of what expands. It shares its family with other Hebrew words expressing abundance and growth. The word evokes the concrete image of something accumulating, extending, filling space — like a crowd growing or an abundant harvest. It is a very stable Semitic root, present in several related languages.
H7227A.emploi: This word appears more than 400 times in the Old Testament, particularly in Genesis, Exodus, and the historical books. It is used to describe quantities (prisoners, plunder, livestock), durations (long delays, periods of waiting), moral or natural qualities (wickedness, divine faithfulness), and states (strength, power, intensity). Its meaning varies according to context: in "The LORD saw that the wickedness was great," it qualifies the extent of evil; in "many peoples," it counts a multitude. The French translation changes according to context: great, numerous, many, several, depending on whether one emphasizes size, number, quantity, or intensity.
H7227A.portee: This word reminds us that God sees and knows the real extent of things — both evil and good. It helps the reader grasp the importance of what is at stake in biblical history: the stakes are high, the challenges numerous, but so are the resources and grace of God. When the Bible emphasizes that wickedness was "great" or that divine faithfulness is "great," it invites the believer to measure the gravity of sin and the infinite generosity of their God.

sens: One who commands, who leads a troop or a group of warriors
One who is at the head of a service or an institution
The most important, the principal
H7227B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a military commander: a chief of warriors, someone who leads troops into battle. This is exactly the role of Nebuzaradan, "chief" of the guards of the king of Babylon (2 Kings 25:8), who leads the royal guard and carries out the king's orders during the capture of Jerusalem.
2. By extension, it refers to one who is responsible for a service or an important function in an administration or court. The context of Esther 1:8 suggests characters of authority charged with official functions.
3. More generally, the word designates what is great, numerous, or principal. The common idea is that of precedence: one who is "rav" is not equal to others, but above or in front of them.
H7227B.origine: The word "rav" is linked to the idea of multiplicity and majority: it comes from a root that means "to be great" or "to be numerous." A chief is one who prevails over others, who has the majority of authority. This root is found in other Hebrew words like "rab," which also means "master" or "great." Aramaic uses similar forms, notably in the word "rabhréban" (noble, great lord), which shows how this notion of importance and authority has developed.
H7227B.emploi: The word "rav" appears about 28 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical accounts of the 2nd Book of Kings and the Book of Jeremiah. The dominant context is that of Babylonian administration: Nebuzaradan, chief of the guards of King Nebuchadnezzar, recurs regularly in the accounts of the fall of Jerusalem and the exile (2 Kings 25:8-26, Jeremiah 39-52). It is also encountered in other administrative or military contexts (Esther 1:8 refers to court officials, Daniel 1:3 a chief of the eunuchs, Jonah 1:6 the "master" of the ship). In all these uses, the word designates someone who exercises concrete authority over others.
H7227B.portee: This word reminds us that authority in the Bible is always linked to a charge, to a responsibility towards those one leads. Nebuzaradan is not a capricious tyrant: he is an officer who executes his duties, who sometimes even shows justice (he entrusts survivors to Gedaliah in Jeremiah 40:5). Recognizing chiefs is recognizing the order established by God, even when they are foreigners or enemies.

sens: Of large size, of considerable importance
Important in power or influence
H7227G.detail:
1. The Hebrew word rav designates what is great in size or extent. In the two provided uses, it qualifies Sidon: "Sidon the great" (Joshua 11:8 and 19:28) evokes the major Phoenician city of antiquity, renowned for its commercial importance and power.

2. More broadly, rav can qualify what is great in quantity, rank, or authority — hence its link with the notions of "chief" or "captain" mentioned in the source definition. It is the greatness that confers power and command.
H7227G.origine: Rav comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of growth and extent. The word is related to concepts of multiplicity and importance: a "great" thing is often abundant, numerous, and by extension, influential. In the Hebrew Bible, rav serves as an adjective to qualify physical greatness, quantities, or positions of prestige.
H7227G.emploi: The word rav appears twice in the provided uses, both in the book of Joshua, to qualify Sidon. This historical place was indeed a renowned Phoenician metropolis. In Joshua 11:8, during the pursuit of the defeated Canaanite kings, the Israelite army advances "up to Sidon the great." In Joshua 19:28, this same Sidon is mentioned as a geographical landmark in defining tribal boundaries. The epithet "great" emphasizes the eminent status of this city in the ancient world.
H7227G.portee: For the Christian reader, this mention of "Sidon the great" reminds us that Israel's conquests are measured against the scale of the powers of the known world. Sidon represents human splendor, earthly greatness — that which God subjects to His plan for His people. It is a subtle invitation to distinguish true greatness (that of the Lord) from that which the nations cherish.

sens: one who shoots with a bow, a soldier armed with a bow
one who hits the mark, who wounds without missing the target
image of cruelty or threat
H7228.detail:
1. The archer is primarily a warrior who fights with a bow, a feared weapon of war in antiquity. In Jeremiah 50:29, God calls for archers to be raised against Babylon, showing that they are recognizable and mobilizable soldiers — the bow is an elite weapon.
2. The word then evokes one who does not miss: his arrows "surround" the victim and pierce her, as described in Job 16:13, where the archer symbolizes an unrelenting threat that always hits its target. It is an image of deadly efficiency.
3. By extension, the archer becomes a moral image of one who wounds, destroys, or oppresses — Proverbs 26:10 compares the fool who hires the first passerby to an archer who "wounds everyone," meaning he harms all indiscriminately, without discernment.
H7228.origine: The word rav comes from the root rva ("to shoot"), which describes the action of the bow. The same root produces other words related to the archer and shooting. In Greek, the word for archer (toxotès) often translates rav in the Greek Old Testament. The word primarily evokes the concrete image of the warrior facing his drawn bow.
H7228.emploi: The word appears 3 times in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 16:13, it describes the arrows of the archer as an image of inevitable suffering — Job feels pierced like a target. In Proverbs 26:10, the archer embodies the reckless man who wounds thoughtlessly. In Jeremiah 50:29, the archers are summoned as a real force of war against Babylon. Each time, the word carries either the idea of deadly precision or that of an unrelenting threat: the archer does not miss.
H7228.portee: This word reminds the reader that the word of God can strike like an arrow — certain, precise, inevitable. It also invites reflection on divine justice: God is not a blind archer, but he hits the mark. For the Christian, it is an image of the vigilance necessary against spiritual dangers, and of trust in God's protection against threats.

sens: Of considerable size, importance, or power
One who possesses authority, a high position
H7229.detail:
1. Great designates what exceeds ordinary measure by its size, extent, or intensity. The statue that King Nebuchadnezzar sees in a dream is "immense" and of extraordinary splendor (Daniel 2:31): it strikes by its dimensions and terrifying appearance. God himself is called the "great" God who reveals the future (Daniel 2:45), emphasizing his unmatched power.
2. Great can also refer to one who occupies an important position, a position of authority. Belshazzar is the "chief" of the magicians (Daniel 4:9), and King Belshazzar organizes a "great" feast for his nobles (Daniel 5:1): the word qualifies both the high-ranking person and the event that reflects his status. It conveys the sense of "chief," one who commands or presides.
H7229.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of growth, increase, of becoming great. In biblical Hebrew, rav first denotes what is numerous or abundant (material sense of quantity), then what is important or powerful (figurative sense of authority or prestige). The word is used to describe both things (a great statue, a great feast) and people (a great king, a chief).
H7229.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the provided usages, almost exclusively in the books of Daniel and Ezra, texts from the exile and the Persian period. It describes impressive objects (the giant statue of Daniel 2) and royal prestige events (feasts, ceremonies). It also qualifies powerful people: kings are "great," the chief magicians bear this title. The context is always that of visible, earthly greatness, often linked to pagan kingdoms — Babylon, Persia — whose magnificence is praised or whose formidable power is described. The word does not carry a moral connotation in itself: it simply observes the extent or rank.
H7229.portee: This word reminds us that true greatness, in the eyes of the Bible, is not that of statues, royal feasts, or titles of chief. Daniel's visions show "great" kingdoms that will be broken and replaced by God's eternal kingdom. Meditating on this contrast helps the believer not to be impressed by the splendor of the world, but to recognize that only God is truly great and enduring.

sens: A large number of people or things gathered together
An abundant, copious quantity
The majority, what is in greater number
The intensity, strength, or greatness of something
H7230.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a numerous assembly of people or objects. When the angel promises Hagar a "numerous" offspring (Genesis 16:10), he speaks of a posterity so great that it cannot be counted.
2. It also expresses abundance, richness in quantity: Job speaks of an "abundance of wisdom" (Job 26:3), and Proverbs notes that "it is by the strength of oxen that one must have an abundance of income" (Proverbs 14:4).
3. The word can designate what predominates or surpasses: "the multitude of your iniquities" (Jeremiah 13:22) means that the sins are so numerous, so massive, that they explain the punishment.
4. It can finally qualify greatness or power: the king boasts of the "multitude of his chariots" (2 Kings 19:23), meaning his massive military strength.
H7230.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be many, to abound." It evokes the idea of a mass, an accumulation that manifests itself through its volume and weight. The word can apply to quantities (gold, silver, provisions), to people (troops, nations), or to abstract qualities (wisdom, iniquity, glory).
H7230.emploi: The word appears 144 times in the Old Testament, especially in historical narratives and wisdom literature. It is very common in the books of Kings and Chronicles to describe the wealth of kings (1 Kings 10:27, 2 Chronicles 9:27), the importance of religious assemblies (2 Chronicles 5:6), or the strength of armies (1 Samuel 13:5, Judges 7:12). In the Psalms, it expresses trust in God: "It is not by the multitude of warriors that one is victorious" (Psalms 33:16). The word can also qualify what harms (multitude of sins, Jeremiah 13:22) or what enriches (abundance of wisdom, Job 26:3).
H7230.portee: This word reminds the believer that God masters numbers and forces: he promises a multitude of descendants to Abraham, but he also teaches that strength resides in him alone, not in the multitude of warriors or riches. It is an invitation not to place trust in what appears great or massive, but in the one who holds all abundance.

sens: Increase in number, become numerous
Become great, significant in quantity or strength
Grow, abound, proliferate
H7231.detail:
1. This verb describes the action of growing in number: people, animals, objects become more numerous. In Genesis 6:1, "when men began to multiply on the face of the earth" shows the increasing population. It is a natural and visible process: things that were few become many.
2. The word also denotes becoming great, significant, or powerful in quantity. In Deuteronomy 7:7, Israel did not "surpass in number all the peoples": it is not because it is the largest number that God chose it. It conveys the idea of measurable greatness.
3. Finally, "multiply" expresses abundance, accumulation: our transgressions are "many" (Isaiah 59:12), our enemies rise "many" (Psalms 3:2). It is a flourishing, a profusion that impresses or overwhelms.
H7231.origine: The Hebrew root רבב (rav) fundamentally means "many" and "great." The verb naturally derives from it: the basic idea is that of quantity that grows, of what becomes abundant. The same root is found in the adjective rab ("numerous, great") and in related words. This root expresses everything that exceeds ordinary measure, everything that accumulates or extends.
H7231.emploi: This verb appears 21 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Psalms, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. It is used literally to describe a population or an army that grows (Genesis 6:1, Psalms 144:13: "our flocks multiply by thousands"), or to measure an impressive quantity. It is also used figuratively to express the abundance of what is negative: numerous enemies, accumulating sins, multiplied transgressions. The context determines whether the accumulation is joyful or feared.
H7231.portee: This word invites the believer to contemplate how God multiplies His blessings: a numerous offspring, an abundance of resources (Psalms 144:13). But it also confronts him with his own multiplied transgressions (Isaiah 59:12): sin also accumulates and extends. It is a reminder that everything that "multiplies" — both good and evil — reveals our condition and our need for grace.

sens: Shoot arrows, bolts, or any projectile
Launch a strike, a repeated attack
Multiply blows or shots abundantly
H7232.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to shoot an arrow or bolt from a bow: archers launch their projectiles. Genesis 49:23 speaks of archers who have launched arrows against someone with determination.
2. More broadly, it means to launch a blow, an attack — to strike repeatedly with force. The image is that of a warrior who multiplies his blows.
3. By extension, to multiply something abundantly, in great number: Psalms 18:15 says that God launched His arrows and multiplied the bolts of lightning to scatter His enemies. The verb evokes the idea of profusion and irresistible power.
H7232.origine: The verb comes from a root that suggests the idea of shooting, projecting with force. It is related to the image of the warrior or hunter who deploys his weapon — bow or arrows. The word appears rarely in the Hebrew Bible (only twice), making it a colorful and poetic verb, especially used in songs of war or victory.
H7232.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 49:23, it describes the archers who pursue someone with relentless arrows — an image of violence and repeated harassment. In Psalms 18:15, in a song of victory, it shows God launching His arrows and multiplying lightning to defeat His enemies. In both cases, the word paints a vigorous and repeated action, often with a military or divine connotation.
H7232.portee: This verb reminds us of the power of divine action: God does not strike once, He multiplies His blows with assurance and majesty. For the Christian, it is an image of God's certain victory over evil, and of His limitless strength when He acts to save His own.

sens: The number ten thousand, or an uncountable large quantity
A group or multitude organized of warriors or soldiers
A very large quantity of blessings, descendants, or riches
A numerous and impressive assembly of celestial or divine beings
H7233.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes the number ten thousand, but more broadly, a quantity so large that it cannot be precisely counted. In Judges 20:10, "ten thousand" men are referred to as a considerable military force that is divided to seek provisions. 2. In war songs (1 Samuel 18:8 and 1 Samuel 29:5), "ten thousand" contrasts with "thousand" as a much greater glory: David was attributed ten thousand victories, Saul only a thousand, which made the latter jealous. The word evokes legions, massive armies. 3. In Genesis 24:60, Rebecca receives the blessing of becoming "myriads": it is not exactly ten thousand children, but a lineage so numerous that it appears infinite, like grains of sand. 4. In Deuteronomy 33:2, Moses speaks of the "holy myriads" that surround God: these are the countless celestial beings, the angels who form His divine and formidable court.
H7233.origine: The Hebrew word רְבָבָה comes from a root that expresses the idea of multiplicity and accumulation. It is related to other Hebrew words that mean "great number" or "to multiply." The word is used in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) to translate the same numerical and symbolic realities: an immense quantity, whether counted (ten thousand precisely) or immeasurable (an infinite crowd). In biblical thought, the myriad represents less an exact number than an image of divine abundance and power.
H7233.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the historical books (Samuel, Judges) and poetic books (Psalms). In war songs (1 Samuel), it measures glory in battle: David accumulates ten thousand, which provokes Saul's jealousy. In blessings (Genesis, Leviticus), it symbolizes an endless abundant lineage. In theophanies (Deuteronomy, Psalms), it describes the angelic army that accompanies God in majesty. In Ezekiel 16:7, Jerusalem itself grows "in myriads" like a multitude of people. The meaning thus shifts from concrete number to symbolic greatness and irresistible power.
H7233.portee: This word reminds us that God, in the Bible, is not measured by small human numbers. When we speak of myriads in His presence or in His name, we emphasize the immensity of His power, His promises, and His majesty. For the believer, being blessed with a "myriad" offspring or being protected by "the myriads" of heaven is to receive or contemplate the infinite within the finite: a grace that exceeds all measure.

sens: To cover a surface by spreading fabric, blankets
To cover in order to beautify or protect
H7234.detail: 1. The word evokes the action of covering a surface — a bed, a floor — by spreading fabric, blankets, or rugs over it. It is a concrete gesture: the woman in Proverbs says, "I have adorned my bed with coverings, with Egyptian linen" (Proverbs 7:16), which literally means that she has covered her bed by spreading precious fabrics on it. 2. By extension, the verb takes on the meaning of beautifying or decorating: to adorn something is to cover it in a way that makes it more beautiful or more attractive. The primary idea remains that of covering by spreading, but it is enriched with an aesthetic intention.
H7234.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that describes the action of covering a surface by spreading something — fabric, covering, coating. This image of covering by spreading is at the heart of the word. The context of Proverbs (draperies and rugs) reflects this initial meaning well: to adorn one's bed is to cover it with fine fabrics.
H7234.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible: in Proverbs 7:16, in the discourse of the adulterous woman who seeks to seduce. She enumerates the luxuries of her chamber — a bed adorned with coverings and rugs imported from Egypt — to illustrate the comfort and allure with which she surrounds it. The context is not trivial: what adorns, covers, and beautifies can also conceal. The word remains attached to this image of a covered surface, whether to seduce or to protect.
H7234.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hide the reality of seduction and temptation: it describes it with clarity and detail. Here, the adornments of the bed are not presented as innocent, but as part of a seduction strategy. For the Christian reader, this passage invites vigilance: external allure and sensual pleasures, even if they may seem harmless, conceal spiritual traps.

sens: To become numerous, to increase in quantity
To become great or powerful
To abound, to be in great quantity
To increase, to make grow
To commit more, to transgress greatly
H7235A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of growth in number: living beings that reproduce and become numerous. When God says to the fish and the birds, "Be fruitful, multiply, and fill the waters of the seas" (Genesis 1:22), He commands these creatures to increase in number and grow in population. It is the natural image of fertility and generation.
2. The word can also mean "to become great" in the sense of greatness, power, or importance. When David takes "a large quantity of bronze" (2 Samuel 8:8), the word describes what has become considerable, abundant, imposing by its volume or mass.
3. Sometimes it marks accumulation and abundance: many things gathered or present together. During the plagues of Egypt, God says, "I will multiply my miracles" (Exodus 7:3), expressing the increase and repetition of the same phenomenon.
4. The verb can also mean "to increase" or "to make grow" in an active sense: the Law requires to multiply the tax for numerous livestock (Leviticus 25:16), meaning to increase the amount.
5. In some moral contexts, "to multiply" means "to do much" or "to transgress greatly": to multiply sins is to increase their number and severity.
H7235A.origine: The root rab means "many, great" and expresses the idea of quantity and greatness. The verb ra-vah is derived from it, expressing the movement toward this state of multiplicity: to become many, to become great. In Hebrew, the family also includes nouns like rab (the great) and rabba (the multitude). This ancient and common root describes one of the most tangible experiences: observing something that grows, reproduces, accumulates.
H7235A.emploi: This verb is among the most frequent in the Old Testament (211 occurrences). It appears as early as Genesis with the blessings of fertility (Genesis 1:22, 9:1, 17:2), where God promises a numerous offspring to Abraham and his sons. It also characterizes the growth of the people of Israel in Egypt despite slavery (Exodus 1:7, 1:12). The word extends to all increase: of goods, wealth (2 Samuel 12:2), wisdom (1 Kings 4:29), transgressions (Exodus 11:9). Proverbs uses it to express the fruits of just governance: "When the righteous increase, the people rejoice" (Proverbs 29:2). The nuance varies: beneficial growth, material accumulation, or sometimes aggravated transgression.
H7235A.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God controls growth: He blesses, He multiplies, He gives abundance. The promises made to Abraham — a numerous offspring — are expressed forcefully here. But the word also invites reflection: the multiplication of number or goods is not an end in itself; what matters is the divine blessing that accompanies it. When transgressions multiply, it is a danger and a call to repentance. The word teaches us that everything grows or diminishes according to God's will and grace.

sens: To shoot an arrow with a bow
Figuratively: to launch, to send with force
H7235B.detail: 1. To shoot with a bow means to release an arrow. Ishmael, the son of Abraham, "grew up in the wilderness and became an archer" (Genesis 21:20): this means he developed the skill of handling the bow, an essential skill for hunting and warfare in the ancient Near East. This verb describes the concrete action of projecting an arrow toward a target. 2. The meaning can extend figuratively to evoke the launching of something with force or at a distance, as one sends an arrow.
H7235B.origine: The Hebrew verb רָבָה (ravah) is formed from a root that expresses the idea of projecting, launching, or shooting. Its primary meaning is related to the action of using a bow, a typical projectile instrument of warriors and hunters in the biblical Near East. This root reflects a reality of ancient life, where mastery of the bow was a major skill.
H7235B.emploi: This verb appears once in the Bible, in Genesis 21:20, where it describes Ishmael becoming an "archer." The text emphasizes growth and learning: Ishmael grows up in the wilderness and acquires this warrior skill. It is a key moment in his story, marking his transition to adulthood and independence. The term is used in its most concrete sense, without figurative nuance in the available biblical sources.
H7235B.portee: For the reader, this image of Ishmael becoming an archer reveals how God accompanies the development of a child, even far from his family. It shows that growth includes the acquisition of practical skills and abilities: God trains His children for life, not just for the spiritual. It is a reminder that human maturation is also God's concern.

sens: Increase in size, volume, extent
Become larger, more powerful, more important
Increase, multiply in number or quantity
H7236.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to become larger in dimensions. The tree in Daniel "had become great and strong, its height reached to the heavens" (Daniel 4:11): it grew, it extended upwards. The hair of Nebuchadnezzar grew "like the feathers of eagles" (Daniel 4:33): it lengthened.
2. The word also applies to power and authority: the king became "great and strong, whose greatness increased and reached to the heavens" (Daniel 4:22). It is no longer just the size of the body, but the extent of dominion that grows.
3. It can denote an increase in number or quantity: the king received "many" gifts (Daniel 2:48). Here the word expresses abundance, multiplication.
H7236.origine: The Hebrew verb רבּה (revah) belongs to the family of words that describe increase and enlargement. It evokes the concrete image of something that pushes, rises, becomes larger — like a growing tree or a developing body. This verb has produced nouns like "greatness" and "multitude" in the Hebrew Bible.
H7236.emploi: This verb appears five times in the book of Daniel, always in Aramaic (the language of this section). It primarily describes the growth of Daniel's symbolic tree (chapters 4:11 and 4:20), the increasing power of King Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4:22), and phenomena of physical multiplication such as the growth of the king's hair (Daniel 4:33). A figurative use also appears with "many gifts" (Daniel 2:48), where the verb expresses abundance rather than gradual growth.
H7236.portee: This verb invites us to meditate on what grows and increases in our lives and in the world: the power of human kingdoms grows, but it remains unstable and subject to God. It can decrease as suddenly as it has grown, like the tree of Nebuchadnezzar. It reminds us that only God's kingdom grows in a way that lasts and will never pass away.

sens: Capital of the Ammonite, beyond the Jordan
Royal fortress and center of Ammonite power
Subject of military conflicts between Israel and the Ammonites
Target of prophetic judgments against the nations
H7237.detail:
1. Rabbah is the main city of the kingdom of Ammon, located east of the Jordan, in the lands that correspond to present-day Jordan. It was a fortified and well-established city: Deuteronomy 3:11 mentions a gigantic iron bed belonging to Og, king of Bashan, which was kept there as a testimony.
2. The city was the seat of Ammonite power, a royal residence where kings and their officials resided. Jeremiah 49:3 calls it "the royal city" of this people, showing its political and military importance.
3. Rabbah became the theater of wars between Israel and the Ammonites. David and Joab conducted a long siege there during which the incident of Bathsheba occurred (2 Samuel 11-12). Joab eventually took the "royal city" (2 Samuel 12:26-29), almost completely destroying it (1 Chronicles 20:1).
4. The prophets Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Amos all announce the ruin of Rabbah as punishment against Ammon: Jeremiah 49:3 cries to the "daughters of Rabbah" to mourn, for God's judgment is falling upon the entire Ammonite nation.
H7237.origine: The Hebrew name Rabbah literally means "the Great," reflecting its status as a major capital. It comes from the root rabbâ (ר-ב-ה), which means "to become great, to be numerous." It was indeed the largest city in the Ammonite territory, dominating regional trade and political life.
H7237.emploi: Rabbah appears fourteen times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical and prophetic books. It is first mentioned as a well-established city at the time of conquest (Deuteronomy 3:11, Joshua 13:25), then becomes famous from the reign of David as the theater of war against the Ammonites (2 Samuel 11:1, 12:26-29). David commands the siege from Jerusalem while Joab leads the troops. During the exile, the prophets cite it as an example of God's judgment on Israel's enemies: Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Amos all refer to it to announce its destruction and the end of the Ammonite nation.
H7237.portee: Rabbah embodies in biblical history the earthly power that God humiliates according to His justice. The destruction of this great royal fortress reminds us that no empire, no fortification escapes divine judgment. For the reader, it is an invitation not to fear powerful nations: God judges and breaks them according to His will, and His justice is exercised over all without exception.

sens: Splendor and power of a king or empire
Brilliance, magnificence, and prestige that inspire respect
Scope of the dominion and authority of a sovereign
H7238.detail:
1. Greatness is primarily the visible splendor and concrete power of a king or empire: it is what strikes the eye and commands respect. In Daniel 4:22, King Nebuchadnezzar saw his greatness increase and rise to the heavens, an image of his growing power that fills all dimensions of heaven and earth.
2. It also denotes magnificence, what makes someone or something worthy of admiration and reverence. In Daniel 5:18-19, Nebuchadnezzar received from God "the empire, the greatness, the glory, and the magnificence," and this greatness was so imposing that peoples, entire nations trembled before him.
3. Finally, it is the scope of dominion: the extent of reign and authority over others, the ability to elevate or lower, to give life or death. In Daniel 7:27, the greatness of the kingdoms of the earth is given to the people of the saints, symbolizing the ultimate victory of God's reign.
H7238.origine: The Hebrew word רְבוּ (rebou) comes from the root רבה (rbh) which means "to become great," "to increase," "to multiply." This root first describes physical or numerical growth, then extends to the prestige and power that "grow." The word expresses the idea of amplification: something grows in extent, strength, brilliance. This family of roots often appears in the Old Testament to speak of the increase of the people, prosperity, or divine majesty.
H7238.emploi: The word רְבוּ appears five times in the book of Daniel (4:22, 4:36, 5:18, 5:19, 7:27), always related to royal or divine power. It denotes the greatness of King Nebuchadnezzar, given and then taken away by God according to the circumstances of his pride or submission. In Daniel 4:22, it is at the peak of its growth; in Daniel 7:27, it passes from earthly reign to the eternal reign of the saints. The context is always that of political power and absolute authority, but also of divine sovereignty that distributes and takes back greatness according to His will.
H7238.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that all earthly greatness — political power, wealth, prestige — comes from God and belongs to Him. Nebuchadnezzar had to learn through humiliation that his power was merely divine loan. But even more, Daniel prophesies that the ultimate greatness, the eternal reign, belongs to the people of the saints: the final victory will never be that of the kings of this world, but that of the Most High God and those who obey Him.

sens: The number ten thousand, a thousand times ten
A very large number, an innumerable multitude
H7239.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the number ten thousand in its strict sense. It is found in the census of peoples and inventories of treasures: when Ezra counts the assembly of the return from exile, he enumerates "forty-two thousand three hundred sixty people" (Ezra 2:64). It is a concrete and precise number, used to express large quantities.
2. In a secondary sense, ten thousand evokes a multitude so considerable that it exceeds what can be counted or even imagined. In this figurative register, the word paints the idea of extreme abundance, almost inexhaustible. Thus, when the Bible speaks of an army or a crowd numbering tens of thousands of soldiers or people, it emphasizes less the exact number than the overwhelming numerical superiority.
H7239.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that refers to the idea of quantity and mass. It belongs to the same family as the Aramaic word "ribbo," which is spelled identically. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates this same number for inventories and censuses, thus remaining faithful to its original usage in Hebrew.
H7239.emploi: This word appears in several biblical contexts, always to express very important quantities. It is found in the historical accounts of the return from exile (Ezra, Nehemiah), where it quantifies the crowds and treasures in gold and silver. It is also encountered in warrior contexts (Daniel 11:12), where it measures the size of armies. In Psalm 68:18 and Jonah 4:11, it takes on a broader dimension: it becomes almost an image of what cannot be counted, of infinity. The usage remains constant: it is always a large number, but sometimes poetically expressed as an image of excess and abundance.
H7239.portee: For the believing reader, this number reminds us that God governs countless multitudes and directs the history of peoples numbering in the tens of thousands. It is also an invitation to feel, in the face of these overwhelming figures, the magnitude of the divine plan and His ability to order multitudes.

sens: An immense, incalculable number: ten thousand times ten thousand
H7240.detail: 1. This word designates a considerable number, obtained by multiplying ten thousand by ten thousand. In Daniel's vision, it serves to express a quantity so enormous that it exceeds calculation: the heavenly beings standing before the throne of God are so numerous that they cannot be counted. The text plays on the accumulation of large numbers to suggest infinity (Daniel 7:10).
H7240.origine: The Hebrew word ribbo means first "ten thousand," the largest unit of number that the Hebrews commonly used. In Aramaic, the form ribbo retains this meaning. Multiplying ten thousand by ten thousand ("ten thousand millions") was the biblical way of saying "a multitude without number," far beyond what can be counted. It is a poetic device to evoke infinity.
H7240.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 7:10, in the grand description of the throne of the Ancient of Days. Daniel sees a river of fire flowing before the divine throne, and the heavenly creatures who serve Him are in an incalculable number. The use of the plural "ten thousand millions" accumulates the figures to reinforce the idea of a multitude that no number can truly express: it is the countless throng of the heavenly armies.
H7240.portee: This vision shows the reader that the court of heaven overflows with an incomprehensible power and majesty. The believer discovers that God is served by a multitude so great that it escapes all measure, which reinforces the assurance that the Almighty governs the universe with absolute wisdom and strength.

sens: Water falling from the sky in generous quantity, capable of watering the earth and bringing life to it
Blessing and fertility that God sends to make the harvest grow
Divine influence that spreads and transforms, as raindrops nourish the greenery
Divine punishment withheld when the people turn away from God
H7241.detail:
1. The word describes abundant, generous rain that falls in numerous drops and waters the entire earth. It is a life-giving rain, the one that makes seeds sprout and greens the meadows after drought: it "soaks" the furrows of the farmer and blesses his seed (Psalms 65:11).
2. This rain is also a symbol of divine blessing, the gift that only God can grant. It nourishes without human effort: the remnant of Jacob will be "like dew from the Lord, like droplets on the grass" that "do not rely on man" (Micah 5:6).
3. Figuratively, abundant rain represents the teaching and divine word that spread and penetrate hearts: "Let my word fall like dew, like showers on the greenery" (Deuteronomy 32:2).
4. Finally, its absence is a punishment: the withholding of rain marks God's judgment against an unfaithful people. Jeremiah proclaims: "The rains have been withheld," and asks: "Is it not You, Lord our God?" who controls the rain (Jeremiah 3:3; 14:22).
H7241.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of falling drop by drop, accumulating in quantity. It specifically designates rich and beneficial rain, not mere dew or a passing shower. In biblical imagery, abundant rain always embodies what comes from above to transform and revive the parched earth.
H7241.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the Psalms and the prophets. It is used literally to describe the agricultural benefits of rain (Deuteronomy 32:2; Psalms 65:11; 72:6), but also as an image of the prophetic word that spreads (Deuteronomy 32:2). It also appears in judgment oracles, where its absence signifies divine wrath (Jeremiah 3:3; 14:22). The Segond translates it sometimes as "rain," sometimes as "shower" or "droplets," depending on the poetic context.
H7241.portee: This abundant rain teaches us that all blessing comes from God alone, not from our efforts or false deities. It invites us to receive the divine word as rain that transforms and revives the soul. It also reminds us that the absence of blessing is never by chance: it is God who withholds or grants according to the state of the people's heart.

sens: Chain or metal ornament worn around the neck
Adornment of prestige and honor
Mark of distinction and power
H7242.detail:
1. The necklace is a chain or metal ornament — usually gold — that is worn around the neck as jewelry. In Genesis 41:42, Pharaoh places a gold necklace around Joseph's neck to publicly honor him.
2. The necklace symbolizes distinction and honor: it is a visible mark of prestige and favor from the one who gives it. Joseph receives this necklace along with fine clothes and authority over Egypt, showing that he becomes someone important.
3. The necklace can also represent the ornament and beauty added to someone or something. In Ezekiel 16:11, God describes adorning Jerusalem with necklaces, bracelets, and other ornaments: the image evokes the tenderness with which one beautifies the beloved.
H7242.origine: The Hebrew word rāvid comes from a root that evokes the idea of sewing or braiding together threads or chains. The necklace is thus etymologically what is braided or united to form an ornament. This type of ornament was common in the ancient Near East, worn by the great, the kings, and those to be honored.
H7242.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 41:42, Joseph receives a gold necklace from Pharaoh as a sign of his appointment to a high office: it is a public reward and a badge of the power conferred upon him. In Ezekiel 16:11, the necklace is part of the ornaments with which God symbolically adorns Jerusalem to show the love and favor with which He has covered her. In both contexts, the necklace is linked to honor, dignity, and the relationship of favor between the giver and the receiver.
H7242.portee: The necklace reminds us that God can elevate those who are faithful to Him and entrust them with responsibilities, as He did for Joseph in Egypt. It also shows us that God adorns His beloved with beauty and dignity, not as a reward earned, but as a gift of His tenderness. This image invites us to recognize in ourselves the marks of honor and grace that God bestows upon us.

sens: Which comes after three others in an order of succession
Part divided into four equal parts
Generation or degree of kinship in the fourth rank
Measure of capacity or volume equal to a quarter
H7243.detail:
1. The fourth day: the natural order of things. In Genesis 1:19, it is the day when God creates the luminaries (sun, moon, stars). The word simply designates what occupies the number four position in an ordered series. It can apply to a child (the fourth son of Josiah in 1 Chronicles 3:15), to a year of reign (1 Kings 6:1: the fourth year of Solomon), or to a rank in a list.
2. Quarter or portion: a fraction that divides the whole into four. Numbers 15:4 speaks of a quarter of hin of oil for the offering: it is not about the number four, but a measure equal to a quarter of the container. It is also a quarter of a shekel or a quarter of an ephah.
3. Successive generation: in Genesis 15:16, the expression "to the fourth generation" means to the fourth descendant. It is a measure of distance in genealogical time.
4. Fixed rank or place: Ezekiel 10:14 describes the four flying creatures around the divine throne, each having a fourth identical face. The word emphasizes the regular and complete ordering of the cosmos according to divine will.
H7243.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root שׁרבע (arba, four), with the suffix -i which makes the adjective ordinal (like French "three" becomes "third"). It expresses the idea of fourth rank in a numbered series from one to four. The same root produces arba (four), arbaim (forty), arbaà (to square), and is found in words like "crossroads" (place where four paths meet). It is a very ancient word, common throughout biblical Hebrew and even in Aramaic (revi'ay).
H7243.emploi: The word appears 55 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Pentateuch, historical and prophetic books. It can designate a rank pure and simple (fourth son, fourth year, fourth day) or a fraction (quarter of measure). In Exodus and Numbers, it often recurs in the prescriptions of offerings and measures of worship, where a quarter of hin or a quarter of ephah is precise and repeatable. In the books of Jeremiah, it marks key years of the reigns of kings (the fourth year of Jehoiakim). Sometimes it carries a theological nuance: the fourth generation in Genesis 15:16 and Exodus 20:5 symbolizes the time before God's judgment on a family line. In the context of counting or succession, it remains purely descriptive.
H7243.portee: This word reminds us that the order created by God is also expressed in time, generations, and measures. When the Bible speaks of the fourth year or the fourth generation, it teaches us that God counts, that He waits patiently or executes His judgment according to a precise calendar. The prescriptions for offerings of a quarter of hin show that even in worship, mathematical regularity reflects divine order and holiness. For the reader, it is an invitation to see God as master of time and measure, not as someone who acts capriciously.

sens: Which comes after three others in an order of succession
Which occupies the number four rank in a listing
Element that closes a series of four things
H7244.detail: 1. The word simply designates what comes in fourth position in an ordered sequence. In the Book of Daniel, it qualifies a kingdom that follows three other kingdoms in the prophetic vision (Daniel 2:40: "There will be a fourth kingdom, strong as iron"), and likewise an animal in the night visions (Daniel 7:7: "there was a fourth beast, dreadful, terrible, and exceedingly strong"). 2. It is a word of pure numerical arrangement: it precisely situates the place of a thing among four. When Daniel "looks" or "desires to know the truth," it is always on this fourth term that he focuses (Daniel 3:25: "the appearance of the fourth is like that of a son of the gods"), marking its particular importance in the series. 3. The prophetic context gives it a special significance: the fourth element stands out from the first three, often by a force or strangeness surpassing the others (Daniel 7:23: "different from all the kingdoms").
H7244.origine: It is the Aramaic from the Book of Daniel. The word comes from the root שׁמע (raba), "four," and carries the suffix -ɪ which marks the ordinal (the rank in the series). In classical Hebrew, the equivalent word is רְבִיעִי (revi'i) — same form, same meaning. It is simply the number four put into ordinal form, like "first," "second" in French.
H7244.emploi: The word appears only in the Book of Daniel, five times, always in chapters 2, 3, and 7. It describes the four kingdoms of the prophetic vision and the four beasts of the night visions. Daniel repeats it to emphasize the importance of the fourth term: in Daniel 2:40 and 7:23, he speaks of the "fourth" kingdom; in Daniel 7:7, 7:19, 7:23, of the "fourth" beast. What stands out is that each time the fourth is distinctly different from the first three by its raw power (iron, iron teeth, bronze claws) and its devastating character. The word remains a simple ordinal, but the rhetoric of the visions makes it a central axis.
H7244.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites recognition that God orders the events of history according to a precise and numbered plan. The "fourth" is the last and often the most fearsome of the kingdoms, reminding us that earthly power has a limit — it does not exceed God's count. It is a lesson in trust: even empires that seem invincible are contained within a design that precedes them.

sens: City of Issachar
H7245.detail: Rabbith is a city in the territory of Issachar, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of cities assigned to Issachar during the division of the promised land (Joshua 19:20).
H7245.origine: The name Rabbith comes from a Hebrew root meaning "multitude" or "abundance," which perhaps suggests that this city was an important population center or a gathering place.
H7245.emploi: Rabbith appears only once in the biblical text, in Joshua 19:20, where it is listed among the cities entrusted to the tribe of Issachar during the distribution of lands after the conquest of Canaan. It is mentioned between Kishion and Abets. Nothing else is known about its history or significance in the life of Israel.

sens: to cook in hot oil
to mix while stirring during cooking
H7246.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to cook food in hot oil. This is how the Segond translates this word: the grain offerings are "fried" in oil, as in Leviticus 6:14 where the fine flour is brought "fried," or in Leviticus 7:12 where "cakes of fried fine flour mixed with oil" are mentioned.
2. The word also evokes the action of mixing and stirring: frying implies stirring the dough or food in boiling oil so that it cooks evenly and does not burn, as when preparing a treat by constantly stirring.
H7246.origine: This Hebrew verb expresses the idea of mixing, of stirring together. Its image is one of movement: one stirs, one mixes, one shakes. It appears three times in the sacrificial laws, always to describe the cooking of the offerings presented to God. The word belongs to the vocabulary of Levitical worship.
H7246.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Bible, exclusively in the context of grain offerings and cakes to the Lord. In Leviticus 6:14, it describes how the grain offering of fine flour must be "fried" in oil. In Leviticus 7:12, it qualifies the "cakes of fried fine flour" brought during a thank offering. In 1 Chronicles 23:29, it appears in the enumeration of the tasks of the Levites, who prepared "fried cakes" among other things. The word always applies to the preparation of foods consecrated to worship.
H7246.portee: This verb reminds us that the worship offered to God engages all details, including how to prepare the food: God has prescribed how His offerings should be cooked. This shows that piety is not a purely spiritual matter, but is concretely expressed in ordinary gestures, cooking, and the work of hands. The care taken to properly fry a cake of offering was a form of obedience and respect towards God.

sens: Location on the eastern border of Israel
H7247G.detail: Riblah is a city mentioned in the description of the borders of the land promised to Israel. It is located east of Ain, in the eastern region, and serves as a landmark to delineate the southeastern boundary of the country (Numbers 34:11). The name evokes the idea of fertility, suggesting that this area was well-watered and productive.
H7247G.origine: The Hebrew name Riblah (רִבְלָה) literally means "fertility" or "abundance," derived from a root that evokes wealth and agricultural abundance. This root reflects the geographical and agricultural characteristics of the region.
H7247G.emploi: Riblah appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 34:11, in the context of the precise enumeration of the borders of the territory that Israel is to conquer and occupy under the leadership of Joshua. This detailed description served as an official reference for the delineation of the lands to be divided among the tribes.

sens: city in Syria located in the land of Hamath
strategic point on the road between Babylon and Palestine
place of condemnation and execution of prisoners
H7247H.detail: Riblah was an important city in the land of Hamath, Syria, situated on the major trade and military route connecting Babylon to Palestine (2 Kings 23:33). It served as a headquarters or royal residence for conquerors: it was there that Pharaoh Necho held King Josiah in chains, and later that the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar established his seat and pronounced sentences against the captives of Judah (Jeremiah 39:5). The name evokes the fertility of the place, as it was located in a fertile region. It is also the place where the sons of Zedekiah and the leaders of Judah were executed in the presence of the king of Babylon (Jeremiah 39:6).
H7247H.origine: The name Riblah (דִּבְלָה in Aramaic, diblah) means "fertility" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes abundance and agricultural wealth. The place, although remote from Judah and Babylon, was a prosperous oasis on the routes of the Euphrates, which explains why it served as a seat of power during conquests.
H7247H.emploi: Riblah appears ten times in the Bible, primarily in 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39-52, and only in accounts of conquest and captivity. Pharaoh Necho held Josiah prisoner there around 610 B.C. (2 Kings 23:33), and then, a few decades later, Nebuchadnezzar established his headquarters there during the siege of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. It is in this city that the Babylonian king pronounced his sentences against Zedekiah and the survivors of Judah, and where the execution of the princes of Judah took place (2 Kings 25:6, 21; Jeremiah 39:5-6). The city is still mentioned as the place where the justice (or vengeance) of the conqueror was exercised upon the defeated.

sens: Babylonian officer during the time of Nebuchadnezzar
H7248.detail: Rab-mag is a title or name of a Babylonian officer that appears during the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. The term designates a high official of Nebuchadnezzar, probably the chief of the magicians or diviners, or chief of the Babylonian princes — scholars debate the exact meaning of the title. He is among the military and administrative leaders sent by the king of Babylon to take the city and carry off the captives.
H7248.origine: The Hebrew word rav-mag is composed of two elements: rav ("great," "chief") and mag (related to the magicians, scholars, and diviners of the Babylonian court). It is a Babylonian administrative title, not a personal Hebrew name. The term reflects the hierarchy and functions of the Babylonian imperial system.
H7248.emploi: Rab-mag appears twice in the Bible, both times in the book of Jeremiah during the final siege of Jerusalem. In Jeremiah 39:3, he is among the Babylonian officers who sit at the Middle Gate after the city is taken. In Jeremiah 39:13, he is mentioned again, this time ordering the release of the prophet Jeremiah on the orders of Nebuchadnezzar. These two mentions show a high-ranking officer, responsible for both military administration and the execution of royal decisions.

sens: High dignitary of the court of the king of Assyria
Chief of the eunuchs of the Assyrian palace
H7249G.detail:
1. Rab-Saris is a title of a high official at the court of the king of Assyria. The name literally means "chief of the eunuchs" (rab = chief, saris = eunuch), but it actually designates a person of very high rank, not just a responsible official of the harem. It is a prestigious title comparable to that of minister or secretary of state.
2. In the biblical context, Rab-Saris is one of the three high officers sent by the king of Assyria to negotiate the surrender of Jerusalem alongside Tartan and Rabshakeh (2 Kings 18:17). His presence shows the importance of this embassy: only the highest dignitaries of the Assyrian kingdom were entrusted with such a diplomatic and military mission.
H7249G.origine: The Hebrew name רַב־סָרִיס (rav-saris) is a composition: rab means "chief" or "great" in Hebrew, and saris comes from Akkadian and refers to a court eunuch or officer. This Assyrian administrative title was borrowed by the Hebrews, who recognized the structures of foreign power. The word "rab" appears elsewhere in Hebrew in other official titles (for example, "Rab-Mag," chief of the magicians).
H7249G.emploi: Rab-Saris appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 18:17. He is mentioned as one of the three high officers sent by the Assyrian king Sennacherib to besiege Jerusalem during the reign of King Hezekiah. This moment constitutes one of the most serious crises in the history of the Kingdom of Judah: the Assyrians had already conquered the Kingdom of Israel to the north and now threatened the capital of the southern kingdom.
