Rab-Saris participates in this negotiation for surrender, which will not succeed due to divine intervention.
H7249G.portee: The mention of Rab-Saris recalls the historical reality of God's judgment upon His people: Judah is confronted with the imperial power of Assyria, and its survival depends solely on divine intervention. This character embodies the arrogant earthly authority in the face of the sovereignty of the God of Israel.

sens: Title of a high Babylonian official
Chief of the eunuchs or royal officer
H7249H.detail: Rab-Saris is a title or name of a Babylonian function, not a mere personal name. It designates a high dignitary of the royal palace of Babylon, responsible for the eunuchs of the court. This title appears during the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C., when Nebuchadnezzar invaded the city: Rab-Saris is among the generals who present themselves at the Middle Gate after the capture of the fortress (Jeremiah 39:3). He is one of the trusted officers of the Babylonian king, tasked with leading the captives and the orders of the monarch (Jeremiah 39:13). His importance in the military and administrative hierarchy of Babylon makes him a key figure in the siege.
H7249H.origine: The name is composed of two Hebrew words: "rav" (ר־ב) means "great" or "chief," and "saris" (סָרִיס) refers to a eunuch or palace officer. Together, "rav-saris" literally means "great of the eunuchs" or "chief of the eunuchs." It is a bureaucratic title of the Babylonian court, borrowed from the Assyrian and Babylonian administration. Other similar titles appear in the Bible, such as Rab-Mag (chief of the magicians) or Rab-Shakeh (chief of the cupbearers).
H7249H.emploi: Rab-Saris is mentioned twice in the book of Jeremiah, in chapters 39 to 40. He first appears in Jeremiah 39:3, among the Babylonian officers who enter Jerusalem after its fall. He is named alongside other generals and dignitaries sent by Nebuchadnezzar. Then, in Jeremiah 39:13, we see him giving orders to Gedaliah and others regarding the custody of the prophet Jeremiah: the Babylonian king had indeed instructed his officers to keep Jeremiah safe. These two occurrences show him both as a military figure and as an executor of royal orders.
H7249H.portee: Rab-Saris embodies the brutal and organized power of Babylon, an instrument of divine judgment upon Jerusalem. His presence underscores that the fall of the city is not an accident, but the execution of a plan set by God; at the same time, his respect for Jeremiah (obeying the king's orders to protect him) shows that even in the midst of defeat, the word of God and His messengers are not without protection. This detail reminds Israel that foreign domination has limits set by the Lord.

sens: To stretch out to rest
To unite carnally, particularly in an illicit or unnatural manner
H7250.detail:
1. The verb describes the physical action of lying down, stretching out for rest or sleep. This is the most basic and bodily sense of the word.
2. In the three biblical usages provided, the word takes on a sexual meaning: it denotes carnal union, particularly in contexts of prohibition. In Leviticus 18:23 and 20:16, it refers to relations between a woman and a beast, an act presented as a defilement and severely punished. In Leviticus 19:19, the same verb applies to the mating of animals of different kinds, which the Law forbids. The word evokes each time a transgression of the order that God has established.
H7250.origine: The Hebrew verb רָבַע (ra.va) comes from a root that denotes the act of lying down or stretching out horizontally. Its primary meaning is simply physical and neutral. However, in the context of the purity laws of Leviticus, it takes on a moral and religious charge: it names illicit or abnormal sexual union as a confusion of the created order.
H7250.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in Leviticus, at the heart of the Mosaic purity laws. In Leviticus 18:23 and 20:16, it denotes the abomination of a woman who lies with a beast, an act punished by death for both the woman and the animal. In Leviticus 19:19, it applies to the forbidden mating of animals of two different species. These three occurrences show that the Law governs not only human sexual life but also the natural and animal order, all of which fall under the ritual and moral purity that God requires of Israel.
H7250.portee: These verses remind the Christian reader that God has established an order in creation — boundaries between species, between the pure and the impure, between human and animal — and that He expects His people to respect these limits. Far beyond the ancient letter, these texts invite us to recognize that human sexuality is not a lawless domain: it is situated within God's order and can only be exercised within the limits He sets.

sens: Having four equal sides and four right angles
Having a regular and symmetrical shape
H7251.detail: 1. The word first describes the geometric shape: an object or surface whose four sides are of equal length and whose angles are right. This is the most concrete image. The altar of burnt offerings had a square base, five cubits long and five cubits wide (Exodus 27:1), and the altar of incense was also square, one cubit by one cubit (Exodus 30:2). In Solomon's temple, the beams of the doors formed square frames on each level (1 Kings 7:5). 2. Figuratively, the word more broadly designates what is regular and well-proportioned, balanced in its structure. The courtyard of the temple measured by Ezekiel formed a perfect square of one hundred cubits by one hundred cubits (Ezekiel 40:47), symbolizing divine order and the holiness of the place. This geometric shape appears as a sign of what is just, measured, and in accordance with God's plan.
H7251.origine: The Hebrew root *raba'* means literally 'to form in four,' as it is related to the number four (*arba'*). In Hebrew, geometry and number are often linked: the word expresses the idea of a figure whose four elements are equal and ordered. This root is used in contexts where divine order and measure are essential.
H7251.emploi: This word appears 12 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in passages that describe the precise dimensions of the tabernacle, its furnishings, and the temple. Exodus 27, 30, and 37-39 show it applied to the altar and the breastplate of the high priest, both of which are square. The account of the temple's construction in 1 Kings 7 uses it to describe the architecture of the doors and windows. Ezekiel, who describes the future temple with meticulous precision, uses this word for the courtyard, the altar, and various dimensions of the sacred building (Ezekiel 40, 41, 43, 45). The context is always that of sanctification and order: sacred objects or worship spaces are square, thus marking that they reflect divine order and perfection.
H7251.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God loves order and measure. The precise dimensions of the tabernacle and the temple are never unnecessary details: they manifest the holiness of God, who is never chaotic or approximate. The square, symmetrical, and regular shape symbolizes the stability and perfection of what comes from God. It is an invitation to recognize that our God is a God of beauty, structure, and clarity.

sens: To stretch out on a bed or on the ground to rest or sleep
To be extended, lying in a horizontal position
H7252.detail:
1. To lie down means to stretch out on a bed or on the ground to sleep or rest. It is the action of moving from a standing position to a lying position. In Psalm 139:3, the psalmist says to God: 'You know when I walk and when I lie down' — this ordinary gesture of lying down symbolizes the intimate moments of daily life, those when one is vulnerable and alone.
2. To be lying down is the state of being extended, lying horizontally. It is not just the action of lying down, but the state that follows, the rest of the body on a bed or the ground. The psalmist expresses thereby that God knows all his postures, all his states, from movement to rest.
H7252.origine: The Hebrew verb רֶבַע (rebaa) evokes the image of a body that stretches out, that lies down. Its root is related to the idea of spreading out, of being horizontal. The family of the word in Hebrew speaks of rest, relaxation, and the vulnerability of the human body in a lying position.
H7252.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Psalm 139:3. In this context, it describes one of the most ordinary and intimate gestures of human life: the moment one lies down to sleep. The psalmist uses it to express God's omniscience — He knows not only our great actions (walking) but also our moments of rest, our private and intimate life.
H7252.portee: This word reminds us that God is aware of every aspect of our lives, including our most ordinary and private moments. There is no gesture, no rest, no moment of weakness or solitude that escapes His attention. It is both a word of comfort — we are never alone — and a call to humility: we live constantly under the gaze of a God who loves us.

sens: Face, edge, or direction of an object that has four parts
A quarter of a measure or quantity
H7253.detail:
1. The word designates one of the four faces, edges, or directions of an object that is square or has four distinct sides. In Ezekiel's vision, the heavenly creatures "went in their four sides" (Ezekiel 1:17), which means they could move in all four directions without needing to turn. The altar described in Ezekiel 43:16 "was square by its four sides," emphasizing that each of the four edges was equal to the others.
2. The word can also mean a quarter of a measure, the fourth part of a whole. When a lamb was offered as a sacrifice, a "quarter of a hin of olive oil" was offered (Exodus 29:40) and "a drink offering of a quarter of a hin of wine": these are precise measurements, each equivalent to a quarter of a hin. Similarly, in 1 Samuel 9:8, the servant possessed "a quarter of a shekel of silver," meaning a quarter of the weight of silver called a shekel.
H7253.origine: The Hebrew word revá comes from a root that fundamentally means "four." It is directly related to the word for "four" (arba'), and its primitive meaning refers to something that is divided into four parts or has four sides. The form of the word indicates something that is by nature or by construction quadrangular. This root is common in Semitic languages.
H7253.emploi: This word appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in contexts of detailed description: in the laws concerning sacrifices in Leviticus and Exodus (measures of flour and oil), in historical accounts (the currency in 1 Samuel), and especially in the prophetic visions of Ezekiel where he describes the heavenly creatures and the temple altar. The meaning varies slightly depending on the context: it can refer to the four directions of movement (the creatures of the divine throne), the four edges of a square object (the altar), or simply a quantifiable fraction (a quarter of a measure or weight).
H7253.portee: This word reminds us that precision matters in worship: each offering, each measure was calculated accurately according to God's law. In Ezekiel's visions, the four sides and four directions emphasize the perfection and omnipresence of God's throne, which sees and acts in all directions. It is an invitation to respect the order and measure that God establishes for our approach to Him.

sens: One of the five kings of Midian
Midianite prince vassal to King Sihon
H7254.detail: 1. Reba was one of the five kings of Midian, killed by the Israelites during their conquest of the Midian territory, at the time when the prophet Balaam also fell (Numbers 31:8). 2. He was also counted among the princes of Midian who were subject to Sihon, king of the Amorites, and who lived in the land (Joshua 13:21). His name means "four" in Hebrew, which was common as a king's name in this context of the ancient Near East.
H7254.origine: The name Reba literally means "four" in Hebrew. It was a name of a Midianite king, borne by one of the five rulers who governed the territories east of the Jordan during the time of the Exodus and the conquest.
H7254.emploi: Reba appears twice in the Bible, both times during the conquest of the land of Canaan. He is mentioned in Numbers 31:8 as one of the five kings of Midian killed during the campaign led by Moses against Midian, after the incident with Balaam. He reappears in Joshua 13:21, where he is identified as a prince (and no longer a king) of Midian, under the domain of Sihon, king of the Amorites. This evolution of the title suggests that he held a high rank in the political structure of that region.

sens: one of the four equal parts of a whole
a unit of capacity for liquids or solids
a small quantity of something
H7255.detail: 1. A quarter is one of the four equal parts of a whole: when something is divided into four, the quarter is one portion (Numbers 23:10: "the quarter of Israel" means a quarter of the people). 2. A quarter is also a unit of measure, particularly for dry or semi-dry materials: in 2 Kings 6:25, the "quarter of a kab" (the kab being a container) refers to a very small quantity, sold at a high price during the famine. 3. By extension, the word evokes a tiny or precious portion, especially in a context of scarcity.
H7255.origine: The Hebrew word רֹבַע (ro'va) comes from the root רבע (r-b-'), which fundamentally means "to be the fourth" or "to count by four." This root expresses the idea of division into four parts. The word thus naturally designates the fraction obtained: a quarter.
H7255.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Numbers 23:10, Balaam speaks of the "quarter of Israel" to designate a part of the people; the meaning is that of a portion or division. In 2 Kings 6:25, during the siege of Samaria, a "quarter of a kab" of dove's dung becomes a precious commodity and is sold for a high price: the word takes on the value of a very small measure. In both contexts, the quarter expresses either an arithmetic division or a concrete unit of measure.
H7255.portee: This word reminds us that God knows His people in detail: even when divided into portions, each part matters in God's eyes. It also shows how the Bible speaks of tiny quantities, revealing that in extreme famine, the smallest measures become precious and valuable.

sens: The rank of four in a succession
The fourth generation of a family descending from an ancestor
H7256.detail:
1. This word simply designates the number four and its order in a series: it is what comes after the third. It applies to duration in generations, that is, in successive family lineages.

2. In the Bible, it specifically refers to the fourth generation of the same family, that is, the great-great-grandchildren of an ancestor. Exodus 20:5 speaks of the iniquity of the fathers that is punished "to the third and fourth generation" of those who hate God: this means that the consequences of a father's sin can reach his children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren.
H7256.origine: This word comes from the Hebrew root that means "four." It is the ordinal adjective formed from this number: just as one says "third" for the number three in French, Hebrew says "fourth" (rib.be.a) for four. This is a common way in Hebrew to form ordinal numbers from cardinal numbers.
H7256.emploi: The word appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible, each time related to God's justice and mercy. It appears in four parallel or very close texts: Exodus 20:5, Exodus 34:7, Numbers 14:18, and Deuteronomy 5:9. All state the same principle: God punishes the iniquities of the fathers to the third or fourth generation, thus showing that sin has effects that extend beyond the guilty party themselves, but also that this scope is not infinite. This repetition emphasizes the importance of this principle in Israel's theology.
H7256.portee: This term invites the reader to meditate on two realities. First, the actions of the fathers have real consequences for the children: our choices do not concern us alone. Secondly, this limit to the fourth generation tempers fear: the curse is not eternal or unlimited. God remains a God of justice and mercy, who punishes but also "keeps His love to a thousand generations" (Exodus 34:7), reminding us that His goodness far surpasses His judgment.

sens: To lie down, to recline for rest or sleep
To be laid out, to remain stretched out
To remain still in ambush or lurking
To rest peacefully, to enjoy calm security
To weigh on someone like a burden or a threat
H7257.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word is the action of lying down horizontally: to lie down to sleep or rest. Job 11:19 states it clearly: "You will lie down without anyone to make you afraid," describing the rest of the righteous. It is the simple and concrete image of the body lying horizontally.
2. From this comes the idea of being extended, laid out in place. Isaiah 11:6 beautifully illustrates this: "the leopard will lie down with the goat" — wild beasts rest peacefully next to their usual prey, all danger dissipated.
3. The word can also mean to remain still, hidden, ready to act: sin "crouching at the door" (Genesis 4:7) is a creature lurking, waiting for the moment to pounce. It is the image of an animal in ambush.
4. When it is said that shepherds make their flocks "lie down" (Jeremiah 33:12), the word expresses a tranquil, secure rest, a well-being where the animal can finally lie down without fear.
5. Finally, the word can evoke a burden weighing on you: the donkey that "falls under its burden" (Exodus 23:5) is literally crushed, overwhelmed — the weight pins it to the ground.
H7257.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the physical image of lying flat. The verb belongs to a family of words expressing rest and stillness. In biblical context, the Old Testament uses it to describe both animal rest (lions, leopards, livestock) and human tranquility, or conversely a lurking threat.
H7257.emploi: This verb appears 30 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the poetic and prophetic books. It describes the rest of livestock and wild beasts (Isaiah 11:6, Ezekiel 34:14-15), the sleep of the righteous (Job 11:19), the regained peace of a land (Jeremiah 33:12, Isaiah 14:30). But it also carries a threatening nuance when sin "crouches at the door" (Genesis 4:7), or when a beast threatens to collapse under its load. The context transforms simple rest into an image of imminent danger or overwhelming weight.
H7257.portee: This word reminds us that true rest is not a luxury: it is a deep need, a blessing from God. The images of livestock that can rest in safety speak to every Christian: rest exists only when the threat disappears and God ensures our protection. Conversely, the image of sin crouching at the door warns us: evil is constantly lurking, ready to strike if we let our guard down.

sens: Place where one rests, where one dwells
Place where animals lie down, where they spend the night
Refuge, safe shelter
Enclosure or pasture serving as a dwelling for livestock
H7258.detail: 1. It is primarily a place to rest and dwell, like a lodging or a house: in Proverbs 24:15, it refers to the "place where the righteous rests," his dwelling. 2. The word also designates the den or lair where animals lie down at night: in Isaiah 35:7, the "den of jackals" is that deserted place where these beasts retreat and sleep. 3. It can mean a refuge or a safe shelter, a place of protection: the "fold" of the flock in Jeremiah 50:6 is the place to which the sheep must return safely. 4. For livestock, it is a pasture or an enclosure where the herds gather and rest: in Isaiah 65:10, the "fold of the fat cattle" in the valley of Achor is that field where the animals find food and rest.
H7258.origine: The Hebrew word révets comes from a root that evokes the idea of lying down, stretching out, resting. It is related to the verb that means "to stretch out" or "to lie down." The image is that of a place where one lays down their body, whether a human or an animal, to find rest and security.
H7258.emploi: This word appears four times in the Old Testament, always to describe a place of rest or refuge. In Proverbs 24:15, it refers to the house of the righteous as a personal place. Isaiah uses it twice: first in 35:7 for the den of jackals in the desert, and then in 65:10 for the pasture of livestock. Jeremiah in 50:6 uses it in the figurative sense of the "fold," the refuge to which God's flock must return. The word thus applies to both humans and animals and can take on a spiritual significance when it concerns God's people.
H7258.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize the importance of rest and security, not only materially but also spiritually. God's "fold" reminds us that God's people have a place of refuge and return, a promised dwelling where they find peace and protection. It is an image of God's pastoral tenderness towards His people.

sens: Woman from Abraham's family, daughter of Bethuel and sister of Laban
Wife of Isaac, mother of Esau and Jacob
Woman whose beauty and grace marked God's plan for Abraham's descendants
H7259.detail: 1. Rebecca is a woman from Abraham's lineage, born into the family of Bethuel in Mesopotamia (Genesis 22:23). She is the sister of Laban and belongs to the kinship from which Abraham's wife also came. 2. Abraham's servant recognizes her at the well and asks for her hand in marriage for Isaac (Genesis 24:45): she agrees and becomes Isaac's wife, heir to the promise made to Abraham. Isaac loves her and finds comfort in her after the death of his mother Sarah (Genesis 24:67). 3. Rebecca becomes the mother of Esau and Jacob (Genesis 25:21), the two twin sons of whom the elder is to serve the younger according to the Lord's word. She plays a decisive role in the history of salvation: she helps Jacob receive the blessing that his father Isaac intended for Esau (Genesis 27:6-15), thus fulfilling the divine plan despite the deception.
H7259.origine: The name Rebecca literally means "to ensnare" or "she who binds." It evokes the image of one who captures or binds, which can symbolize her ability to unite and influence events. In Hebrew, it is a feminine name borne by a key woman in the Old Testament. This name also appears in Greek in the New Testament as Rhébekka (Romans 9:10).
H7259.emploi: Rebecca is mentioned 29 times in Genesis, from chapter 22 to chapter 49. She first appears as one of Bethuel's daughters (Genesis 22:23), then as the woman that Abraham's servant goes to find for Isaac in Mesopotamia (Genesis 24). The entire chapter 24 recounts how she is chosen, how she agrees to leave her family to follow the servant, and how she becomes Isaac's wife. The following narratives show her as a caring mother to her sons and as a woman of action: she listens to the Lord's words regarding her children's destiny (Genesis 25:23) and intervenes to ensure God's will is fulfilled, even through cunning (Genesis 27). She is also presented as a woman of great beauty (Genesis 26:7).
H7259.portee: Rebecca shows how God leads His people through women of faith and courage. She leaves her family and country to follow God's plan, becoming an instrument of a promise that transcends her own children. She teaches that God uses our choices, our convictions, and even our human cunning to accomplish His plans. Her story reminds the reader that God does not change His purposes and can use anyone, woman or man, to bless and guide His people.

sens: Of large size or importance
Powerful, capable of great things
Who speaks or acts with excessive pride, arrogance
H7260.detail:
1. The word primarily describes what is vast or considerable in size or scope. Daniel 4:3 speaks of God's "great" signs and wonders — works so spectacular that they impress. Daniel 7:3 and 7:7 describe "great" beasts and "great" teeth, emphasizing their impressive and threatening nature.
2. It then denotes power, authority, the ability to command. In Daniel 2:48, the king gives Daniel "rich" gifts and establishes him as chief ruler — the word here expresses the greatness of the status and influence conferred upon him.
3. Finally, it characterizes one who speaks or behaves with excessive pride, with arrogance. In Daniel 7:8 and 7:11, the horn has "a mouth that spoke arrogantly" and utters "arrogant words" — the word highlights the insolence, the haughty pride of a creature that stands against God.
H7260.origine: The Hebrew word rav.rav is an intensive form (repetition of the same term) of the word rav ("great," "numerous"). This repetition reinforces the idea of greatness or, when applied to character, that of marked and persistent arrogance. The root expresses breadth, fullness, and when it pertains to speech or attitude, it evokes excess, lack of measure.
H7260.emploi: This word appears eight times in Hebrew in the book of Daniel, concentrated in chapters 2, 4, and 7. It is first used to describe the signs and wonders of God (Daniel 4:3), then the creatures of the prophetic vision — terrifying beasts (Daniel 7:3, 7:7). It takes on a moral color when it qualifies the words or attitude of the little horn, threatening and blasphemous (Daniel 7:8, 7:11). The context of Daniel 2:48 also shows its meaning of "rich" or "considerable" applied to royal gifts. Each time, the term emphasizes the extraordinary, whether divine, natural, or threatening.
H7260.portee: This word helps the reader understand that visible greatness is not necessarily a sign of virtue: the little horn, despite or because of its arrogance, will ultimately be destroyed, while God's signs endure forever. It invites a distinction between true greatness (that of God and His work) and false greatness (human pride that stands against Him).

sens: person of high rank
powerful and influential man in the kingdom
dignitary or council of the king
H7261.detail:
1. The word designates a person who occupies a high position in the hierarchy of power. In Daniel 4:36, after Nebuchadnezzar regains his sanity, his "great ones" (the dignitaries of the kingdom) come to seek him out to lead the government again, showing that they are his advisors and main collaborators.
2. It refers to a man of power and influence in the service of the king. At Belshazzar's feast (Daniel 5:1), the king gathers his "great ones" numbering a thousand: these are the high officials, military leaders, and statesmen of the kingdom who share the privilege of drinking with the sovereign.
3. The word can also collectively refer to the nobility or entourage of royal power. In Daniel 5:9, when the hand appears on the wall, the king's "great ones" are dismayed along with him, showing that they form a coherent group of high-ranking individuals at the throne.
H7261.origine: The word is Aramaic rabbān (רַבְרְבָן), which comes from the root rav (רַב), meaning "chief" or "principal." This same root is found in classical Hebrew with the same notion of superiority and high rank. The Aramaic rabbān has retained and developed this sense of dignity, designating not only one who is great or important but specifically a man vested with an official charge and authority.
H7261.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the book of Daniel, exclusively in chapters 4 to 6, which report events at the Babylonian court. It is used to designate the dignitaries and advisors of the king. In Daniel 4:36, the "great ones" ask Nebuchadnezzar to resume his role; in Daniel 5:1-3, they share the royal feast and participate in the profanation of the temple vessels; in Daniel 5:9-10, they witness the supernatural events and the king's panic. This court and political power context defines the use of the term throughout Scripture.
H7261.portee: This word reminds the reader that earthly kingdoms, even the most powerful, are organized hierarchically and that their "great ones" do not escape God's providence. The nobles of Babylon, despite their prestige and influence, witness the hand of God writing judgment and discover that their power is nothing before the God of Israel. It is a lesson in humility in the face of divine dominion: no earthly rank protects from eternal judgment.

sens: High Assyrian officer sent as an ambassador
Military chief and diplomat of the king of Assyria
Spokesman for the Assyrian king to Jerusalem
H7262.detail:
1. Rabshakeh is a historical figure, a high-ranking officer at the court of the king of Assyria. His title literally means "chief of the cupbearers" or "first cupbearer" in Aramaic, but he performs a much broader function: that of military commander and diplomatic envoy. He first appears in 2 Kings 18:17 as one of three emissaries sent by the king of Assyria with a powerful army to intimidate Jerusalem and its king Hezekiah.

2. His main role in the Bible is that of negotiator and propagandist. He speaks on behalf of the Assyrian king, shouting loudly in the Judean language so that the people can hear (2 Kings 18:28). He seeks to convince the Judeans that their resistance is futile and that their God cannot save them, thus attempting to provoke their surrender without fighting.

3. He embodies the pride and blasphemy of the nations hostile to God. His words insult the living God (2 Kings 19:4) and disdain King Hezekiah's trust in the Lord. However, his mission fails: God protects Jerusalem, and Rabshakeh retreats defeated.
H7262.origine: The name "Rabshakeh" comes from Aramaic and means "chief of the cupbearers" or "first cupbearer" (rab = chief, great; shakeh = cupbearer, one who pours drinks). At the Assyrian court, this title designated a very high-ranking officer, often tasked with diplomatic and military missions, far beyond his court functions. It is the same administrative title found in ancient Near Eastern courts.
H7262.emploi: Rabshakeh appears sixteen times in the Bible, all in the same historical events: 2 Kings 18—19 and Isaiah 36—37. These two passages recount the same episode, that of the invasion of the kingdom of Judah by the Assyrian king Sennacherib. Rabshakeh is most often mentioned as the emissary who speaks on behalf of the king, intimidating the inhabitants of Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:17, 28), then retreats after God's miraculous intervention (2 Kings 19:8). His fiery and blasphemous speech reveals Assyria's vain confidence in its own power.
H7262.portee: This character illustrates how God humiliates the proud who stand against Him and His people. Rabshakeh represents the power of the world hostile to faith, attempting through words to persuade believers that they have no hope. Yet, it is God who has the final word: those who entrust their lives to the Lord need not fear the threats of the powerful of the world, regardless of their titles or armies.

sens: A piece of compacted earth, generally irregular in shape
Earth that clumps together or hardens
An image of what is humble and earthly
H7263.detail:
1. A clod is a block or piece of solidified earth, about the size of a handful or larger. It is the concrete image of the word: earth that has compacted and hardened. In Job 38:38, God questions Job about the clods of earth — how they stick together when dust becomes moist.
2. The word emphasizes the idea of cohesion, of earth that clumps and binds. When rain falls, fine dust transforms into solid clods; this is a phenomenon that every ancient farmer observed.
3. The clod of earth becomes an image of what is mundane, earthly, subject to the laws of nature. In Job 21:33, the clods of the valley are light — this is a poetic detail to show that even after death, one returns to the ordinary of the earth, like everyone else.
H7263.origine: The Hebrew word regev comes from the root rāgab, which evokes the idea of sinking or compacting. A clod is earth that has compacted and hardened, becoming solid. The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Job, a book that meditates a lot on human fragility and the power of nature.
H7263.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, exclusively in Job. In Job 21:33, it describes the clods of the valley with a certain poetic lightness — suggesting that even after death, one is reduced to the ordinary, to common earth. In Job 38:38, it refers to clods that stick together under moisture: God poses this rhetorical question to Job to humiliate him, reminding him that he does not even understand the basic mechanisms of creation. In both cases, the clod symbolizes earthly reality, far from prestige or the exceptional.
H7263.portee: This simple word reminds the believer that we are all made of earth, and that death brings us back to this fundamental humility. In the face of God's greatness and the mysteries of creation, human beings must recognize their ignorance: we do not even understand how water and earth transform. It is a lesson in wisdom and modesty.

sens: To sway, to be physically agitated: of a person who is afraid or cold, or of something that is shaken
To be strongly shaken by an external power: the earth trembles during a disaster, a house shakes
To be troubled internally, disturbed in spirit or emotions
To become irritated, to become angry or to show emotional agitation
To cause someone fear, trouble, or anger
H7264.detail: 1. To tremble primarily means to sway, to shiver physically. It is the involuntary movement of one who is afraid or shivering (Isaiah 32:11, "Tremble"). 2. The word also describes the shaking of massive objects: the earth trembles during God's judgment (2 Samuel 22:8, "The earth shook and trembled"), the foundations of the mountains tremble (Psalms 18:8). 3. It expresses an inner disturbance, a perturbation of the soul: to be moved, destabilized, anxious (1 Samuel 28:15, Saul who fears Samuel). 4. The word also designates irritation, the onset of fury: to be angry is to "tremble" with indignation (Isaiah 5:25, the anger of the Lord that burns). 5. In the active form, "ragaz" can also mean to make someone furious or to irritate them (Ezekiel 16:43, "you have provoked me").
H7264.origine: This Hebrew verb primarily expresses physical agitation, swaying. Its root evokes the image of a body moving uncontrollably, of earth losing its stability. The word belongs to the family of expressions of movement and disturbance: "ragaz" shares a common atmosphere with other verbs describing trouble (fear, anger, destabilization). In religious texts, trembling often becomes the image of divine judgment: the earth trembles when God acts.
H7264.emploi: The verb appears about forty times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms, among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Joel) and in historical narratives (Samuel, Kings). Its two major usages are: (1) Physical or cosmic trembling (fear, cold, or shaking of the world during divine intervention): this is its most common meaning in poetry and the Psalms (Psalms 18:8, 99:1; Joel 2:10). (2) Emotional or moral agitation (anger, disturbance, anxiety): very present among the prophets to describe the turmoil of nations or judgment (Isaiah 5:25, 13:13). The verb can take an object (to provoke someone) or remain intransitive (to be troubled). This polysemy reflects the Hebrew link between physical disorder and emotional disorder.
H7264.portee: This word reminds us that God's power shakes not only material creation but also the hearts of men. Trembling can express reverential fear before God, or on the contrary, the anger that overtakes one who refuses His will. For the believer, this verb invites recognition of the stability that only God can provide, in the face of the agitations of the world and the heart.

sens: To anger, to provoke someone's fury
H7265.detail: 1. To irritate means to provoke someone's anger or indignation, particularly that of God. In Ezra 5:12, the people of Israel "irritated" the God of heaven by their unfaithfulness, which led to their punishment: God delivered them into the hands of King Nebuchadnezzar, who destroyed the temple and deported the people. It is a verb that expresses how human actions provoke a divine reaction.
H7265.origine: The Aramaic word "ragaz" (to irritate) is related to the Hebrew "ragaz" (H7264), which primarily means "to tremble" or "to agitate." The underlying image is one of violent agitation, physical or emotional. When one irritates someone, one sets them in motion, making them "tremble" with anger. In Aramaic, the verb takes on an active nuance: to make someone irritated, to put them in a rage.
H7265.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Aramaic Bible, in Ezra 5:12, in the context of the Babylonian exile. It is a retrospective reflection on the causes of the destruction of the first temple: the ancestors irritated God, and this irritation triggered divine punishment. The verb emphasizes the moral causality between the people's unfaithfulness and the punishment they suffered.
H7265.portee: This word reminds us of a major truth of the biblical faith: God is not indifferent to our actions, particularly our disobedience and unfaithfulness. To irritate God is to reject His covenant and commandments. For the believer, the text invites understanding that the painful consequences of Israel's history are not due to chance, but to a moral reality: our choices provoke a response from God. It is both a warning and an invitation to obedience.

sens: Fierce anger, outburst
State of intense agitation of the soul
Fury that drives to action
Indignation expressed through words or actions
H7266.detail:
1. The word denotes a fierce and sudden anger, a surge of rage that seizes someone. This is what King Nebuchadnezzar feels when he learns that three young men refuse to bow down before his idol: he is "irritated and furious" (Daniel 3:13), a double expression that shows the intensity of his outburst.

2. The word also evokes inner agitation, the deep turmoil of one who loses their calm. It is more than a mere annoyance: it is a state where the person is shaken, destabilized by anger.

3. This irritation is never passive: it drives to action. Nebuchadnezzar does not merely remain angry; he "gives the order" immediately, showing that rage produces concrete and often dreadful effects.
H7266.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the Hebrew verb "ragaz" (רָגַז) which means "to tremble, to be agitated." The basic image is that of convulsive movement, of trembling: a person in the grip of irritation "trembles" with anger. The root thus emphasizes the physical nature of anger, a state that agitates both body and soul.
H7266.emploi: This word appears only once in the Aramaic Bible, in Daniel 3:13. It is a pivotal moment in the story of the three companions in the fiery furnace: the king, upon learning of their refusal, is seized by a violent irritation that drives him to act immediately. The context is one of a conflict of religious conscience, where insubordination triggers the anger of human authority.
H7266.portee: This word reminds us how anger can blind judgment. Nebuchadnezzar, in his fury, acts without thinking, without listening. For the Christian reader, it is a lesson: do not let irritation dominate you, but seek wisdom and restraint, especially when you have power over others.

sens: Restless and troubled movement, physical or inner agitation
State of disorder or disturbance
Noise or rumbling that emanates from something
Intensity, fervor, bubbling of a force
H7267.detail: 1. The word first describes an incessant and troubled movement, an agitation of one who cannot find rest. In Job 3:17, the wicked who are agitated without end are contrasted with the weary who finally find rest — it is the image of perpetual unease. 2. It also designates the state of a person who is upset or in distress: in Job 3:26, Job says that trouble has seized him, meaning he knows neither tranquility nor peace. 3. The word can evoke a noise that rumbles or trembles: in Job 37:2, it is the trembling of the voice of God, the rumbling that comes from His mouth — a powerful and impressive manifestation. 4. It also expresses the fervor, the intensity of a force that bubbles: the eagle in Job 39:27 burns with fervor and devours the land, unable to contain itself.
H7267.origine: The Hebrew word rogez comes from a root that evokes movement, agitation, and disturbance. It is related to verbs meaning to shake, agitate, or tremble. The starting image is physical — a movement that shakes, disturbs — before it applies to emotional or inner states. The same root produces words denoting trepidation or fear.
H7267.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the book of Job (6 occurrences) and once in Isaiah. In Job, it describes either the agitation of the wicked without rest, or the trouble and anxiety of one who suffers, or an impressive noise. In Job 37:2, during God's speech in the storm, rogez evokes the rumbling of the divine voice — a powerful and holy agitation. In Job 39:27, applied to the eagle, it expresses the fervor, the irresistible drive of a creature in full strength. In Isaiah 14:3, the context speaks of rest after agitations — a peaceful cessation of trouble.
H7267.portee: This word reminds the biblical reader that the absence of God or disobedience produces perpetual agitation, an impossibility of finding peace. Conversely, resting in God is a concrete blessing. It also shows that God Himself can be a force that rumbles, that stirs — impressive and fearsome. For the believer, knowing rest in God rather than agitation becomes a matter of faith.

sens: In the grip of physical and emotional tremors
Restless, tormented, without inner peace
H7268.detail:
1. The word first evokes the image of a person who trembles, who cannot remain stable or calm — the body and mind shaken by involuntary agitation. In Deuteronomy 28:65, this describes the heart made agitated by the Lord: a deep agitation that paralyzes, that takes away all peace.
2. More broadly, it is the state of one who finds no rest anywhere, who is constantly troubled and anxious. The same phrase adds "you will not have a place of rest for the sole of your feet," showing that the agitation of the heart leads to the impossibility of stopping or settling down.
H7268.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses disturbed movement, instability. It evokes the image of something that vibrates, trembles, that cannot remain still — an agitation that comes from within and manifests through visible signs. It is the opposite of rest and stability.
H7268.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (in Deuteronomy 28:65). It is part of the list of curses that the Lord will send upon the unfaithful people: the agitation of the heart figures as one of the worst punishments, more terrible than mere deprivation, because it deprives man of all tranquility. It is an agitation that affects the heart itself, the seat of will and emotional balance.
H7268.portee: This word reminds us that distance from the Lord does not bring freedom but constant agitation. It shows that true peace — that of the heart and inner rest — comes from God alone. For the believer, it is an invitation to seek stability and rest in Him, rather than living in perpetual anxiety.

sens: Shiver or agitation of the body
Movement of inner unease that translates into physical disturbance
H7269.detail:
1. The word first denotes the visible trembling of the body, this convulsive shiver that seizes someone under the effect of fear, cold, or strong emotion. It is the primary physical image: the body that trembles involuntarily.
2. But the biblical context broadens the meaning: this trembling reveals a deep unease, an anxiety that invades the whole person. In Ezekiel 12:18, the prophet must eat and drink with trembling and anxiety — this ordinary gesture, emptied of its natural calm, becomes the visible sign of inner distress, of a disturbance that even affects the simplest acts.
H7269.origine: The Hebrew word rog-zah comes from a root that expresses oscillating movement, agitation, shaking — like a leaf trembling in the wind, or an object vibrating. It is not a common word in the Bible; it appears rarely, which makes it all the more striking when the text uses it. It belongs to the same family as other Hebrew terms related to trembling and shaking.
H7269.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 12:18. The prophet Ezekiel is commanded to eat and drink with trembling and anxiety: it is a prophetic theatrical act, where each gesture of the body speaks to the people. The choice of this rare word reinforces the weight of the message: this is not an ordinary trembling, but the bodily expression of prophetic distress that announces imminent judgment. The context shows that this trembling is linked to the destruction of Jerusalem and the approaching exile.
H7269.portee: This word reminds us that unease and fear manifest in the body — we cannot hide them entirely. But more deeply, it invites us to consider how our ordinary acts can become witnesses of what is happening within us. When the people see the prophet trembling, they are called to ask: what justifies such distress? It can be a lesson on conscience: sometimes our physical trouble reveals a spiritual truth we have tried to ignore.

sens: To go back and forth on foot, to move, to walk
To secretly observe a country or a city in order to report information
To send someone for military reconnaissance
To report malicious words about someone, to slander
H7270.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is simply to walk, to move on foot. This is the basic idea of the word: using one's feet to move from one place to another.
2. When looking at a place 'on foot,' by traversing it, one observes it closely. This is why the word transitions to the idea of exploring or scouting a territory. Joshua sends his men to 'explore' Jericho (Joshua 6:25) and the tribes of Judah do the same with the land of Laish (Judges 18:14).
3. In a military context, it means sending men ahead to examine the enemy's defenses and weak points in order to prepare for an attack. Joseph accuses his brothers of being 'spies' who have come to observe 'the weak places of the land' of Egypt (Genesis 42:9).
4. Finally, 'to go back and forth' can also mean to spread gossip, to carry malicious words about others. It is to walk while sowing discord, hence 'to slander.'
H7270.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the movement of feet, the act of walking or circulating. The basic image — traversing a territory on foot — naturally enriches the meanings of 'looking closely while moving' and, in a military context, 'to send for reconnaissance.' The family of the word also includes the idea of training or getting accustomed to something (like teaching a child to walk). In biblical Hebrew, this same root can refer to one who accompanies or follows, hence the idea of messenger or bearer of news.
H7270.emploi: The word 'espionner' appears 24 times in the Hebrew Bible. Its uses are distributed across two main areas. First, military or civil reconnaissance: the twelve men sent by Moses to scout Canaan traverse the land (Deuteronomy 1:24), Joshua sends scouts before attacking Jericho (Joshua 6:25), and the northern tribes explore the territory before migrating (Judges 18:14). The most striking geopolitical context is in Genesis 42, where Joseph's brothers are suspected of being spies sent to probe Egypt. Secondly, the moral and social domain: one also 'spies' by carrying malicious words (Psalms 15:3), aiming to weaken the community as one weakens a fortress. The two meanings — reconnaissance and slander — share the idea of circulating to observe and report.
H7270.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on two opposing realities. On one side, exploring and scouting are legitimate when preparing a just action (the entry into the promised Canaan). On the other, spying and slandering are crimes against the community, weapons of one who undermines the trust of others. The Bible thus contrasts the loyal scout with the informer. The word reminds us that our words, like our movements, have visible consequences — they 'explore' and 'report' who we really are.

sens: The part of the human or animal body that touches the ground, from the heel to the toes
The position or base of a structure, that on which it rests
In a figurative sense: power, authority, domination
H7271.detail:
1. The foot is the lower part of the leg, the part that allows one to walk and stand. In Nebuchadnezzar's vision, the colossal statue has feet partly of iron and partly of clay (Daniel 2:33, 2:34) — this fragile material shows that the final kingdom will lack solidity. The lion in Daniel's vision, stripped of its wings, is 'made to stand on its feet like a man' (Daniel 7:4), meaning restored to a position of being alive and active.
2. The foot is also the base on which something rests. The feet and toes of the statue symbolize the unstable foundation of the last kingdom, divided and divisible (Daniel 2:41, 2:42).
3. To walk or trample means to exercise absolute domination. The fourth terrible beast 'trampled what remained' (Daniel 7:7) of the previous creatures — an image of conquest and victory.
H7271.origine: The Aramaic word regual (ריגל) comes from the same family as the Hebrew regel (רֶגֶל), which designates the foot. The Hebrew root refers to the idea of walking, of moving. In biblical Hebrew, the foot also appears figuratively to indicate a manner, a conduct, an authority.
H7271.emploi: The word regual appears 7 times in the Aramaic New Testament of Daniel. It appears exclusively in chapters 2 and 7, both filled with symbolic visions. In chapter 2, the feet of the statue materialize the instability of the last kingdom of men before divine judgment. In chapter 7, the beastly creatures act with their feet: they stand or trample what they conquer. The meaning remains concrete (the part of the body), but the prophetic context imbues it with a political and eschatological dimension.
H7271.portee: These prophetic visions remind us that human kingdoms, even seemingly powerful, rest on fragile foundations. Only the kingdom of God is unshakeable. When we see the feet of these beasts or this statue, we are invited not to place our trust in the powers of this world, but to await the final judgment and the establishment of the eternal reign.

sens: The part of the body that touches the ground and allows one to walk
The lower limb of an animal or a celestial creature
The lower base of an object (table, support)
A trace, an imprint left by walking
The rhythm or cadence of movement ('according to the foot of')
An occurrence or a time (in the sense of countability)
H7272.detail:
1. The foot is literally the part of the human body that rests on the ground: it is with the feet that one walks, advances, and stands. The dove in the Ark found nowhere to 'set its foot' (Genesis 8:9), meaning no dry land to rest on.
2. Animals, celestial creatures, and even gods (in a figurative sense) have feet. The cherubim of Solomon's temple 'stood on their feet' (2 Chronicles 3:13), reminding us that in Hebrew, even supernatural creatures are described in the image of earthly creatures.
3. An object can have 'feet' — it is the base on which it rests. Thus, the footstool of the divine throne (Psalms 99:5) is the lower surface on which one places their feet, a symbol of submission and respect towards God.
4. The foot evokes the trace of the journey: 'a path that his foot had never trodden' (Isaiah 41:3) means a road he had never traveled before.
5. 'According to the foot of' means 'at the rhythm of,' that is, going slowly so that everyone can follow at the same pace (Genesis 33:14).
6. The word can also designate a unit of countability: 'three times' (Numbers 22:33) literally uses 'three feet,' hence the meaning of 'three occasions' or 'three times.'
H7272.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of 'walking' or 'making an imprint.' The same family of words also gives the idea of 'footprint,' 'path,' and 'following.' In ancient Hebrew, the foot is primarily the organ of movement, travel, and concrete presence.
H7272.emploi: The word 'foot' appears 232 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the literal sense: these are the feet of the human body (one removes sandals before the Lord in Exodus 3:5), the feet of animals and celestial creatures, the feet of idols. It also takes on derived meanings: 'footstool' (the support where one places their feet, a symbol of domination), 'following' or 'accompaniment' (to follow in someone's footsteps), and sometimes 'time' or 'occasion' (one foot = one step, hence the idea of countability). In Exodus 12:11, eating 'with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet' describes a hurried travel attire. Jonathan climbs using 'hands and feet' to scale (1 Samuel 14:13). The term is very concrete: it truly designates what we see and touch.
H7272.portee: The foot reminds us of the walk of faith: having our feet firmly planted on the ground means advancing confidently in the will of God. It is also a symbol of humility (to bow at someone's feet), of domination (to place one's foot on the enemy), and of consecration (washing feet was an act of love and service). For the Christian, meditating on the foot engages us to see God as close to our concrete reality, capable of 'treading' the paths of the world with us.

sens: Soldier who marches on foot, as opposed to a cavalryman
Ordinary man without military status
H7273.detail:
1. An infantryman is a soldier who fights on foot, typically equipped with a melee weapon such as a sword. Exodus mentions "six hundred thousand foot soldiers" who came out of Egypt (Exodus 12:37), and Saul summons "two hundred thousand" to fight Amalek (1 Samuel 15:4), indicating that these are organized troops. The contrast with cavalry and chariots highlights this meaning: when David captures Syrian chariots and horses, the text distinguishes "one thousand chariots" from "forty thousand foot soldiers" (1 Chronicles 19:18).
2. More broadly, the word refers to any man who moves on foot, as opposed to one who rides a horse or is in a chariot. He is not necessarily a warrior: he is simply someone who walks, who is on foot rather than mounted.
H7273.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "foot." In Hebrew, an adjective formed from this root refers to what relates to feet or to one who moves on his feet. The image is very concrete: it is the man who advances on his own legs, unlike the cavalryman who is carried by a horse.
H7273.emploi: This word appears twelve times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in military lists and war narratives. It is mainly found in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) to count the troops. The texts regularly use it to compare two forces: chariots and cavalry on one side, infantrymen on the other. For example, when the Syrians are defeated, the narrative distinguishes the one thousand captured chariots from the forty thousand slain infantrymen (1 Chronicles 19:18). This formulation shows that it is a well-established military category in antiquity.
H7273.portee: This word reminds us that in ancient armies, the majority of warriors were infantrymen on foot, armed and trained. It illustrates the concrete organization of biblical peoples and their ability to mobilize significant forces. For the Christian reader, this shows the historical reality of the conflicts described in Scripture, far from any romanticism.

sens: Location in the highlands east of the Jordan
Region of Gilead associated with Barzillai
H7274.detail:
1. Roguelim is a location situated in the highlands east of the Jordan, in Gilead. The name means "place of the fullers," those workers who treated and cleaned fabrics. This topography likely reflects an ancient economic activity related to the textile industry in this region.
2. Roguelim is known in the story of David primarily through Barzillai the Gileadite, who lived there. When David flees Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion, Barzillai comes to join him at Mahanaim with provisions and supplies (2 Samuel 17:27), and then he accompanies the king to the Jordan to escort him back (2 Samuel 19:31).
H7274.origine: The Hebrew name Roguelim comes from a root meaning "to tread" or "to treat" (as in treating fabrics). This etymology suggests that the place was a center of textile activity or a locality known for this trade in antiquity. The suffix "-im" (plural) possibly indicates several workshops or a district encompassing multiple fullers.
H7274.emploi: Roguelim appears only twice in the Bible, both in 2 Samuel. It first appears in 2 Samuel 17:27 as the residence of Barzillai the Gileadite, who brings aid and provisions to David in flight. It reappears in 2 Samuel 19:31 when Barzillai descends from Roguelim to accompany the king across the Jordan. These two mentions frame a crucial moment in David's story: his temporary defeat by Absalom and his support from the inhabitants of Gilead.

sens: To kill someone by throwing stones at them
To execute judicially by stoning
To punish by death according to Mosaic Law
H7275.detail:
1. The most direct meaning is the physical action of killing by throwing stones: stones are thrown at a person until death. This is the material act described literally in the texts.

2. In the context of Mosaic Law, to stone refers to a form of judicial execution reserved for certain serious crimes. Leviticus 20:2 and 20:27 show that those who give their children to Molech or consult the spirits of the dead must be stoned. This is a death sentence pronounced by the entire community.

3. Stoning also appears as a political punishment: in 1 Kings 12:18, the people stone Adoram, the king's officer, revealing how the people can rise up against authority. This shows that stoning can be an act of revolt, beyond the strictly religious framework.
H7275.origine: The Hebrew verb ragam comes from a root that evokes the action of throwing or piling up stones. The noun ragam also means stone or pile of stones. This action was well known in antiquity as a form of execution: it involved the entire community in the punishment, reinforcing its character as a collective act and a popular sentence.
H7275.emploi: The verb is used 15 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of Law (Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and history (Kings, Chronicles). In Leviticus 24:14-16, stoning concerns the blasphemer: the entire assembly participates in the judgment. In Numbers 14:10 and 15:35-36, it punishes idolatry and the violation of the Sabbath. Joshua 7:25 reports the stoning of Achan after his disobedience. These uses show that stoning is an established practice, ordained by God in the Law, and executed by the whole people as an expression of communal judgment.
H7275.portee: This word reminds the reader of the absolute holiness of God and the gravity of sin in the ancient Law. It shows that the community of Israel was called to participate together in the application of divine justice, not just a few judges. For the Christian, this contrasts with the grace brought by Christ: where the Law commanded stoning, Jesus grants forgiveness to the adulterous woman (John 8). The word invites reflection on the transition from Law to grace.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Jahdai and descendant of Caleb
H7276.detail: Regem is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:47. He is the son of Jahdai and belongs to the lineage of Caleb, one of the great names in the history of Israel. He is listed among his brothers: Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph. His name means "friend" in Hebrew, but the Bible tells us nothing else about his life or actions.
H7276.origine: The name Regem comes from Hebrew and literally means "friend." It carries the same meaning as the Hebrew word regam, which evokes the notion of friendship or companionship. It is a name with a blessing connotation, common during the monarchical period of Israel.
H7276.emploi: Regem appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:47. This passage lists the descendants of Caleb and his wives, tracing the genealogies of the tribe of Judah. Regem is mentioned among the sons of Jahdai, with no additional details provided about his life or role in the history of Israel.

sens: A pile of stone or accumulated material
A group of people gathered, a crowd or multitude
H7277.detail: 1. The word primarily evokes a heap or a concrete accumulation, like piled stones — this is the basic material image. 2. By extension, it designates a gathering of people, a crowd or a large company; in Psalms 68:28, it qualifies the troop, that is, the multitude that accompanies and supports the leaders of Judah, evoking the idea of people gathered around their leaders.
H7277.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to throw" or "to cast." The primary image is that of stones thrown and piled together — hence the meaning of "heap" or "pile." This image of things thrown together has naturally led to designating a multitude of people gathered, like a crowd where people press against one another.
H7277.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 68:28, where it describes the troop of the leaders of Judah — that is, the multitude that surrounds and follows them. In this context of praise and celebration of the tribes of Israel, the term emphasizes the idea of a large and organized company around its leaders. Its unique appearance makes it a rare poetic term from the Psalm.
H7277.portee: This word reminds us that the people of God are made up of multitudes, communities gathered around their leaders. It invites reflection on the strength of numbers and unity — how believers, gathered together, form a visible and powerful presence. It is also an image of the Church as a collective body, numerous yet one under the same Lord.

sens: Man from the time of Exile and Return
Sent by the exiled people to consult the temple
H7278.detail: Regem-Melech is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at a time when the Jews returning from Babylonian captivity were questioning their religious practices. In Zechariah 7:2, he is seen sent by the exiles from Bethel with others to go to the temple in Jerusalem and seek counsel about fasting: should they continue to fast as they did during the exile, now that the temple was rebuilt? His role shows how dispersed communities sought the wisdom of the prophets to guide their return to normal life.
H7278.origine: The Hebrew name Regem-Melech literally means "the heap of the king" (regem = heap or pile; melekh = king). It is a typical compound name of the time, where each element carries a meaning that can evoke an image (a royal heap) or a parental aspiration. No other biblical mention tells us where this character came from or how he became the envoy of his community.
H7278.emploi: Regem-Melech appears only once in the Bible, in Zechariah 7:2. He is sent by the people returned from captivity at Bethel to go to the temple in Jerusalem and ask the priests and prophets about the relevance of fasting. This act shows that the returned exiles needed spiritual guidance to reorient their lives after years of deportation. His name and mission illustrate the importance of envoys and mediators in the community of the Return.
H7278.portee: This passage reminds us that returning to normalcy after a spiritual crisis requires wisdom and counsel. Regem-Melech and his companions sought to understand how to honor God in the new circumstances. It speaks to us about the importance of faithfully questioning God and His prophets when our past practices must adapt to new realities.

sens: Express dissatisfaction in a low voice, secretly
Whisper, speak softly
Report the words of others to sow discord
Criticize quietly without daring to speak openly
H7279.detail:
1. To murmur primarily means to express dissatisfaction by speaking softly, without directly confronting the one responsible. The Israelites in the desert "murmured in their tents" (Psalms 106:25): they complained among themselves, away from Moses and God, instead of presenting their request openly. It is a veiled complaint, sometimes shameful.
2. The word also evokes whispering, that muffled sound that is barely heard. It is to speak softly so that others do not hear well, or to give weight to a confidence.
3. To murmur can designate someone who repeats the words of others to create misunderstandings and conflicts. Proverbs 16:28 and 26:22 describe the "reporter" whose words bring down discord "to the depths of the bowels" — like poison that penetrates deeply. This reporter divides friends (Proverbs 16:28) by transmitting what was not meant to be repeated.
4. To murmur is also to criticize in the background, without confronting directly. It undermines trust and obedience through insinuations and sly remarks rather than through honest contestation.
H7279.origine: The Hebrew root רגן (ragan) evokes whispering and muffled words. It carries the image of secrecy, of what is said in the ear and should not be known publicly. The word belongs to a family of Hebrew terms that describe hidden, murmured, or malicious words — those that harm in silence.
H7279.emploi: This word appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in Proverbs and in the desert narratives. In Deuteronomy 1:27 and Psalms 106:25, it describes the murmuring of the Israelites in the desert: they criticized God and Moses by speaking softly among themselves, without daring to openly rebel. This murmuring reflects a form of sly disobedience and lack of faith. In Proverbs 16:28, 18:8, 26:20, and 26:22, the word rather designates the reporter, the one who spreads words in secret to sow discord. Four times Proverbs warns against these "words of the reporter" which, like delicacies, fascinate and do harm. Thus the word shifts from the meaning of murmuring (hidden complaint) to the meaning of gossiping (repeated words in secret).
H7279.portee: To murmur is to complain in secret instead of trusting or saying things to someone's face. It is a form of soft but serious disobedience — the Israelites murmured instead of believing. For the modern reader, this word reminds us of the danger of hidden words, murmurs, and gossip that dig trenches without anyone being able to respond frankly. It is a call to transparency and frankness rather than insinuation.

sens: Stir, move with force
Happen suddenly, instantly
Disturb, unsettle
H7280A.detail:
1. To raise primarily means to put a mass in motion, to stir it with force: the sea rises, its waves lift and roar. It is the image of power creating ripples, tumultuous movement (Job 26:12, Isaiah 51:15).
2. The word can also evoke something that happens in an instant, very quickly, almost in the blink of an eye: the lying tongue lasts only a moment, it is brief and fleeting (Proverbs 12:19).
3. In a context of threat or sudden divine action, to raise expresses the idea of surging or acting in a flash: God says, "Suddenly I will make Edom flee," meaning very quickly, without warning (Jeremiah 49:19).
H7280A.origine: The Hebrew root ragaï evokes the idea of rapid movement and agitation. It is related to words that designate an instant or a very brief moment, as if the action were done in the blink of an eye. The primary image is that of a jolt or vibration — something sudden and violent.
H7280A.emploi: This verb appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom and prophetic books. Three times, it describes God's action raising the sea and its waves (Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah), an image of His dominion over creatures and chaos. Twice in Jeremiah, it expresses the imminence of divine action: God suddenly drives away the peoples. Once in Proverbs, it designates the brevity of a lying word. The meaning thus varies between physical agitation and rapidity, even instantaneousness.
H7280A.portee: This word teaches the power and sovereignty of God: He alone masters the chaotic forces of creation, raises them, and dominates them. It also reminds us that divine action can be sudden and unexpected, without delay. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize that what seems stable or eternal is actually fragile, and that God acts according to His will, not according to our expectations.

sens: state of calm and stillness, absence of movement
tranquility of the soul and heart, inner peace
cessation of an action or violence
H7280B.detail:
1. Rest is primarily physical stillness, the act of ceasing to move or act. This is what Israel experiences as it walks toward its place of rest after exile (Jeremiah 31:2), or what the sword of the Lord must find when it returns to its sheath (Jeremiah 47:6).
2. More profoundly, it is the tranquility of the heart and mind. A person who does not find rest lives in constant agitation: the one who transgresses the covenant will have an agitated heart and languishing eyes, unable to find a moment of peace (Deuteronomy 28:65).
3. It is also the result of the cessation of a threat or violence. To give rest to a land is to restore stability and security after the ravages of war (Jeremiah 50:34).
H7280B.origine: This verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of relaxation and calm. In Hebrew, the same root gives the noun that means an instant, a moment — the idea that is also found in words translated as tranquil and calm. The basic image is that of a pause, a stop of movement or agitation.
H7280B.emploi: This verb appears about ten times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the prophets of the exile. When the people transgress the covenant, God denies them rest: neither inner peace nor physical security (Deuteronomy 28:65). But after punishment, God promises His people rest, a return to stability (Jeremiah 31:2). The word also applies to the forces of nature: the sword that rests, the land that finds rest when conflicts cease (Jeremiah 47:6, 50:34). In all cases, rest is the gift of God that follows the end of judgment.
H7280B.portee: For the believer, this word teaches that true peace is not the absence of fatigue, but the absence of agitation of the heart before God. It is a rest that only God can give, after removing the threat of judgment. This rest is a comforting promise for those who submit to God: the rest that follows exile symbolizes the restoration and renewal that God grants to His repentant people.

sens: To split, to crack on the surface
To harden and form a crust
To dry out and become chapped (skin, earth)
H7280C.detail:
1. The word first describes a rupture of surface: skin that splits, a crust that cracks. In Job 7:5, the skin of the sick person "cracks," fissuring under the effect of illness and suffering.
2. The underlying image is one of hardening: the skin or the earth hardens, then this hardness breaks into cracks. It is the transition from flexibility to rigidity, then to rupture.
3. The word also evokes the action of time and dryness: overly dry skin, earth scorched by the sun that splits. Job's illness is characterized by a progressive decay of the body.
H7280C.origine: The root ראג (rag) expresses the idea of becoming hard, stiff, rigid. The verb ragas evokes what stiffens and cracks — the opposite of living flexibility. The image is that of a living material (the skin) losing its elasticity and fissuring: it is death that gains on the body.
H7280C.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 7:5. Job, ravaged by illness, describes his state of decay: his body is covered with worms, a crusty earth forms on his skin, and this skin cracks. It is a cry of extreme suffering, where the sick person sees his own body disintegrate. The context is one of lament: Job exposes to God the horror of his physical condition.
H7280C.portee: This word reminds us that illness and suffering attack the body down to its substance: they render it unrecognizable, repugnant. For the reader, it is an invitation to empathize with extreme suffering, not to judge too quickly those who weep or cry out. It is also a reminder that our flesh is fragile and perishable.

sens: A very short span of time, a moment that passes very quickly
A fraction of a second when something happens suddenly
The adverb: "in an instant," "for an instant," marking the brevity or suddenness of an action
H7281.detail:
1. The word first designates a very short interval of time, so rapid that it can barely be grasped — like a blink of an eye. The Lord tells Moses that a single instant of His presence among the people would consume him (Exodus 33:5), so brief compared to divine eternity.
2. It is also the precise moment when an event occurs, especially when it is brutal or unexpected. The psalmist says that the wicked are destroyed in an instant (Psalms 73:19) — not gradually, but all at once, in a second.
3. The adverb describes an action that lasts barely a moment or happens suddenly. When Jeremiah announces that calamity comes suddenly (Isaiah 47:9), he means that the blow will strike without warning, so fast that no one can evade it.
H7281.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "trembling" or "quivering" — hence its initial image: a small moment that makes one shiver, that passes in a quiver. In Aramaic, a word from the same family also means "moment." It is a simple and direct word, without elaborate metaphor, that paints the extreme brevity of time.
H7281.emploi: This word appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the wisdom books and among the prophets. In Job, it is found several times to say that the prosperity of the wicked lasts only an instant (Job 20:5, Job 21:13), or that God tests man at all moments (Job 7:18). The psalms use it to describe the sudden destruction of the wicked (Psalms 73:19) or the joy that lasts an instant (Psalms 30:6). Among the prophets, especially Isaiah and Jeremiah, it emphasizes the trial or destruction that falls upon the people "in an instant" — which reinforces the sense of surprise and irreversibility.
H7281.portee: This word invites the believer to meditate on the extreme brevity of human life and the things of this world. When calamity comes in an instant (Job 34:20), or when the prosperity of the wicked lasts only an instant (Job 20:5), the Bible teaches us that nothing belongs to us in our own right, and that only what endures with God has eternal value. It is an invitation to seek what lasts, not what vanishes.

sens: Who is calm, peaceful, without agitation
Who lives in peace, without trouble or threat
H7282.detail:
1. The word designates someone who enjoys calm and peace, without noise or agitation: it is the state of one who rests, who is not troubled. In Psalms 35:20, the psalmist speaks of the "calm people of the land," the peaceful inhabitants whom the wicked target with their deception.
2. It is also one who lives in safety, protected from threats: calm then means "without fear," "at peace." The enemies of the psalmist attack precisely those who are calm, that is, vulnerable and defenseless.
H7282.origine: The Hebrew verb expresses the idea of rest and calm. It is related to the realm of serenity and absence of trouble. This word belongs to the semantic field of peace and well-being: one who is calm is not agitated, not anxious.
H7282.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 35:20. It describes the ordinary people of the land who live in peace and calm, precisely those whom the wicked target with their lies and deception. The context shows that "calm" means "without suspicion," "exposed to danger precisely because one does not expect it."
H7282.portee: This word reminds us that the righteous can be vulnerable: being calm and living in peace does not immunize against the malice of others. The psalmist invites us to recognize this threat and to rely on God rather than on our own innocence.

sens: A noisy and disorderly agitation of a crowd
A confused noise of voices and movements
An inner agitation, a fermentation of emotions or thoughts
H7283.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a tumultuous agitation, a crowd in loud and confused movement — like the rumbling of a multitude in upheaval. It is the concrete image of people stirring together, speaking loudly, creating disorder (Psalms 2:1, "Why do the nations rage?").
2. By extension, it refers to a confused noise, the rumor and agitation that arise from it — not only the physical tumult but also the mental confusion it creates.
3. Figuratively, it represents an inner agitation, a fermentation of emotions, plots, or rebellious thoughts. In Psalm 2, the nations are in tumult not only because they are agitated externally, but because their minds conspire against God: it is a fermentation of hostile feelings.
H7283.origine: The Hebrew root ragash evokes the image of a crowd that ferments, stirs, and conspires together. The word belongs to a family of terms describing tumultuous and confused movement. The Aramaic equivalent regash has exactly the same meaning: to create tumult, to gather in noise and disorder.
H7283.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Psalms 2:1), in a highly dramatic context: the Psalmist contemplates the nations rising in tumult against God and His anointed. The word expresses not only the physical agitation of the peoples rebelling but also the inner conspiracy, the fermentation of hostile thoughts. It paints the image of a restless, noisy multitude in organized revolt — a rebellion that arises from an underground fermentation.
H7283.portee: This word shows how hostility toward God never arises in isolation: it ferments in hearts and minds, then expresses itself in collective agitation and organized rebellion. Psalm 2 invites us to see how human plots against divine order are futile and noisy — much tumult for nothing, in the face of Him who sits in heaven.

sens: To arrive in a crowded, agitated, disordered manner
To insist forcefully with someone, to keep pressing the issue
H7284.detail:
1. This word describes a crowd arriving in a rush, in agitation and disorder. The image is of a multitude pressing forward, jostling to move together. In Daniel 6:6, the officials and satraps "came tumultuously before the king": they arrive in mass, full of zeal and urgency.
2. By extension, the word also expresses the idea of returning repeatedly, insisting energetically. In Daniel 6:15, these same men "insist" before the king: they press him, harassing him with their repeated demands to confirm the decree against Daniel.
H7284.origine: The Aramaic root rgsh (or rgz in other forms) evokes movement, agitation, the noise that rises from a multitude. It carries the idea of tumult, of uproar. In biblical Aramaic, it also denotes the manifestation of collective emotion: a crowd that stirs, that rumbles, that moves together.
H7284.emploi: This verb appears three times in the book of Daniel, in chapters 6:6, 6:11, and 6:15, all in the context of the plot against Daniel. Each time, it describes the attitude of Daniel's adversaries: first "tumultuously" when they come to the king, then "tumultuously" again when they enter to arrest Daniel in prayer, and finally "insisted" when they ask the king to confirm the irrevocability of the decree. The word emphasizes the urgency, agitation, and pressing insistence of these men.
H7284.portee: This word shows how evil often proceeds: not by a single blow, but through collective and repeated pressure, a harassment that mounts. The reader sees that Daniel's persecution is not the work of a single quiet enemy, but of an agitated and insistent pack. It reveals the carnal energy expended by those who oppose justice and God's righteousness.

sens: A large group of assembled people
A compact gathering of people sharing a common moment
