H7285A.detail: 1. This word denotes a large group of people gathered in the same place — the image of a dense crowd where people are close together. In Psalm 55:15, the psalmist remembers those times when he went to the house of God in the company of the crowd: it is not just a theoretical idea, but the lived experience of an assembly of believers walking together toward the temple. 2. More broadly, this word evokes the idea of a united community, a human mass sharing a common moment or purpose — here, a religious pilgrimage where everyone participates in collective worship.
H7285A.origine: The Hebrew word regesh comes from a root that expresses the idea of movement, noise, and agitation (hence "trembling," "shaking"). The crowd is exactly that: a living, moving whole that vibrates. The word appears only once in the Bible, making it a rare and precise term to describe this moment of collective communion.
H7285A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible: in Psalm 55:15. The psalmist, going through a period of betrayal and spiritual loneliness, finds comfort in recalling the happy days when he walked toward the temple in the company of the crowd of believers. This unique usage places the word in a context of nostalgia and lost communion — the crowd represents not only a physical multitude but also an experience of religious brotherhood.
H7285A.portee: This word reminds the believer of the strength of communal worship: the presence of other believers ascending to God together is not a distraction but a grace. It also protects us, for in the "crowd" that worships, each finds comfort and is strengthened in faith. This image from the psalmist can speak today to those who, alone or isolated, remember the warmth of an authentic Christian assembly.

sens: A group of people who stir and make noise together
A turbulent and agitated crowd conspiring or plotting
A confused and tumultuous assembly of voices or movements
H7285B.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes a group, a band of people who stir together and make noise — like a crowd in movement or in animated discussion. It is a concrete image: you see people, you hear them. In Psalms 64:3, the psalmist prays to be protected "from the noisy troop of wicked men": he speaks of a crowd of evildoers conspiring against him, whose very agitation — their murmurs, their comings and goings — reveals their malice. 2. The word thus takes on a nuance of plotting or conspiracy: it is not just noise, but the noise of a crowd organizing against someone. The agitation is not innocent; it is that of people scheming together. The image is of a confused but threatening group, where voices mingle around a wicked project.
H7285B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses agitation, tumult, and confused movement. The starting image is that of boiling, commotion — something that moves, that stirs noisily. It is a feminine noun, formed to describe an action or atmosphere rather than an isolated person: the quality of being a tumultuous crowd.
H7285B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 64:3. It is used in a prayer of trust: the psalmist asks God to protect him from the plots and malice of a band of wicked men. The "noisy troop" evokes both the noise of conspiracy and its confused, disorganized character — yet still dangerous. It paints the atmosphere of collective malice.
H7285B.portee: This word helps the reader recognize collective malice and the danger it represents, even when it seems disorganized or noisy. It reminds us that wickedness often acts in groups, and that noise, agitation, and rumor can be weapons of conspiracy. For those who fear opposition, it also speaks of turning to God alone in the face of a hostile crowd: it is God who must safeguard the one who is alone.

sens: Flatten or beat something to stretch and widen it
Submit, dominate, reduce under one's power
Lower, defeat, bring down an opponent
H7286.detail:
1. Extend: this means to flatten something by striking or working it to make it more flat and wide. In 1 Kings 6:32, the craftsman "extends" the gold over the cherubim and palm trees of the temple, meaning he strikes and flattens it to delicately cover the sculptures, as one would do with a sheet of gold that is hammered.
2. Subjugate: this means to submit someone to one's authority, to reduce them under one's power. The psalmist says in Psalms 144:2 that God "subjugates" his people, meaning he places this people under his protection and benevolent dominion.
3. Bring down: this means to knock down, defeat, or overthrow an enemy. In Isaiah 45:1, the Lord holds Cyrus by the hand to "bring down" the nations before him, signifying that he will subdue and defeat them militarily.
H7286.origine: This verb comes from a root that evokes the action of striking, beating. The same root is found in other Hebrew words that describe the action of striking or flattening. The initial image is very concrete: that of a hammer striking to extend, flatten, subdue. Depending on the context and grammatical nuance, the word can emphasize the physical action of extending (for example, extending a sheet of gold) or its figurative meaning: to submit, dominate, as if one is "flattening" the resistance of an enemy.
H7286.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the sense of striking, extending, or subjugating. In 1 Kings 6:32, it describes the technical work of the goldsmith who "extends" the precious gold over the sculptures of the temple, a very concrete and material usage. In Psalms 144:2 and Isaiah 45:1, it shifts to the figurative sense of submitting, dominating, or bringing down: submitting a people, defeating nations. The warrior or political context gives the verb all its power: it is an act of power, of domination, that "flattens" resistances.
H7286.portee: This word reminds us that God has absolute power, not only over the events of history (he brings down nations through Cyrus), but also over his people whom he "subjugates" — not to break them, but to protect and keep them. It also invokes the humble image of gold extended in the temple: it is by submitting that we become precious in God's eyes, like gold that shines all the more as it allows itself to be shaped.

sens: Exercise authority, power over someone or something
Control, subjugate, enslave
Command, direct, have charge
Trample, crush, oppress
Triumph over, defeat
H7287A.detail:
1. Exercise sovereign authority over a creature or domain: it is the power to control, direct, govern. Genesis 1:26 shows man created to dominate over all the animals of the earth and the seas. It is a right and responsibility entrusted by God.
2. Submit someone to one's power, particularly by force or enslavement. Leviticus 25:46 forbids the Israelites from dominating harshly over their brothers, showing that domination can be just or unjust depending on the manner and intention.
3. Command as a leader or responsible person: to have direction, authority. In 2 Chronicles 8:10, the leaders placed at the head of the people and charged with overseeing them dominate over them as governors.
4. Crush, trample, reduce to helplessness: dominate then takes on a connotation of violence or oppression. In Isaiah 14:6, the one who dominates over the peoples does so with a relentless anger that strikes without rest.
5. Prevail, triumph: dominate over one's enemies, defeat and enslave them. In Isaiah 14:2, Israel will dominate over those who had taken them captive, overturning oppression.
H7287A.origine: The Hebrew verb radah comes from a root expressing the idea of treading, trampling, then conquering and commanding. The basic image is that of a foot that steps on, of power that is exercised by physical force and then by authority. The root also evokes crushing, brutal domination. The word carries within it the ambiguity of power: it can be legitimate and beneficial (the king who governs justly) or tyrannical and destructive (the oppressor who crushes).
H7287A.emploi: The verb radah appears 22 times in the Old Testament, mostly in legislative and wisdom texts. It first designates the right granted to man to dominate over creation (Genesis 1:26, 1:28). Then it qualifies the exercise of royal and political power: King Solomon dominated over the conquered lands (1 Kings 4:24), the leaders dominate over the people (2 Chronicles 8:10). The Law imposes clear limits: the Israelites must not dominate harshly over foreigners or servants (Leviticus 25:43, 25:46), revealing an ethics of power. The verb also applies to the oppression suffered (Nehemiah 9:28: enemies dominate over Israel) and the prophetic overturning of power relations (Isaiah 14:2: Israel will dominate over its oppressors). It finally expresses divine or royal sovereignty deployed over the nations.
H7287A.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the nature of power: the one who "dominates" bears a responsibility before God. Genesis 1:26 shows that to dominate is not an absolute right, but a charge entrusted, a stewardship of creation. The laws of Leviticus remind that one who exercises authority must do so with justice and mercy, without harshness. For the Christian, radah sheds light on the call to serve rather than tyrannize, to govern with wisdom and to recognize that all authority comes from God and must be exercised according to his will.

sens: Remove or seize something with the hand
Exercise authority over someone, dominate
Trample, crush
H7287B.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to take something in hand, to remove it from a place. Samson "took" the honey from the lion's carcass (Judges 14:9) — he seized it, removed it, and ate it on the way. It is the simple action of grasping with the hand.
2. Dominate or command someone: to exercise authority, a grip. The priests "dominate" under the guidance of false prophets (Jeremiah 5:31) — they govern, they control. The word describes a power that one exercises over others.
3. Trample, walk on by crushing. At the time of the harvest, one "treads" the grapes in the press (Joel 3:13) — one tramples them to extract the juice. It is the idea of crushing underfoot.
H7287B.origine: The Hebrew verb radah comes from a root that evokes the action of scraping, rubbing, or treading. In Hebrew, the same root can describe the elementary gesture of scraping or removing something from a surface. By extension, the word comes to mean seize, take in hand, then dominate or crush. It is a word that follows the concrete logic of physical action, of the body's gesture, before applying to power and authority.
H7287B.emploi: The verb radah appears three times in our usages: twice as "take" (Judges 14:9), once as "dominate" (Jeremiah 5:31), and once as "tread" (Joel 3:13). The context changes the nuance: with a concrete object (the honey), it is "take"; with people and the idea of authority exercised, it is "dominate"; with an agricultural product that is crushed, it is "tread". The verb thus describes a manual, physical action, which varies according to what one does — seize, command, or crush.
H7287B.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, power and authority are often described by concrete images — the gesture of the hand that seizes, dominates, crushes. For the reader, this shows how unjust domination (the priests who command according to false prophets) is placed on the same level as the brutal trampling of grapes: evil has a tangible and destructive reality. Conversely, "taking" in hand what is good (the honey) speaks of legitimate appropriation.

sens: Son of Jesse and brother of David
The fifth son of Jesse
H7288.detail: 1. Raddaï is a man from the tribe of Judah living during the time of the united monarchy. He is one of the sons of Jesse, the father of King David. His only biblical mention is found in 1 Chronicles 2:14, where he is listed in the genealogy of Jesse's family. 2. He is specifically the fifth son of Jesse, coming after Nethanel in the genealogical order. Although he is the brother of David and several other sons of Jesse (Eliab, Abinadab, Shimeah, Ozem, Elihu, and the sisters Zeruiah and Abigail), Raddaï appears only once in the Scriptures and has no personal story recorded.
H7288.origine: The name Raddaï means "he who treads" or "trampling" in Hebrew, evoking the action of walking on or crushing something. The name suggests an image of strength or dominance. It is a name borne by this historical figure from Jesse's family during the Old Testament period.
H7288.emploi: Raddaï appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:14. He is mentioned in Jesse's genealogy, which lists the sons of David's father. This passage provides no details about his life, actions, or significance. He is simply listed as a member of Israel's royal family during the time of the united monarchy, with no further information.

sens: A wide and light piece of fabric worn on the body
A loose and flowing garment, cloak or cape
H7289.detail:
1. The word refers to a veil or fabric that one drapes over oneself. In the Song of Solomon, the young girl has her veil taken away by the guards who encounter her: it is a garment she wears and can be removed, which covers and protects the one who wears it.
2. It can also mean a looser garment, an outer garment or a light cape. In Isaiah, the prophet lists the adornments of the women of Jerusalem and mentions "light outer garments" as part of this adornment: these are outer garments, light and loose, worn over others.
H7289.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to spread". It designates something that extends, that covers widely. The same Hebrew verb expresses the idea of unfolding, covering with a wide surface, which explains why the name applies to fabrics that envelop the body.
H7289.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. First in Isaiah 3:23, where it is among the feminine ornaments that God threatens to take away from the women of Jerusalem: it is translated as "outer garments" or "light tunics". Then in the Song of Solomon 5:7, where the veil is a garment that the young girl wears when she goes out and is taken from her. These two contexts show that it is a garment worn, either a veil or a loose outer garment, which is part of the adornment of women.
H7289.portee: This word reminds us that in biblical culture, certain garments, including the veil, played an important role in daily life and social identity. Understanding these concrete details helps us better grasp the scenes and symbols of the Bible.

sens: to be plunged into a heavy and deep sleep
to be unconscious, lose consciousness
to be struck by dizziness or torpor
to be paralyzed or frozen in fear
H7290.detail:
1. The word describes a very deep sleep, a total numbness of the senses. Sisera, the military leader, falls into such a deep sleep beside Jael that he does not wake up when she drives a tent peg into his temple (Judges 4:21): it is the very image of sleep from which one does not rise.
2. More broadly, the word means to be unconscious or out of oneself, unable to react. Daniel, terrified by the heavenly vision, falls "struck by dizziness, face to the ground" (Daniel 8:18): it is a state of torpor and loss of consciousness, not ordinary sleep.
3. In some contexts, the word expresses a paralyzing torpor or numbness: Jonah goes down to the bottom of the ship and falls "deeply" asleep during the storm (Jonah 1:5), indifferent to the panic around him.
4. Metaphorically, the word can denote inertia or drowsiness in the face of danger: the one who "sleeps" during the harvest (Proverbs 10:5) is struck by a sleep of indifference.
H7290.origine: The Hebrew verb radám comes from a root that expresses the idea of falling heavily, of being numb. The word paints the image of a body collapsing into unconsciousness. It also appears in the biblical concept of the "sleep of God" or His apparent silence in the face of danger: Jacob's warriors fall asleep at the threat of the mighty God (Psalms 76:7).
H7290.emploi: The verb radám appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible. It always depicts a sleep or state of unconsciousness that is particularly deep, not ordinary. In historical narratives, it shows the invulnerability or inertia of the sleeper (Sisera, Jonah). In vision texts (Daniel), it describes fainting or shock in the presence of the supernatural. Finally, it is used figuratively for apathy in the face of one's duties (Proverbs). The context determines whether it refers to actual physical sleep or metaphorical unconsciousness.
H7290.portee: This word teaches that deep sleep can signify vulnerability and a lack of spiritual vigilance. For the believer, it invites one to remain alert in faith and not to fall asleep in response to God's calls. It also reminds us that only God never sleeps and is always attentive to the cries of His people.

sens: To run after someone or something to catch it
To chase, drive away, repel an enemy
To persecute, harass, do harm to someone
To seek eagerly, to search insistently
H7291.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to run after someone to catch them: Abram "pursued" the kings as far as Dan to recover his nephew (Genesis 14:14), and the Israelites could "pursue" their fleeing enemies in the desert (Judges 8:5).
2. In military combat, the word also refers to chasing the enemy, routing them, and not letting them escape: after Joshua's victories, the Israelite army "pursued" and struck the fleeing Canaanites (Joshua 8:24, Joshua 10:10).
3. More cruelly, the word can mean to persecute, to do harm to someone repeatedly and intentionally, as a torturer would: God says He will "pursue" His enemies (2 Samuel 22:38), or the psalmists complain that their enemies persecute them without cause (Psalms 38:21).
4. Figuratively, "to pursue" can also mean to seek something eagerly: the corrupt leaders in Isaiah "run" after rewards (Isaiah 1:23), meaning they seek them greedily.
H7291.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of staying behind someone, closely following them, from which the sense of pursuit naturally derives. This image of rapid movement and perseverance in hunting or combat permeates the word. The root is akin to the verb "to follow" or "to be in the wake of," but with a nuance of intention: not only to follow someone but to pursue them with a specific aim.
H7291.emploi: This verb is very common in the Hebrew Bible: it appears 135 times, notably in the warrior narratives of Genesis and Joshua (military pursuits after victories), in Judges and Samuel (hunts against Israel's enemies), and in the Psalms and the Prophets (persecutions and divine punishments). Its military uses dominate: in Egypt, Pharaoh "pursues" the Hebrews (Exodus 14:4-9), and the Israelites regularly "pursue" their defeated adversaries. Gradually, the word also takes on a moral hue: in the Psalms, persecution becomes a motif of lamentation and a cry for help to God. The verb can also express an ardent quest or covetousness: seeking good (Psalms 38:21) or rewards (Isaiah 1:23).
H7291.portee: This word helps the reader understand the violence and urgency of biblical battles, but above all to grasp how God Himself "pursues" His adversaries and protects or punishes according to His purposes. For the persecuted believer, the word resonates with their own sufferings: the Psalms show them that even the righteous are sometimes "pursued," but that God sees this injustice. Finally, the use of the word for an ardent quest reminds us that our search for God and justice must be as persistent as that of a hunter or a warrior.

sens: To fill with trouble, confusion, or anxiety
To press someone insistently, to harass
To strengthen, to give confidence or assurance
H7292.detail:
1. Troubler means to fill someone with confusion, agitation, or distress. It is a disturbance that comes from outside and disrupts inner peace. In Song of Solomon 6:5, the beloved's eyes trouble the one who gazes upon them: they put him in turmoil, disturbing him with their beauty.
2. Importuner means to press someone insistently, to harass them with repeated requests until they are put in difficulty. In Proverbs 6:3, the son who has fallen into slavery is urged to go and prostrate himself and make pleas to his creditor: he must importune him with his supplications.
3. In contrast, rassurer or fortifier means to give confidence, to strengthen the soul by putting it out of trouble. In Psalm 138:3, the speaker acknowledges that God has reassured him and strengthened his soul when He answered him.
H7292.origine: The Hebrew verb rāhab originally evokes the idea of agitation, tumult, or force that stirs. It is a movement that sweeps away, that shakes. The word carries several nuances depending on the context: it can denote hostile agitation (to importune, to oppress), emotional agitation (to trouble, to move), or, when confidence prevails, the action of giving strength and stability to one who was troubled.
H7292.emploi: This verb appears four times in the Hebrew Bible according to our usages. In Psalms 138:3, it takes on the meaning of reassuring or spiritually strengthening: God answers the prayer and strengthens the psalmist's soul. In Proverbs 6:3, it describes the action of importuning someone with urgent requests. In Song of Solomon 6:5, it expresses the trouble and turmoil caused by the beloved's gaze. In Isaiah 3:5, in a context of social oppression, the young and the worthless continually oppress or importune their elders and superiors. Thus, the same verb oscillates between the idea of disruptive agitation and that of energetic action capable of transformation: this is why it can mean to trouble, to importune, or, on the contrary, to strengthen and reassure.
H7292.portee: This word invites the Christian to recognize God's power to bring peace amid trouble. When the psalmist confesses that God has reassured him, he testifies that the heard prayer is not limited to external resolution, but it strengthens the soul itself. At the same time, the warnings from Proverbs and Isaiah remind us of the danger of yielding to inner turmoil or the malicious importunity of others, and the importance of seeking help from the one who alone can give true and lasting peace.

sens: Symbolic name for Egypt
Image of pride and arrogance
H7293.detail:
1. Rahab is a poetic and symbolic name given to Egypt in the Hebrew Bible, particularly in the psalms and prophecies. This term appears mainly to designate Egypt in a context where the psalmist enumerates the peoples who know God: "I proclaim Egypt and Babylon among those who know me" (Psalms 87:4). It is a poetic usage, akin to referring to "perfidious Albion" for England.
2. The name Rahab literally means "pride" or "arrogance." It evokes Egypt's pride, its sense of power and superiority. This choice of name is not neutral: it portrays Egypt not only as a nation but as an embodiment of an attitude of defiance toward God, as shown in the context of Isaiah 30:7 where Egypt is contrasted with trust in God.
H7293.origine: The word Rahab comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to swell, to be filled with pride." It is a speaking name: it does not simply describe what Egypt is geographically, but the spirit that characterizes this power — arrogance, rebellion against God. The same word or related words are sometimes used to describe pride in general in the Scriptures.
H7293.emploi: Rahab appears twice in the provided passages to designate Egypt. In Psalm 87, it is a poetic term among other names of nations (Babylon, land of the Philistines, Tyre, Ethiopia), listed to show that peoples of all origins are spiritually born in Zion. In Isaiah 30:7, the context indicates that this name highlights Egypt's attitude of rebellion. This usage shows that the name is never neutral: it always colors the perception of Egypt by presenting it as a power dominated by pride.
H7293.portee: For the Christian reader, Rahab serves as a reminder that pride — whether national, personal, or religious — is incompatible with the recognition of God. Egypt, despite its greatness, is brought back to its spiritual essence: a proud nation that ignores or rejects the living God. This term invites us to discern within ourselves and in our societies this spirit of Rahab, this temptation to trust ourselves rather than God.

sens: Mythical monster of primordial chaos
Symbolic designation of Egypt
H7294.detail:
1. Rahab is a legendary creature, a sea monster that ancient Near Eastern peoples imagined as the embodiment of primordial chaos. In biblical texts, this name evokes storm, arrogance, and untamed power. God crushes it like a carcass, symbolizing His absolute victory over the forces of disorder (Psalms 89:11; Isaiah 51:9).
2. By symbolic extension, "Rahab" becomes the prophetic name for Egypt, representing the proud and chaotic nation that the Lord crushes just as He crushed the primordial monster. This parallel is rooted in the memory of the Exodus, where God frees His people from Egyptian slavery by exercising His sovereign power.
H7294.origine: The name Rahab literally means "width" or "expanse," perhaps evoking the tumultuous immensity of the sea. It originally designates a chaos monster recognizable in Mesopotamian and Canaanite mythologies: a rebellious aquatic creature that only God can dominate. By applying it to Egypt, the Bible connects this country to the image of human powers that oppose God and that His arm crushes.
H7294.emploi: Rahab appears four times in the Bible: twice in direct parallel with the idea of monster or chaos (Job 9:13 and Job 26:12), and twice as a prophetic designation of Egypt (Psalms 89:11 and Isaiah 51:9). In the passages from Job, the term retains its mythical sense of a creature from the depths. In the psalms and Isaiah, it takes on a historical and theological significance: the God who crushes Rahab in ancient times is the same who breaks the power of Egypt and frees His people. The contexts emphasize the invincibility of the Lord in the face of any opposition.
H7294.portee: This name reminds believers that God reigns over chaos and that His power is infinitely superior to that of human empires, even the mightiest. It invites God's people to place their trust not in earthly forces, but in the Lord alone who breaks obstacles and frees His children. Rahab concretely represents: no hostile power, whether mythical, political, or spiritual, escapes divine mastery.

sens: One who displays pride, who considers themselves superior to others
One who defies, who opposes with arrogance
One who despises others and refuses to submit
H7295.detail:
1. A proud person is someone who displays pride and believes themselves superior to others. The image is that of a person lifting their head, elevating themselves in front of others. In Psalm 40:5, the Lord calls blessed the one who does not turn to the proud, meaning who is not seduced by those who display this arrogant pride.
2. The proud one is also one who defies, who opposes arrogantly. It is an attitude of rebellion: instead of accepting or obeying, one stands against, refusing to bend. This defiance marks a closing of the heart to correction or authority.
3. Ultimately, the proud despises others and refuses any submission. This attitude manifests itself through hardness, a refusal to acknowledge one's dependence or limitations.
H7295.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of standing up, rising with pride. This same root produces other words related to pride and rebellion. The central image is that of a body that elevates itself, of a head that lifts up — a gesture of pride and contempt.
H7295.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalm 40:5. In this context of blessing, the author lists the characteristics of the blessed man: it is the one who places their trust in the Lord and does not look to the proud and the liars. This association with liars suggests that pride goes hand in hand with deceit and dishonesty. The psalmist warns that proximity to the proud diverts from true happiness, which rests on trust in God.
H7295.portee: Psalm 40 invites the Christian to examine their influences and role models. Turning away from the proud means refusing to follow those whose hearts are closed to God, those who seek to impress with their pride rather than submit to divine grace. It is a call to vigilance: the promised happiness belongs to the one who chooses humility and trust in God rather than admiration of the proud.

sens: excessive self-esteem
overconfidence in one's own strength or dignity
the sense of glory derived from one's years or accomplishments
H7296.detail: 1. Pride is this excessive self-esteem that inflates us with too high an opinion of ourselves. In Psalm 90:10, men take pride in their years and prolonged life, as if the length of their days were a title to personal glory. 2. It is also misplaced confidence in one's own strength or dignity: one imagines oneself to be someone great, capable, worthy of honor. But the text in Psalms explains well: this kind of pride does not last, it vanishes with the passing life. 3. More broadly, it is the sense of glory or esteem that one attributes to oneself for one's accomplishments — one's years, health, works — instead of recognizing the gift of God.
H7296.origine: The Hebrew word rohav comes from the root rahab, which primarily evokes noise, commotion, agitation — the idea of something that swells and makes noise. Pride is precisely what swells within us and makes us noisy with our ego, instead of listening to God. This sense of 'swelling' of self is at the heart of all the words in this family: it is the image of a vesicle, a bubble that inflates.
H7296.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 90:10. Moses, the author of this psalm, speaks of the brevity of human life: the years pass, and those who live long are tempted to take pride in their longevity, as if it were a reason for personal pride. But the psalmist describes this pride as being only 'pain and misery,' and it 'passes quickly': there is nothing lasting to be gained from it. The word thus designates the vain and ephemeral pride of mortals.
H7296.portee: This word reminds the believer of a humbling and salutary truth: all that we take pride in — our years, our successes, our health, our dignity — is ephemeral and perishable. Pride based on these things is only vanity. True wisdom, as shown in Psalm 90, consists in recognizing the brevity of life and asking God for 'a wise heart.' Better is the fear of God than self-pride.

sens: To experience a fear that shakes the body
To waver internally in the face of a threat
H7297.detail:
1. This verb describes the physical trembling caused by fear or fright: the body shudders, the limbs move involuntarily under the grip of fear. It is an instinctive reaction to danger or threat. In Isaiah 44:8, God commands His people: 'Do not fear, and do not tremble,' paralleling inner fear and its bodily expression.
2. More broadly, to tremble also means to waver internally, to be seized by an anxiety that shakes confidence. Trembling then becomes the visible sign of fear or uncertainty that grips the heart.
H7297.origine: The Hebrew verb רָהָה (rahah) belongs to a family of words expressing fear and fright. Its formation suggests a physical and emotional disturbance. The word evokes the image of a body agitated, a person shaken from within by a strong emotion.
H7297.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 44:8. God encourages His people not to tremble in the face of uncertainty: He affirms that He has long announced the future and that He is the only true God. The context invites us to see trembling as the opposite of faith — the one who trembles doubts, while the one who does not tremble relies on the divine word.
H7297.portee: This word teaches us that true faith dispels trembling: not that it removes the respectful fear of God, but that it extinguishes panic and doubt in the face of life's uncertainties. To believe the divine promise is to find firmness of heart despite troubling circumstances.

sens: Hollow container, usually made of stone or wood, used to water animals
Basin or bowl from which water is drawn for livestock
H7298A.detail:
1. A trough is a hollow and shallow container, made of stone, wood, or another solid material, specifically intended to water livestock. It is an object of pastoral life, essential for providing water to sheep, goats, or other animals. In Exodus 2:16, the daughters of the priest of Midian fill the troughs to water their father's flock.
2. By extension, a trough can also refer to the hollow or cavity itself where water accumulates for the animals. In the story of Jacob (Genesis 30:38 and 30:41), the troughs are basins where Jacob places peeled branches to influence the sheep when they come to drink: the hollow, as such, is the place where the action concentrates.
H7298A.origine: The Hebrew word רַהַט (rahat) comes from a root that evokes the idea of a hollow, a depression, or a cavity. The basic image is that of an object or place whose central part sinks or hollows out, forming a receptacle. The word belongs to the simple and concrete vocabulary of rural and pastoral life, without connection to a specialized field.
H7298A.emploi: The word appears three times in the Bible, only in the narratives of Exodus and Genesis. In Exodus 2:16, it refers to ordinary troughs where the daughters of Jethro fill with water to give to their father's flock. In Genesis 30:38 and 30:41, Jacob uses the troughs as part of a strategy (placing peeled branches before them) to encourage the birth of certain lambs. In all cases, the trough is simply the container or place intended to water the animals of a flock.
H7298A.portee: This word recalls the concrete gestures of biblical pastoral life: caring for entrusted animals, feeding them, and watering them. It also testifies to the ingenuity of ancient shepherds and their attentive observation of animals. For the Christian reader, it is a window into the humble and laborious daily life of the ancestors in faith.

sens: Ring or spiral formed by hair
H7298B.detail: 1. A curl is a natural wave or spiral formed by hair, especially when it is long and thick. The word evokes the beauty of abundant and shiny hair. In Song of Solomon 7:6, the poet says that "the hair of your head is like purple," a royal curl that captivates — the king is literally "bound" by this splendor.
H7298B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that originally designates something curved or rolled. It is a simple and visual image: a ring, a spiral. The name is specifically used for hair curls, this natural beauty that waves and curls.
H7298B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 7:6. It is a poetic and romantic text where the poet celebrates the physical beauty of the one he loves. The curl of the hair is a trait of beauty that symbolizes seduction and attraction, to the point that the king is like a prisoner of it. Its use is very limited, but the context shows that it is a precious and remarkable element of feminine beauty.
H7298B.portee: This passage reminds us that the Bible does not hide the physical attraction between man and woman — it speaks of it with poetry and admiration. The curls of hair symbolize a beauty that captivates and binds. For a believer, it is an invitation to recognize beauty as a gift from God, and to honor one's spouse with sincere and poetic admiration, far from vulgarity.

sens: The outward appearance of a person or thing, what is seen of it
The look, the silhouette, the physical form that catches the eye
H7299.detail:
1. Appearance is what one perceives first when looking at someone or something: their visible look, their general appearance. When Nebuchadnezzar sees in a dream the great statue, Scripture specifies that "its appearance was terrifying" (Daniel 2:31) — it is not its secret essence, but what emanates from it, what is seen, what impresses. It is the image received upon seeing it.
2. This word also designates the silhouette, the recognizable shape of a person. When the three companions of Daniel walk in the midst of the fire, Nebuchadnezzar notices "the figure of the fourth" who "looks like a son of the gods" (Daniel 3:25) — he speaks of what allows identifying and distinguishing this fourth person from the three others.
H7299.origine: The Aramaic word "rev" (רֵו) comes from a root that means "to see." It is related to the Hebrew word "reuth" (רְאוּת), which literally means "the sight, the vision." Appearance is therefore what is seen, what is offered to the view — the visual image that something or someone presents.
H7299.emploi: This Aramaic word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the book of Daniel. In the prophetic dream of the statue of nations (Daniel 2:31), it designates the impressive and terrifying appearance of the statue itself. In the episode of the three young men in the furnace (Daniel 3:25), it describes the recognizable silhouette, the individual appearance of the fourth person who appears alongside Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. In both cases, it is the immediate visual impression that is emphasized.
H7299.portee: This word reminds us that in Scripture, appearance has a place: what is seen of a person or event matters and deserves to be described, not because one should judge by looks, but because God also reveals Himself through what manifests. The visual details in biblical visions and narratives are not superficial — they serve to convey a deep and even divine reality.
